When it ceased, I longed for nothing so much as to be out of the room.
The sofa was not far from the door, but I did not dare to raise my
head, for I knew Mr. Huntingdon was standing near me, and I knew by the
sound of his voice, as he spoke in answer to some remark of Lord
Lowborough’s, that his face was turned towards me. Perhaps a
half-suppressed sob had caught his ear, and caused him to look
round—heaven forbid! But with a violent effort, I checked all further
signs of weakness, dried my tears, and, when I thought he had turned
away again, rose, and instantly left the apartment, taking refuge in my
favourite resort, the library.

There was no light there but the faint red glow of the neglected
fire;—but I did not want a light; I only wanted to indulge my thoughts,
unnoticed and undisturbed; and sitting down on a low stool before the
easy-chair, I sunk my head upon its cushioned seat, and thought, and
thought, until the tears gushed out again, and I wept like any child.
Presently, however, the door was gently opened and someone entered the
room. I trusted it was only a servant, and did not stir. The door was
closed again—but I was not alone; a hand gently touched my shoulder,
and a voice said, softly,—“Helen, what is the matter?”

I could not answer at the moment.

“You must, and shall tell me,” was added, more vehemently, and the
speaker threw himself on his knees beside me on the rug, and forcibly
possessed himself of my hand; but I hastily caught it away, and
replied,—“It is nothing to you, Mr. Huntingdon.”

“Are you sure it is nothing to me?” he returned; “can you swear that
you were not thinking of me while you wept?” This was unendurable. I
made an effort to rise, but he was kneeling on my dress.

“Tell me,” continued he—“I want to know,—because if you were, I have
something to say to you,—and if not, I’ll go.”

“Go then!” I cried; but, fearing he would obey too well, and never come
again, I hastily added—“Or say what you have to say, and have done with
it!”

“But which?” said he—“for I shall only say it if you really were
thinking of me. So tell me, Helen.”

“You’re excessively impertinent, Mr. Huntingdon!”

“Not at all—too pertinent, you mean. So you won’t tell me?—Well, I’ll
spare your woman’s pride, and, construing your silence into ‘Yes,’ I’ll
take it for granted that I was the subject of your thoughts, and the
cause of your affliction—”

“Indeed, sir—”

“If you deny it, I won’t tell you my secret,” threatened he; and I did
not interrupt him again, or even attempt to repulse him: though he had
taken my hand once more, and half embraced me with his other arm, I was
scarcely conscious of it at the time.

“It is this,” resumed he: “that Annabella Wilmot, in comparison with
you, is like a flaunting peony compared with a sweet, wild rosebud
gemmed with dew—and I love you to distraction!—Now, tell me if that
intelligence gives you any pleasure. Silence again? That means yes.
Then let me add, that I cannot live without you, and if you answer No
to this last question, you will drive me mad.—Will you bestow yourself
upon me?—you will!” he cried, nearly squeezing me to death in his arms.

“No, no!” I exclaimed, struggling to free myself from him—“you must ask
my uncle and aunt.”

“They won’t refuse me, if you don’t.”

“I’m not so sure of that—my aunt dislikes you.”

“But _you_ don’t, Helen—say you love me, and I’ll go.”

“I wish you _would_ go!” I replied.

“I will, this instant,—if you’ll only say you love me.”

“You know I do,” I answered. And again he caught me in his arms, and
smothered me with kisses.

At that moment my aunt opened wide the door, and stood before us,
candle in hand, in shocked and horrified amazement, gazing alternately
at Mr. Huntingdon and me—for we had both started up, and now stood wide
enough asunder. But _his_ confusion was only for a moment. Rallying in
an instant, with the most enviable assurance, he began,—“I beg ten
thousand pardons, Mrs. Maxwell! Don’t be too severe upon me. I’ve been
asking your sweet niece to take me for better, for worse; and she, like
a good girl, informs me she cannot think of it without her uncle’s and
aunt’s consent. So let me implore you not to condemn me to eternal
wretchedness: if _you_ favour my cause, I am safe; for Mr. Maxwell, I
am certain, can refuse you nothing.”

“We will talk of this to-morrow, sir,” said my aunt, coldly. “It is a
subject that demands mature and serious deliberation. At present, you
had better return to the drawing-room.”

“But meantime,” pleaded he, “let me commend my cause to your most
indulgent—”

“No indulgence for you, Mr. Huntingdon, must come between me and the
consideration of my niece’s happiness.”

“Ah, true! I know she is an angel, and I am a presumptuous dog to dream
of possessing such a treasure; but, nevertheless, I would sooner die
than relinquish her in favour of the best man that ever went to
heaven—and as for her happiness, I would sacrifice my body and soul—”

“Body and _soul_, Mr. Huntingdon—sacrifice your _soul?_”

“Well, I would lay down life—”

“You would not be required to lay it down.”

“I would spend it, then—devote my life—and all its powers to the
promotion and preservation—”

“Another time, sir, we will talk of this—and I should have felt
disposed to judge more favourably of your pretensions, if you too had
chosen another time and place, and let me add—another _manner_ for your
declaration.”

“Why, you see, Mrs. Maxwell,” he began—

“Pardon me, sir,” said she, with dignity—“The company are inquiring for
you in the other room.” And she turned to me.

“Then _you_ must plead for me, Helen,” said he, and at length withdrew.

“You had better retire to your room, Helen,” said my aunt, gravely. “I
will discuss this matter with you, too, to-morrow.”

“Don’t be angry, aunt,” said I.

“My dear, I am not angry,” she replied: “I am _surprised_. If it is
true that you told him you could not accept his offer without our
consent—”

“Be quiet a moment, will you, Arthur?” said I, “and listen to me—and
don’t think I’m in a jealous fury: I am perfectly calm. Feel my hand.”
And I gravely extended it towards him—but closed it upon his with an
energy that seemed to disprove the assertion, and made him smile. “You
needn’t smile, sir,” said I, still tightening my grasp, and looking
steadfastly on him till he almost quailed before me. “You may think it
all very fine, Mr. Huntingdon, to amuse yourself with rousing my
jealousy; but take care you don’t rouse my hate instead. And when you
have once extinguished my love, you will find it no easy matter to
kindle it again.”

“Well, Helen, I won’t repeat the offence. But I meant nothing by it, I
assure you. I had taken too much wine, and I was scarcely myself at the
time.”

“You often take too much; and that is another practice I detest.” He
looked up astonished at my warmth. “Yes,” I continued; “I never
mentioned it before, because I was ashamed to do so; but now I’ll tell
you that it distresses me, and may disgust me, if you go on and suffer
the habit to grow upon you, as it will if you don’t check it in time.
But the whole system of your conduct to Lady Lowborough is not
referable to wine; and this night you knew perfectly well what you were
doing.”

“Well, I’m sorry for it,” replied he, with more of sulkiness than
contrition: “what more would you have?”

“You are sorry that I saw you, no doubt,” I answered coldly.

“If you had not seen me,” he muttered, fixing his eyes on the carpet,
“it would have done no harm.”

My heart felt ready to burst; but I resolutely swallowed back my
emotion, and answered calmly,

“You think not?”

“No,” replied he, boldly. “After all, what have I done? It’s
nothing—except as you choose to make it a subject of accusation and
distress.”

“What would Lord Lowborough, your _friend_, think, if he knew all? or
what would you yourself think, if he or any other had acted the same
part to me, throughout, as you have to Annabella?”

“I would blow his brains out.”

“Well, then, Arthur, how can you call it nothing—an offence for which
you would think yourself justified in blowing another man’s brains out?
Is it nothing to trifle with your friend’s feelings and mine—to
endeavour to steal a woman’s affections from her husband—what he values
more than his gold, and therefore what it is more dishonest to take?
Are the marriage vows a jest; and is it nothing to make it your sport
to break them, and to tempt another to do the same? Can I love a man
that does such things, and coolly maintains it is nothing?”

“You are breaking your marriage vows yourself,” said he, indignantly
rising and pacing to and fro. “You promised to honour and obey me, and
now you attempt to hector over me, and threaten and accuse me, and call
me worse than a highwayman. If it were not for your situation, Helen, I
would not submit to it so tamely. I won’t be dictated to by a woman,
though she be my wife.”

“What will you do then? Will you go on till I hate you, and then accuse
me of breaking my vows?”

He was silent a moment, and then replied: “You never will hate me.”
Returning and resuming his former position at my feet, he repeated more
vehemently—“You cannot hate me as long as I love you.”

“But how can I believe that you love me, if you continue to act in this
way? Just imagine yourself in my place: would _you_ think I loved
_you_, if _I_ did so? Would you believe my protestations, and honour
and trust me under such circumstances?”

“The cases are different,” he replied. “It is a woman’s nature to be
constant—to love one and one only, blindly, tenderly, and for
ever—bless them, dear creatures! and you above them all; but you must
have some commiseration for us, Helen; you must give us a little more
licence, for, as Shakespeare has it—

However we do praise ourselves,

Than women’s are.”


“Do you mean by that, that your fancies are lost to me, and won by Lady
Lowborough?”

“No! heaven is my witness that I think her mere dust and ashes in
comparison with you, and shall continue to think so, unless you drive
me from you by too much severity. She is a daughter of earth; you are
an angel of heaven; only be not too austere in your divinity, and
remember that I am a poor, fallible mortal. Come now, Helen; won’t you
forgive me?” he said, gently taking my hand, and looking up with an
innocent smile.

“If I do, you will repeat the offence.”

“I swear by—”

“Don’t swear; I’ll believe your word as well as your oath. I wish I
could have confidence in either.”

“Try me, then, Helen: only trust and pardon me this once, and you shall
see! Come, I am in hell’s torments till you speak the word.”

looked at Lord Lowborough. He was at the other end of the room, talking
with Messrs. Hargrave and Grimsby; but I saw him dart towards his lady
and his host a quick, impatient glance, expressive of intense
disquietude, at which Grimsby smiled. Determined to interrupt the
_tête-à-tête_, I rose, and, selecting a piece of music from the music
stand, stepped up to the piano, intending to ask the lady to play it;
but I stood transfixed and speechless on seeing her seated there,
listening, with what seemed an exultant smile on her flushed face to
his soft murmurings, with her hand quietly surrendered to his clasp.
The blood rushed first to my heart, and then to my head; for there was
more than this: almost at the moment of my approach, he cast a hurried
glance over his shoulder towards the other occupants of the room, and
then ardently pressed the unresisting hand to his lips. On raising his
eyes, he beheld me, and dropped them again, confounded and dismayed.
She saw me too, and confronted me with a look of hard defiance. I laid
the music on the piano, and retired. I felt ill; but I did not leave
the room: happily, it was getting late, and could not be long before
the company dispersed.

I went to the fire, and leant my head against the chimney-piece. In a
minute or two, some one asked me if I felt unwell. I did not answer;
indeed, at the time, I knew not what was said; but I mechanically
looked up, and saw Mr. Hargrave standing beside me on the rug.

“Shall I get you a glass of wine?” said he.

“No, thank you,” I replied; and, turning from him, I looked round. Lady
Lowborough was beside her husband, bending over him as he sat, with her
hand on his shoulder, softly talking and smiling in his face; and
Arthur was at the table, turning over a book of engravings. I seated
myself in the nearest chair; and Mr. Hargrave, finding his services
were not desired, judiciously withdrew. Shortly after, the company
broke up, and, as the guests were retiring to their rooms, Arthur
approached me, smiling with the utmost assurance.

“Are you _very_ angry, Helen?” murmured he.

“This is no jest, Arthur,” said I, seriously, but as calmly as I
could—“unless you think it a jest to lose my affection for ever.”

“What! so bitter?” he exclaimed, laughingly, clasping my hand between
both his; but I snatched it away, in indignation—almost in disgust, for
he was obviously affected with wine.

“Then I must go down on my knees,” said he; and kneeling before me,
with clasped hands, uplifted in mock humiliation, he continued
imploringly—“Forgive me, Helen—dear Helen, forgive me, and I’ll _never_
do it again!” and, burying his face in his handkerchief, he affected to
sob aloud.

Leaving him thus employed, I took my candle, and, slipping quietly from
the room, hastened up-stairs as fast as I could. But he soon discovered
that I had left him, and, rushing up after me, caught me in his arms,
just as I had entered the chamber, and was about to shut the door in
his face.

“No, no, by heaven, you sha’n’t escape me so!” he cried. Then, alarmed
at my agitation, he begged me not to put myself in such a passion,
telling me I was white in the face, and should kill myself if I did so.

“Let me go, then,” I murmured; and immediately he released me—and it
was well he did, for I was really in a passion. I sank into the
easy-chair and endeavoured to compose myself, for I wanted to speak to
him calmly. He stood beside me, but did not venture to touch me or to
speak for a few seconds; then, approaching a little nearer, he dropped
on one knee—not in mock humility, but to bring himself nearer my level,
and leaning his hand on the arm of the chair, he began in a low voice:
“It is all nonsense, Helen—a jest, a mere nothing—not worth a thought.
Will you _never_ learn,” he continued more boldly, “that you have
nothing to fear from me? that I love you wholly and entirely?—or if,”
he added with a lurking smile, “I ever give a thought to another, you
may well spare it, for those fancies are here and gone like a flash of
lightning, while my love for you burns on steadily, and for ever, like
the sun. You little exorbitant tyrant, will not _that_—”

“Be quiet a moment, will you, Arthur?” said I, “and listen to me—and
don’t think I’m in a jealous fury: I am perfectly calm. Feel my hand.”
And I gravely extended it towards him—but closed it upon his with an
energy that seemed to disprove the assertion, and made him smile. “You
needn’t smile, sir,” said I, still tightening my grasp, and looking
steadfastly on him till he almost quailed before me. “You may think it
all very fine, Mr. Huntingdon, to amuse yourself with rousing my
jealousy; but take care you don’t rouse my hate instead. And when you
have once extinguished my love, you will find it no easy matter to
kindle it again.”

“Well, Helen, I won’t repeat the offence. But I meant nothing by it, I
assure you. I had taken too much wine, and I was scarcely myself at the
time.”

“You often take too much; and that is another practice I detest.” He
looked up astonished at my warmth. “Yes,” I continued; “I never
mentioned it before, because I was ashamed to do so; but now I’ll tell
you that it distresses me, and may disgust me, if you go on and suffer
the habit to grow upon you, as it will if you don’t check it in time.
But the whole system of your conduct to Lady Lowborough is not
referable to wine; and this night you knew perfectly well what you were
doing.”

“Well, I’m sorry for it,” replied he, with more of sulkiness than
contrition: “what more would you have?”

“You are sorry that I saw you, no doubt,” I answered coldly.

“If you had not seen me,” he muttered, fixing his eyes on the carpet,
“it would have done no harm.”

My heart felt ready to burst; but I resolutely swallowed back my
emotion, and answered calmly,

“You think not?”

“No,” replied he, boldly. “After all, what have I done? It’s
nothing—except as you choose to make it a subject of accusation and
distress.”

“What would Lord Lowborough, your _friend_, think, if he knew all? or
what would you yourself think, if he or any other had acted the same
part to me, throughout, as you have to Annabella?”

“I would blow his brains out.”

“Well, then, Arthur, how can you call it nothing—an offence for which
you would think yourself justified in blowing another man’s brains out?
Is it nothing to trifle with your friend’s feelings and mine—to
endeavour to steal a woman’s affections from her husband—what he values
more than his gold, and therefore what it is more dishonest to take?
Are the marriage vows a jest; and is it nothing to make it your sport
to break them, and to tempt another to do the same? Can I love a man
that does such things, and coolly maintains it is nothing?”

“You are breaking your marriage vows yourself,” said he, indignantly
rising and pacing to and fro. “You promised to honour and obey me, and
now you attempt to hector over me, and threaten and accuse me, and call
me worse than a highwayman. If it were not for your situation, Helen, I
would not submit to it so tamely. I won’t be dictated to by a woman,
though she be my wife.”

wide.text:
“It will be four years next April since I first saw you, Mrs.
Huntingdon—_you_ may have forgotten the circumstance, but _I_ never
can. I admired you then most deeply, but I dared not love you. In the
following autumn I saw so much of your perfections that I could not
fail to love you, though I dared not show it. For upwards of three
years I have endured a perfect martyrdom. From the anguish of
suppressed emotions, intense and fruitless longings, silent sorrow,
crushed hopes, and trampled affections, I have suffered more than I can
tell, or you imagine—and you were the cause of it, and not altogether
the innocent cause. My youth is wasting away; my prospects are
darkened; my life is a desolate blank; I have no rest day or night: I
am become a burden to myself and others, and you might save me by a
word—a glance, and will not do it—is this right?”

“In the first place, _I_ don’t believe _you_,” answered I; “in the
second, if you will be such a fool, I can’t hinder it.”

“If you affect,” replied he, earnestly, “to regard as folly the best,
the strongest, the most godlike impulses of our nature, I don’t believe
you. I know you are not the heartless, icy being you pretend to be—you
had a heart once, and gave it to your husband. When you found him
utterly unworthy of the treasure, you reclaimed it; and you will not
_pretend_ that you loved that sensual, earthly-minded profligate so
deeply, so devotedly, that you can never love another? I know that
there are feelings in your nature that have never yet been called
forth; I know, too, that in your present neglected lonely state you are
and _must_ be miserable. You have it in your power to raise two human
beings from a state of actual suffering to such unspeakable beatitude
as only generous, noble, self-forgetting love can give (for you _can_
love me if you will); you may tell me that you scorn and detest me,
but, since you have set me the example of plain speaking, I will answer
that _I do not believe you!_ But you will not do it! you choose rather
to leave us miserable; and you coolly tell me it is the will of God
that we should remain so. _You_ may call this religion, but _I_ call it
wild fanaticism!”

“There is another life both for you and for me,” said I. “If it be the
will of God that we should sow in tears now, it is only that we may
reap in joy hereafter. It is His will that we should not injure others
by the gratification of our own earthly passions; and you have a
mother, and sisters, and friends who would be seriously injured by your
disgrace; and I, too, have friends, whose peace of mind shall never be
sacrificed to my enjoyment, or yours either, with my consent; and if I
were alone in the world, I have still my God and my religion, and I
would sooner die than disgrace my calling and break my faith with
heaven to obtain a few brief years of false and fleeting
happiness—happiness sure to end in misery even here—for myself or any
other!”

“There need be no disgrace, no misery or sacrifice in any quarter,”
persisted he. “I do not ask you to leave your home or defy the world’s
opinion.” But I need not repeat all his arguments. I refuted them to
the best of my power; but that power was provokingly small, at the
moment, for I was too much flurried with indignation—and even
shame—that he should thus dare to address me, to retain sufficient
command of thought and language to enable me adequately to contend
against his powerful sophistries. Finding, however, that he could not
be silenced by reason, and even covertly exulted in his seeming
advantage, and ventured to deride those assertions I had not the
coolness to prove, I changed my course and tried another plan.

“Do you really love me?” said I, seriously, pausing and looking him
calmly in the face.

“Do I love you!” cried he.

“_Truly?_” I demanded.

His countenance brightened; he thought his triumph was at hand. He
commenced a passionate protestation of the truth and fervour of his
attachment, which I cut short by another question:—

“But is it not a selfish love? Have you enough disinterested affection
to enable you to sacrifice your own pleasure to mine?”

“I would give my life to serve you.”

“I don’t want your life; but have you enough real sympathy for my
afflictions to induce you to make an effort to relieve them, at the
risk of a little discomfort to yourself?”

“Try me, and see.”

“If you have, _never mention this subject again_. You cannot recur to
it in any way without doubling the weight of those sufferings you so
feelingly deplore. I have nothing left me but the solace of a good
conscience and a hopeful trust in heaven, and you labour continually to
rob me of these. If you persist, I must regard you as my deadliest
foe.”

“But hear me a moment—”

“No, sir! You said you would give your life to serve me; I only ask
your _silence_ on one particular point. I have spoken plainly; and what
I say I mean. If you torment me in this way any more, I must conclude
that your protestations are entirely false, and that you hate me in
your heart as fervently as you profess to love me!”

He bit his lip, and bent his eyes upon the ground in silence for a
while.

“Then I must leave you,” said he at length, looking steadily upon me,
as if with the last hope of detecting some token of irrepressible
anguish or dismay awakened by those solemn words. “I must leave you. I
cannot live here, and be for ever silent on the all-absorbing subject
of my thoughts and wishes.”

“Formerly, I believe, you spent but little of your time at home,” I
answered; “it will do you no harm to absent yourself again, for a
while—if that be really necessary.”

“If that be really _possible_,” he muttered; “and can you bid me go so
coolly? Do you really wish it?”

“Most certainly I do. If you cannot see me without tormenting me as you
have lately done, I would gladly say farewell and never see you more.”

He made no answer, but, bending from his horse, held out his hand
towards me. I looked up at his face, and saw therein such a look of
genuine agony of soul, that, whether bitter disappointment, or wounded
pride, or lingering love, or burning wrath were uppermost, I could not
hesitate to put my hand in his as frankly as if I bade a friend
farewell. He grasped it very hard, and immediately put spurs to his
horse and galloped away. Very soon after, I learned that he was gone to
Paris, where he still is; and the longer he stays there the better for
me.

I thank God for this deliverance!




 CHAPTER XXXVIII


December 20th, 1826.—The fifth anniversary of my wedding-day, and, I
trust, the last I shall spend under this roof. My resolution is formed,
my plan concocted, and already partly put in execution. My conscience
does not blame me, but while the purpose ripens let me beguile a few of
these long winter evenings in stating the case for my own satisfaction:
a dreary amusement enough, but having the air of a useful occupation,
and being pursued as a task, it will suit me better than a lighter one.

After calling for a rideshare, Nikki headed for the airport. On the way, she decided to call Meko. Maybe her friend could help her untangle the mess of emotions and revelations she’d been dealing with since Camilla’s arrival.

	“Meko,” Nikki said when her friend answered groggily, “sorry to call so early, but I need to ask you something.”

	“Girl, are you okay? You sound stressed,” Meko replied, her voice still thick with sleep.

	“Do you know anything about Keith’s ex, Camilla?” Nikki asked. “Has Luca ever mentioned her?”

	There was a pause on the other end. “Camilla?” Meko said, now fully awake. “Oh...yeah, I’ve heard her name before. Luca mentioned her once in passing, but you’re not going to like this. She’s friends with Marissa.”

	Nikki’s heart sank. “What?” she said, gripping the phone tightly. “Marissa knows her?”

	“Yeah,” Meko confirmed. “I didn’t think it was a big deal at the time, but Luca said Marissa and Camilla are pretty close. Why? What’s going on?”

	Nikki leaned back against the seat of the car, her thoughts racing. It all made sense now. Marissa, who had been cold and cutting when she saw Nikki at the club, must have set this in motion. Camilla showing up at Keith’s door wasn’t just a coincidence—it was orchestrated.

	“Meko, I’ll explain everything later,” Nikki said, her voice trembling. “I’m heading back to Atlanta. I need to think.”

	“Nikki, don’t let Marissa or anyone else mess with your head,” Meko said firmly. “You and Keith have something special. Don’t throw it away because of them.”

	“I know,” Nikki said, but her voice lacked conviction. She ended the call as her rideshare pulled up to the airport.



	By the time Nikki boarded her flight, she was feeling more conflicted than ever. She had avoided telling Keith she was leaving, and the guilt gnawed at her as she settled into her seat. Her phone buzzed in her hand—Keith’s name flashed on the screen. She hesitated, watching as the call went to voicemail, only for another one to come through immediately after. He was calling her back-to-back now, and each missed call made her heart ache.

	The plane began to taxi down the runway, and Nikki turned her phone to airplane mode, cutting off the calls. Keith would figure out she was gone by now, and she knew he deserved an explanation. But she couldn’t bring herself to answer him—not yet. She needed to think with a clear mind, away from the chaos of Houston and the drama that seemed to follow Keith’s past.



	When the plane landed in Atlanta, Nikki felt a wave of relief as she stepped into the terminal. The familiar sights and sounds of her hometown grounded her, and she felt like she could finally breathe again. She called a car to take her back to her home, and as soon as she walked through the door, she was overwhelmed by the comfort of being home.

	Her phone buzzed again. This time, Keith had left a voicemail. Nikki stared at it for a moment before pressing play.

	“Nikki, it’s me,” Keith’s voice came through, heavy with concern. “I woke up, and you were gone. Please, just...call me. I need to know you’re okay. If I did something to upset you, I’m sorry. I love you, Nikki. Don’t shut me out.”

	Tears welled up in Nikki’s eyes as she listened. She loved Keith too, but the weight of everything that had happened—the chaos with Camilla, the realization of Marissa’s involvement—made her question whether love was enough.

	She sank onto her couch, staring out the window as the sun began to set over Atlanta. She had come back to find clarity, but her heart was still in Houston, tangled up with Keith and the life they were trying to build together. For now, all she could do was sit with her feelings and hope the answers would come in time.



	Nikki’s head was pounding when she woke up the next morning. The bright sunlight streaming through her windows felt like a harsh contrast to the storm swirling in her mind. She groggily reached for her phone, her heart sinking as she saw the screen light up with 15 missed calls from Keith. Her stomach twisted. She had known he would try to reach her, but seeing the number in such a quantity only added weight to the ache in her chest.

	The first call she listened to was a voicemail from Keith. His voice was heavy with confusion, frustration, and concern.

	“Nikki, it’s me. I’ve been calling and texting. Meko told me you went home...I get it, but I hate that you left like this. I don’t understand. I don’t know what’s going on with you, with Marissa, or your past in Houston...but you can’t just leave without talking to me. Please. Call me back.”

	Nikki closed her eyes as she listened, the sound of his voice both comforting and suffocating. Her mind replayed the chaotic events of the past few days—Camilla’s surprise visit, Marissa’s quiet but piercing jealousy, and the nagging feeling that something was off. She had tried to walk away, to give herself space, but now the confusion felt even heavier.

	She hit the “delete” button on the voicemail and placed her phone face down on the bedside table. Her thoughts were spiraling. She had chosen to leave Houston, to return to Atlanta, not just to escape the pressure of the relationship but also to escape the web of entanglements—Marissa, Jordan, and the dark corners of the life she had started to entangle herself in. But now, back home, it all felt unresolved, and Keith’s persistent calls were doing nothing to ease the turbulence she was feeling inside.

	Her hands instinctively reached for the pack of cigarettes tucked away on the kitchen counter. She didn’t smoke often—just a rare habit when she needed to clear her head or unwind—but today, she felt like she needed something to dull the edges of her thoughts. She lit the cigarette and took a long drag, leaning against the counter as the smoke curled upward in slow, steady spirals. The nicotine hit her bloodstream quickly, bringing her the moment of calm she’d been craving. She exhaled slowly, letting the smoke linger before she stubbed the cigarette out in the ashtray.

	Just as she was trying to gather her thoughts, there was a knock at the door. Nikki wasn’t expecting anyone, but when she opened the door, she was greeted by Karen.

That night, Nikki lay on her back on the grass, the cold night air wrapping around her like a blanket as the Northern Lights danced across the sky. Green and violet ribbons of light twisted and turned in the dark expanse above her, as if the universe itself was putting on a show just for her.

	It was breathtaking.

	She had always dreamed of seeing the Northern Lights, but this moment—standing alone, yet feeling more connected to herself than she had in years—felt like something more. It felt like the universe was affirming her decision to leave the past behind, to claim her own freedom and write her own story.

	Nikki never replied to Antwan’s text. She didn’t respond to Keith or anyone else. For the first time in ages, she wasn’t bound by anyone else’s narrative. She was carving her own path, creating the future she wanted. And that future wasn’t defined by anyone but herself.

	She smiled to herself, feeling a quiet contentment settle over her. She was free. And that was all that mattered.



	Chapter 16: A Crossroads

	Nikki stepped off the plane, the warmth of Atlanta’s air wrapping around her like a familiar embrace. Iceland had given her the space she needed to breathe, to reset. The trip had been everything she hoped for—and more. The Northern Lights had been a reminder of the beauty that existed outside of the noise of her everyday life, the peace that could be found in solitude. She was different now.

	Her heart, once weighed down by confusion, felt lighter, more at ease. She had cleared her head, found her own direction. She was ready to take on whatever came next with strength and clarity.

	But as she made her way to baggage claim, Nikki’s phone buzzed in her purse, pulling her from her thoughts. She glanced down, surprised to see the number: Antwan.

	A surge of anxiety tightened her chest, but she pressed the button to unlock her phone anyway. She didn’t know why—maybe it was a part of her that still hoped things would change, or maybe she just couldn’t help herself.

	But when she saw the number of missed calls—22 voicemails from Antwan—Nikki’s stomach dropped. She clicked on the first voicemail, the sound of Antwan’s voice filling her ears.

	“I can’t stop thinking about you, Nikki. I love you. I know it’s complicated, but I want to be with you. I’m not asking you to make a decision now, but please, just… call me back.”

	Her hand shook as she pressed play on the next message.

	“Nikki, I know I’ve hurt you. I just want to make things right. I can’t get you out of my head. You mean everything to me. Please, baby… just let me in.”

	The next voicemail was much the same, his voice cracking with emotion, each word heavier than the last. The urgency, the vulnerability in his tone made her pause. There was love in his words. Real love. The kind that made her heart ache.

	But it also reminded her of everything she had left behind—his family, his girlfriend, his children.

	Nikki closed her eyes, leaning against the baggage carousel as the next voicemail played.

	“You don’t know how much I need you, Nikki. I’ve been a fool. But please don’t shut me out. I love you. I need you. Just give me a chance.”

	The words felt like a weight on her chest, like they were pulling her in different directions. She could hear his pain, feel the longing in his voice. She could almost see him there, standing in front of her, waiting for her to make a decision.

	But she couldn’t.

	She didn’t want to be part of that world again. The world where everything was a mess, where feelings were complicated and love was tangled in responsibilities and promises to others. She had worked too hard to free herself from that.

	Nikki trusted that God would lead her in the right direction. It was something she had been clinging to during her time in Iceland. The peace she felt there, the certainty that the universe would guide her if she listened. And right now, it was telling her that this—whatever Antwan was asking for—was not her path.

	She wasn’t going to be the other woman. She wasn’t going to get lost in someone else’s family drama, in someone else’s mess. Not when she had finally started to build her own future.

	The sound of another voicemail from Antwan interrupted her thoughts, but this time, she didn’t listen.

	She slid her phone into her bag and took a deep breath. She had found her peace. She wasn’t going to let it be shaken by someone else’s emotional turmoil.

	As Nikki made her way out of the airport, the bright Atlanta skyline greeted her, but there was a sense of finality in the air. She was back, but she wasn’t the same.

	The city felt different now. Her life felt different.

	She would not go back to the past. She was moving forward. She had faith that the right things would come to her when the time was right, and she trusted in the choices she had made. She didn’t need to be tied to anyone else's decisions anymore.

	Nikki was taking control of her life—and she was ready to embrace whatever came next.

	Chapter 17: Invitations and Decisions

	Nikki opened the door to her home, the familiar scent of jasmine and cedarwood filling the air. It felt good to be back, to slip back into her space after what felt like a lifetime away. Iceland had changed her, given her the clarity she needed, but now that she was home, there was still the question of what was next.

	She set her purse down on the entryway table and walked over to the small stack of mail sitting by the door. Most of it was bills, flyers, or generic advertisements, but there, in the middle of the pile, was an envelope that immediately caught her eye. It was sleek, modern, and unusually thin. The return address was from Calvin—her old friend, her former colleague, and a man who had recently become a fixture in her mind for a whole new reason.

	She carefully slid her finger along the edge of the envelope, anticipation building in her chest. Inside, instead of a traditional wedding invite, was something far more unique—an invitation on a tablet. She marveled at the technology. The tablet lit up as soon as she pressed a button, and a beautifully designed video began to play.

Today was special—it was Calvin and Leila’s wedding day. The excitement had been building for days, and the hotel was buzzing with energy as guests prepared for the celebration. The ceremony was to take place at a breathtaking venue, one of the many spaces that Calvin had designed. Everything was pristine and beautifully arranged, from the flowers to the delicate touches that made it uniquely their own. Franco had taken care of everything, from the travel arrangements to making sure Nikki had everything she needed. He had been nothing short of amazing, always putting her comfort first.

	She rolled out of bed, stretching, and smiled as she looked around the hotel suite. It was luxurious, and the view of the ocean was unparalleled. She couldn’t believe how far she had come. Just a few months ago, she had been struggling with her past, unsure of what her future would hold. Now, here she was, about to attend a beautiful wedding with someone who truly saw her, truly appreciated her.

	Franco joined her, and the two of them took their time getting ready. Franco looked incredible, his suit perfectly tailored, his dark hair neatly styled. He was the picture of elegance, a man who carried himself with confidence and grace. Nikki, too, felt radiant. She had chosen a stunning gown that fit her like a dream, a dress that emphasized her curves in all the right ways, without being too revealing. It was simple yet elegant, just like the woman she had become. She looked at herself in the mirror, a soft smile creeping across her face as she admired how far she had come.

	“I’m so glad you’re here,” she said as she turned to Franco, her eyes bright. “Thank you for everything.”

	Franco looked at her with a deep, loving gaze, his eyes softening as he took her hand. “I wouldn’t want to be anywhere else, Nikki. You look stunning.”

	She blushed slightly at his compliment, her heart fluttering in her chest. She had never felt more sure of herself, more at peace with who she was. And being with Franco only made that feeling grow stronger.

	Together, they made their way downstairs to the grand ballroom, where the wedding was set to take place. The venue was even more breathtaking than Nikki had imagined. The soaring ceilings, the intricate chandeliers, and the rows of white chairs set the scene for the ceremony, which was about to begin. As guests filed into the space, Nikki couldn’t help but feel a sense of awe. Everything about this day felt like a dream.

“Cheers to us,” she repeated, lifting her glass to his.

	They spent the flight indulging in the kind of easy conversation that made Nikki feel completely at peace. They laughed at silly jokes, reminisced about the first time they’d met, and talked about everything under the sun. By the time they had both finished their second glasses of champagne, Nikki felt giddy with excitement. The tension of the past few weeks had melted away, and she was finally letting herself relax.

	As the plane began its descent into Aspen, the snowy peaks and pristine, mountainous landscape came into view. Nikki had heard about Aspen’s beauty, but seeing it from above was a whole new experience. It was like a winter wonderland, the kind of place that felt magical. She could already feel the weight of the world lifting off her shoulders.

	They arrived at the airport and were whisked away in a sleek black car to the best hotel in Aspen. The hotel was beyond luxurious—everything about it screamed opulence. The marble floors gleamed, the chandeliers hung like works of art, and every corner was designed with impeccable taste. Franco had clearly spared no expense.

	Nikki couldn’t believe this was all for her. She’d always known Franco had a flair for luxury, but this? This was something else entirely. They checked in, and the concierge handed Nikki a small envelope with her name on it.

	“Everything has been taken care of, Ms. Davenport,” the concierge said with a polite smile. “You’re all set for your stay.”

	Franco flashed a playful grin as he took her hand, leading her to their room. “You deserve this, Nikki. Just relax and enjoy. I’ve got everything planned.”

	Nikki didn’t know what to expect.

	That night, after a few hours of unwinding and getting ready for dinner, Franco took her to an intimate but beautiful restaurant nestled in the heart of Aspen. The warm light from the candles flickered against the walls, creating a soft, romantic atmosphere. Franco looked effortlessly handsome in his tailored suit, and Nikki felt like a goddess in her black dress. Everything felt perfect—too perfect.

	As they sat down, Nikki couldn’t help but feel a little bit overwhelmed by how surreal the whole evening was. The ambiance was magical, the food was exquisite, and the wine was flowing, but there was something in the air that made her heart beat just a little bit faster.

	Midway through dinner, Franco leaned in closer, his eyes locking with hers in a way that made her breath catch.

	“Nikki,” he began softly, his voice full of warmth, “there’s something I’ve been wanting to ask you.”

	Before she could even respond, a waiter appeared, holding a velvet box. Nikki’s heart skipped a beat as she realized what was happening.

	Franco took the box from the waiter and opened it to reveal the most stunning diamond ring Nikki had ever seen. It was large and flawless, sparkling in the candlelight like it was made just for her. Her mouth went dry, her heart pounding in her chest.

	“Nikki D,” Franco continued, his voice full of emotion, “I love you more than words could ever express. You’ve changed my life in ways I never thought possible. You make me a better man, and I can’t imagine my future without you in it. Will you marry me?”

	Tears filled Nikki’s eyes, her hands trembling as she reached for the ring. Everything around her seemed to blur as she looked at Franco, the man who had become her partner in every sense of the word. The man who had given her the space to be herself, supported her dreams, and made her feel loved every single day.

	“Yes,” she whispered, her voice cracking with emotion. “Yes, I will.”

	The room erupted into applause, and Nikki’s gaze swept around the restaurant in disbelief. To her shock, her family was there—her mom, Karen, Meko, even Calvin and Leila, who had their baby with them. Every single person who had meant something to Nikki in her life was there, celebrating this moment with her.

	She stood up and walked toward Franco, her heart full to the brim with love and gratitude. He stood, meeting her halfway, and wrapped his arms around her, pulling her close. His lips met hers in a soft, passionate kiss, and the world seemed to stand still for a moment.

	“I love you,” he murmured against her lips, his voice full of promise. “I love you so much, Nikki.”

	The tears that had been threatening to fall now flowed freely down Nikki’s cheeks. She was overwhelmed by the love and joy that filled her heart, the sense of belonging that she had always longed for but never thought she would find.

	Franco took her hand, slipping the ring onto her finger, and she admired the way it glimmered against her skin. It was perfect, just like him. Just like the life they were going to build together.

	The night was a blur of laughter, hugs, and kisses. It was everything Nikki had ever wanted—intimate, joyful, and full of love. Franco had planned the perfect proposal, the perfect evening. But what made it even more special was the way she felt—whole, content, and at peace.

	As the evening drew to a close, they returned to their hotel room, and Nikki sank into the softness of the bed. Franco joined her, pulling her into his arms.

	“Everything feels right,” she whispered, her voice barely audible as she snuggled close to him. “This is where I’m meant to be.”

	Franco kissed the top of her head, his hand gently caressing her hair. “I promise you, Nikki, this is just the beginning. We’ve got so much more ahead of us, and I can’t wait to spend every day with you.”

	And as Nikki drifted off to sleep in Franco’s arms, she knew that their future was as bright as the stars above Aspen. Together, they would conquer anything life threw their way. Together, they would create a life full of love, laughter, and endless happiness.

	It was the beginning of forever.

	And Nikki knew that, for the first time in her life, she had truly found her home.

wide.text:
“Promise me you’ll think about it,” Nikki pressed.

	“I promise,” Meko said, smiling.

	They hugged tightly before parting ways, leaving Nikki feeling both lighter and heavier. The goodbye was harder than she anticipated, but she also felt hopeful. Meko was special, and Nikki was certain their paths would cross again.



	Back at the Airbnb, Nikki was nearly done packing. Her suitcases were lined up by the door, and she was double-checking drawers and corners to make sure she hadn’t left anything behind. The place felt strangely empty now, stripped of the personal touches she had added during her stay.

	As she was zipping up her last suitcase, her phone buzzed. It was a text from Keith.

	Keith: I have that vodka you wanted. Mind if I stop by?

	Nikki smirked, shaking her head. Keith, with his charm and thoughtfulness, had a way of surprising her. She had mentioned the vodka in passing weeks ago, never expecting him to remember, let alone show up with it.

	Nikki: Sure. Come over.

	Fifteen minutes later, there was a knock at the door. Nikki opened it to find Keith standing there, a bottle of vodka in one hand and a playful grin on his face. He looked casual yet impossibly handsome in a fitted navy T-shirt and dark jeans.

	“You really didn’t have to do this,” Nikki said, taking the bottle from him.

	“I wanted to,” Keith replied, stepping inside. “Consider it a send-off gift.”

	She gestured for him to sit, grabbing two shot glasses from the kitchen. They sat on the couch, the mood light but charged with unspoken tension.

	Nikki poured the vodka into the glasses and raised hers. “To Houston. And to you, Keith.”

	“To you, Nikki,” Keith said, clinking his glass against hers.

	They threw back the shots, the vodka burning warmly as it went down. Keith set his glass down and leaned back, his eyes lingering on Nikki. “You know,” he said, his voice softer now, “I’ve been trying to play it cool, but I don’t want you to leave.”

	Nikki’s heart skipped a beat. “Keith…” she began, but he cut her off.

	“I know you have your life in Atlanta, and I would never ask you to change that. But I just… I’ve never met anyone like you, Nikki. You’re amazing.”

	Before she could overthink it, he leaned in and kissed her. It was slow at first, a tentative exploration, but quickly deepened as they gave in to the pull between them. Nikki felt her reservations melting away, replaced by an overwhelming need to be close to him.

	One kiss turned into another, and soon they were tangled together, their emotions spilling over into every touch. Keith lifted her effortlessly, carrying her to the bedroom where their passion ignited fully. The hours that followed were filled with laughter, tenderness, and a connection that felt both intense and comforting.



	As they lay in bed afterward, Keith traced lazy circles on Nikki’s arm. She turned to him, her heart full. “I love you,” she said suddenly, the words spilling out before she could stop them.

	Keith stilled, then smiled. “I love you too,” he said, his voice steady and sincere.

	The admission felt like a release, a moment of pure honesty that left them both vulnerable but deeply connected. They kissed again, their bodies and emotions perfectly in sync.



	When Nikki finally glanced at the clock, she realized with a jolt that she had missed her flight. “Oh my God,” she said, sitting up in bed. “I can’t believe this.”

	Keith propped himself up on one elbow, a smirk playing on his lips. “Guess you’ll have to stay a little longer.”

	“Don’t tempt me,” Nikki said, throwing a pillow at him.

	Keith laughed, leaning over to kiss her forehead. “I have to head to the club soon, but… this doesn’t have to be goodbye, Nikki.”

	“I know,” she said softly.

	As Keith got dressed and left for work, Nikki sat on the edge of the bed, her mind spinning. She was overwhelmed, unsure of what the future held but certain of one thing—her time in Houston had changed her in ways she couldn’t yet fully grasp. And as much as she loved Atlanta, part of her heart would always belong to this city and the man who had stolen it.



	Nikki woke up early the next morning, her mind clear but her heart heavy. After three months in Houston, she was finally heading back to Atlanta. Her emotions were a storm of excitement and longing—she was eager to check on her house, to feel the comfort of home again, but she also felt the ache of leaving Keith behind. Their last night together had been nothing short of magical, and his constant texts since then only solidified what she had begun to realize: Keith might be her person.

	As she packed the last of her belongings into her carry-on, Keith sent another text.

	Keith: Good morning, gorgeous. Let me know when you land safely. Missing you already.

	Nikki smiled at her phone, her fingers hovering over the screen before she typed back.

	Nikki: Morning! I’ll text you as soon as I land. Missing you too.



	The flight back to Atlanta felt longer than usual, and by the time Nikki stepped off the plane, her emotions were a mix of relief and sadness. She had loved Houston, but Atlanta was her heart. The city felt like an old friend as she drove through familiar streets, eventually pulling into the driveway of her beautifully designed home.

	The moment she stepped inside, she felt a wave of calm. The house was pristine, just as she had left it, but Nikki had to walk through each room to make sure. Cameras were great, but there was nothing like seeing and feeling the space in person. Her design touches were everywhere—the soft blush tones in the living room, the curated art pieces on the walls, and the plush rugs that made every step feel luxurious.

	She dropped her bags by the staircase and sank onto the couch. Her phone buzzed with another text from Keith.

	Keith: How’s it feel to be home?

	Nikki: Overwhelming but good. I miss you though.

	Keith: I miss you too. Call me tonight?

	Nikki: Of course.

	Nikki set the phone down and exhaled deeply. She missed Keith more than she expected, and the realization scared her a little. How had he become so important to her in such a short time? She had always been fiercely independent, focused on her career and her goals. But Keith made her feel seen in a way no one else had.

As guests filed into the space, Nikki couldn’t help but feel a sense of awe. Everything about this day felt like a dream.

	The ceremony itself was intimate and beautiful. Calvin and Leila stood before their guests, exchanging vows with love and devotion. The way they looked at each other, the way they held hands, it was clear to everyone in the room that this was a bond built on a deep, unwavering connection. It was the kind of love that Nikki had once dreamed of for herself, the kind of love she had thought she might never find. But now, as she sat beside Franco, watching her dear friends pledge their lives to each other, she realized something important.

	She had already found that love.

	Franco squeezed her hand, and she turned to look at him. His expression was soft, yet full of emotion. “I love you, Nikki,” he whispered, his voice steady and sincere. “I’ve loved you for a while now. I just— I needed to make sure I didn’t rush this. But now... I know. I know it’s real.”

	Nikki felt a lump form in her throat, and her heart swelled in her chest. She had been so unsure of love for so long, afraid to give herself fully to someone else. But Franco had proven that it was possible to love without the fear of losing yourself. He had shown her that love didn’t need to be complicated. It could be simple, pure, and beautiful, just like what she had with him.

	“I love you too, Franco,” she said, her voice thick with emotion. “I’m so glad I found you.”

	The ceremony continued, but for Nikki, the world seemed to stop for just a moment. She was sitting beside the man she had come to care for deeply, who had patiently waited for her to find herself again. And now, here they were, in this breathtaking place, witnessing the beauty of love.

	Later, as the reception began, Nikki couldn’t help but feel a sense of joy and excitement she hadn’t felt in a long time. The music played, the laughter filled the air, and guests danced and celebrated the union of Calvin and Leila. Nikki and Franco moved through the crowd, their laughter mingling with the sounds of the celebration. The atmosphere was lively, fun, and carefree. For the first time in a long time, Nikki felt like she truly belonged—like she had finally found her place, not just in the world, but in her own life.

	The night was filled with moments of joy—dancing with Franco, talking with friends, and celebrating love. But for Nikki, it was also a moment of reflection. She had come so far. She had reclaimed her independence, found her freedom, and discovered that love could be simple and beautiful, without all the complications she had once believed it to have.

	As the night drew to a close, Franco pulled her into a quiet corner of the ballroom, his eyes filled with affection. “Let’s make tonight unforgettable,” he said softly, his hands gently caressing her back. Nikki smiled up at him, feeling a sense of peace and contentment wash over her.

	And as they danced under the stars, surrounded by the warmth of the night and the joy of the occasion, Nikki knew she had finally found the kind of love she had always wanted—the kind of love that was real, steady, and true. And with Franco, she had everything she needed.



	Chapter 28: Building the Future

	The days after their trip to Miami were filled with a vibrant energy that Nikki hadn’t felt in a long time. She and Meko were working tirelessly on their new business venture, a design firm that was already beginning to make waves. They had managed to secure a few high-profile clients, and within just four months, they had made six figures. The success had come faster than either of them had anticipated, and it felt like all of the hard work and sleepless nights were finally paying off.

	Nikki couldn’t help but marvel at how much her life had changed in such a short time. A year ago, she had been uncertain, struggling to find her footing after leaving Houston, unsure of her next move. But now, with Meko by her side, she was building something beautiful—something that was entirely her own. They had started small, with freelance projects and design consultations, but they quickly grew, thanks in no small part to Meko’s relentless drive and Nikki’s sharp instincts. It felt like they were on the verge of something monumental.

	Meko had always been Nikki’s prodigy, the young designer who had once looked up to her as a mentor. Now, Nikki couldn’t help but feel proud as she watched Meko flourish. She had grown into her own as a designer, with a distinct style and a growing list of clients who trusted her vision. Meko’s designs were bold and innovative, yet grounded in the kind of timeless elegance that Nikki had always loved. It was clear that Meko was destined for great things, and Nikki was thrilled to be a part of it all.

She needed space, needed time to clear her head in a place that would strip away the clutter and offer her a new perspective. The idea of leaving everything behind for a while—no texts, no distractions, no complicated relationships—felt liberating. She needed to find herself again, to get back to a version of Nikki who wasn’t tied down by anyone else’s expectations.

	A few days later, she stood at the edge of the Blue Lagoon, the steam rising from the warm, mineral-rich water, contrasting against the cold air around her. It was surreal. The aquamarine waters stretched out before her, and as she dipped her toes into the soothing heat, she could feel the tension of the past months starting to melt away.

	The air was crisp, fresh—almost like she was inhaling new possibilities.

	That night, Nikki lay on her back on the grass, the cold night air wrapping around her like a blanket as the Northern Lights danced across the sky. Green and violet ribbons of light twisted and turned in the dark expanse above her, as if the universe itself was putting on a show just for her.

	It was breathtaking.

	She had always dreamed of seeing the Northern Lights, but this moment—standing alone, yet feeling more connected to herself than she had in years—felt like something more. It felt like the universe was affirming her decision to leave the past behind, to claim her own freedom and write her own story.

	Nikki never replied to Antwan’s text. She didn’t respond to Keith or anyone else. For the first time in ages, she wasn’t bound by anyone else’s narrative. She was carving her own path, creating the future she wanted. And that future wasn’t defined by anyone but herself.

	She smiled to herself, feeling a quiet contentment settle over her. She was free. And that was all that mattered.



	Chapter 16: A Crossroads

	Nikki stepped off the plane, the warmth of Atlanta’s air wrapping around her like a familiar embrace. Iceland had given her the space she needed to breathe, to reset. The trip had been everything she hoped for—and more. The Northern Lights had been a reminder of the beauty that existed outside of the noise of her everyday life, the peace that could be found in solitude. She was different now.

	Her heart, once weighed down by confusion, felt lighter, more at ease. She had cleared her head, found her own direction. She was ready to take on whatever came next with strength and clarity.

	But as she made her way to baggage claim, Nikki’s phone buzzed in her purse, pulling her from her thoughts. She glanced down, surprised to see the number: Antwan.

	A surge of anxiety tightened her chest, but she pressed the button to unlock her phone anyway. She didn’t know why—maybe it was a part of her that still hoped things would change, or maybe she just couldn’t help herself.

	But when she saw the number of missed calls—22 voicemails from Antwan—Nikki’s stomach dropped. She clicked on the first voicemail, the sound of Antwan’s voice filling her ears.

	“I can’t stop thinking about you, Nikki. I love you. I know it’s complicated, but I want to be with you. I’m not asking you to make a decision now, but please, just… call me back.”

	Her hand shook as she pressed play on the next message.

	“Nikki, I know I’ve hurt you. I just want to make things right. I can’t get you out of my head. You mean everything to me. Please, baby… just let me in.”

	The next voicemail was much the same, his voice cracking with emotion, each word heavier than the last. The urgency, the vulnerability in his tone made her pause. There was love in his words. Real love. The kind that made her heart ache.

	But it also reminded her of everything she had left behind—his family, his girlfriend, his children.

	Nikki closed her eyes, leaning against the baggage carousel as the next voicemail played.

	“You don’t know how much I need you, Nikki. I’ve been a fool. But please don’t shut me out. I love you. I need you. Just give me a chance.”

	The words felt like a weight on her chest, like they were pulling her in different directions. She could hear his pain, feel the longing in his voice. She could almost see him there, standing in front of her, waiting for her to make a decision.

	But she couldn’t.

	She didn’t want to be part of that world again. The world where everything was a mess, where feelings were complicated and love was tangled in responsibilities and promises to others. She had worked too hard to free herself from that.

	Nikki trusted that God would lead her in the right direction. It was something she had been clinging to during her time in Iceland. The peace she felt there, the certainty that the universe would guide her if she listened. And right now, it was telling her that this—whatever Antwan was asking for—was not her path.

	She wasn’t going to be the other woman. She wasn’t going to get lost in someone else’s family drama, in someone else’s mess. Not when she had finally started to build her own future.

	The sound of another voicemail from Antwan interrupted her thoughts, but this time, she didn’t listen.

	She slid her phone into her bag and took a deep breath. She had found her peace. She wasn’t going to let it be shaken by someone else’s emotional turmoil.

	As Nikki made her way out of the airport, the bright Atlanta skyline greeted her, but there was a sense of finality in the air. She was back, but she wasn’t the same.

	The city felt different now. Her life felt different.

	She would not go back to the past. She was moving forward. She had faith that the right things would come to her when the time was right, and she trusted in the choices she had made. She didn’t need to be tied to anyone else's decisions anymore.

	Nikki was taking control of her life—and she was ready to embrace whatever came next.

	Chapter 17: Invitations and Decisions

	Nikki opened the door to her home, the familiar scent of jasmine and cedarwood filling the air. It felt good to be back, to slip back into her space after what felt like a lifetime away. Iceland had changed her, given her the clarity she needed, but now that she was home, there was still the question of what was next.

wide.text:
Nikki couldn’t believe this was all for her. She’d always known Franco had a flair for luxury, but this? This was something else entirely. They checked in, and the concierge handed Nikki a small envelope with her name on it.

	“Everything has been taken care of, Ms. Davenport,” the concierge said with a polite smile. “You’re all set for your stay.”

	Franco flashed a playful grin as he took her hand, leading her to their room. “You deserve this, Nikki. Just relax and enjoy. I’ve got everything planned.”

	Nikki didn’t know what to expect.

	That night, after a few hours of unwinding and getting ready for dinner, Franco took her to an intimate but beautiful restaurant nestled in the heart of Aspen. The warm light from the candles flickered against the walls, creating a soft, romantic atmosphere. Franco looked effortlessly handsome in his tailored suit, and Nikki felt like a goddess in her black dress. Everything felt perfect—too perfect.

	As they sat down, Nikki couldn’t help but feel a little bit overwhelmed by how surreal the whole evening was. The ambiance was magical, the food was exquisite, and the wine was flowing, but there was something in the air that made her heart beat just a little bit faster.

	Midway through dinner, Franco leaned in closer, his eyes locking with hers in a way that made her breath catch.

	“Nikki,” he began softly, his voice full of warmth, “there’s something I’ve been wanting to ask you.”

	Before she could even respond, a waiter appeared, holding a velvet box. Nikki’s heart skipped a beat as she realized what was happening.

	Franco took the box from the waiter and opened it to reveal the most stunning diamond ring Nikki had ever seen. It was large and flawless, sparkling in the candlelight like it was made just for her. Her mouth went dry, her heart pounding in her chest.

	“Nikki D,” Franco continued, his voice full of emotion, “I love you more than words could ever express. You’ve changed my life in ways I never thought possible. You make me a better man, and I can’t imagine my future without you in it. Will you marry me?”

	Tears filled Nikki’s eyes, her hands trembling as she reached for the ring. Everything around her seemed to blur as she looked at Franco, the man who had become her partner in every sense of the word. The man who had given her the space to be herself, supported her dreams, and made her feel loved every single day.

	“Yes,” she whispered, her voice cracking with emotion. “Yes, I will.”

	The room erupted into applause, and Nikki’s gaze swept around the restaurant in disbelief. To her shock, her family was there—her mom, Karen, Meko, even Calvin and Leila, who had their baby with them. Every single person who had meant something to Nikki in her life was there, celebrating this moment with her.

	She stood up and walked toward Franco, her heart full to the brim with love and gratitude. He stood, meeting her halfway, and wrapped his arms around her, pulling her close. His lips met hers in a soft, passionate kiss, and the world seemed to stand still for a moment.

	“I love you,” he murmured against her lips, his voice full of promise. “I love you so much, Nikki.”

	The tears that had been threatening to fall now flowed freely down Nikki’s cheeks. She was overwhelmed by the love and joy that filled her heart, the sense of belonging that she had always longed for but never thought she would find.

	Franco took her hand, slipping the ring onto her finger, and she admired the way it glimmered against her skin. It was perfect, just like him. Just like the life they were going to build together.

	The night was a blur of laughter, hugs, and kisses. It was everything Nikki had ever wanted—intimate, joyful, and full of love. Franco had planned the perfect proposal, the perfect evening. But what made it even more special was the way she felt—whole, content, and at peace.

	As the evening drew to a close, they returned to their hotel room, and Nikki sank into the softness of the bed. Franco joined her, pulling her into his arms.

	“Everything feels right,” she whispered, her voice barely audible as she snuggled close to him. “This is where I’m meant to be.”

	Franco kissed the top of her head, his hand gently caressing her hair. “I promise you, Nikki, this is just the beginning. We’ve got so much more ahead of us, and I can’t wait to spend every day with you.”

	And as Nikki drifted off to sleep in Franco’s arms, she knew that their future was as bright as the stars above Aspen. Together, they would conquer anything life threw their way. Together, they would create a life full of love, laughter, and endless happiness.

	It was the beginning of forever.

	And Nikki knew that, for the first time in her life, she had truly found her home.
