XIII

Sommernætter og stille vand og uendelig stille skoger. Intet
skrik, intet fottrin fra veiene, mit hjærte var fuldt som av
dunkel vin.

Møl og sværmere kommer lydløst flyvende ind gjennem mit
vindu, hitlokket av skinnet fra gruven og av duften fra min
stekte fugl. De støter mot taket med en dump lyd, svirrer
forbi mine ører så det farer koldt gjennem mig og sætter sig
på mit hvite krudthorn på væggen. Jeg betragter dem, de sitte1
skjælvende og ser på mig, det er spindere, borere og møl. Jeg
synes at nogen av dem er som flyvende stedmorsblomster.

Jeg træder utenfor hytten og lytter. Ingenting, ingen støl,
alt sover. Luften lyser av flyvende insekter, av myriader svir-
rende vinger. Borte i skogkanten står bregner og stormhat,
melbærlyngen blomstrer og jeg elsker dens små blomster. Tak
min Gud, for hver lyngblomst jeg har set; de har været som små
roser på min vei og jeg gråter av kjærlighet til dem. Et eller
andet sted i nærheten er vild nellik, jeg ser den ikke, men jeg
fornemmer dens duft.

Men nu i nattens timer har pludselig store, hvite blomster
utfoldet sig i skogen, deres ar står åpne, de ånder. Og lodne
tusmørkesværmere sænker sig ned i deres blade og bringer hele
planten til å skjælve. Jeg går fra den ene til den andre blomst,
de er berusede, det er kjønslig berusede blomster og jeg ser
hvorledes de beruses.

Lette fottrin, et menneskes åndedrag, et glad godaften.

Jeg svarer og kaster mig ned på veien og omfavner de to knær
og den fattige kjole.

Godaften, Edvarda! sier jeg endnu en gang, utslitt av lykke.

Hvor du er glad i mig! hvisker hun.

Hvor jeg kan være taknemmelig! svarer jeg. Du er min og
mit hjærte ligger hele dagen stille i mig og tænker på dig. Du
er den skjønneste pike på denne jord og jeg har kysset dig.
Ofte blir jeg rød av glæde når jeg bare husker på at jeg har
kysset dig.

Hvorfor er du blit så glad i mig just i kvæld? spør hun.

Og det var jeg blit av utallige grunde, jeg hadde bare behøvet
å tænke på hende for å bli det. Dette blik under de buede øien-
bryn høit op i panden og denne mørke, hulde hud!

Skulde jeg ikke være glad i dig! sier jeg. Jeg går og takker
hvert træ for at du er frisk og har din helse. Engang på et ball
var det en ung dame som sat over dans efter dans og alle lot
hende sitte. Jeg kjendte hende ikke, men hendes ansigt gjorde
indtryk på mig og jeg bukket for hende. Nu? Nei hun rystet
på hodet. Frøkenen danser ikke? sa jeg. Kan De begripe det,
svarte hun, min far var så smuk og min mor var en fuldkommen
skjønhet, og min far seiret over min mor med storm. Men jeg
blev halt.

Edvarda så på mig.

Lat os sætte os, sa hun.

Vi satte os i lyngen.

Vet du hvad min veninde sier om dig? begyndte hun. Du
har dyreblik, sier hun, og når du ser på hende gjør du hende
gal. Det er som om du berører hende, sier hun.

translation.text:
Every day, every day I met her. I confess the truth,
I was glad to meet her, yes, my heart took flight. This year it is two
years ago; now I think of it only when I wish, the whole adventure
amuses and distracts me. And as for the two green bird feathers,
I shall explain that shortly.
We had several places where we could meet, by the mill, on the road,
yes, even in my hut; she came wherever I wished. Good day! she always
called first, and I answered good day.

You are happy today, you are singing, she says, and her eyes sparkle.

Yes, I am happy, I answer. You have a spot there on your shoulder;
it is dust, perhaps it is mud from the road; I want to kiss that spot,
oh, do let me kiss it. Everything about you affects me tenderly,
I am so distraught over you. Last night I did not sleep.

And it was true; for more than one night I lay sleepless.

We walk side by side along the road.

What do you think, am I behaving as you like? she says. Perhaps
I talk too much? No? Yes, but you must tell me what you think.
Sometimes I think to myself that this can never turn out well....

What is it that will not turn out well? I ask.

This thing between us. That it will not turn out well. Whether you
believe it or not, I am walking here shivering now; a chill runs
down my back merely when I come near you. It is from happiness.

Yes, the same with me, I answer; a chill also runs through me merely
when I see you. Oh, it will surely turn out well. Besides, I shall pat
you a little on the back to warm you.

She reluctantly lets me do it; I pat a little harder, only in jest;
I laugh and ask whether it does not help.

Oh no, do not be so kind as to thump me on the back anymore, she says.

Those few words! It sounded so helpless to me when she said:
do not be so kind.

Then we went on along the road. Is she displeased with me because
of my jest? I asked myself, and I thought: let us see.
I said:

I happen to remember something. Once, on a sleigh ride, there was
a young lady who took a white silk handkerchief from around her own neck
and tied it around mine. In the evening I said to the lady: You shall
have Your handkerchief back tomorrow; I shall have it washed. No,
she answered, let me have it now; I want to keep it as it is,
just as You have worn it. And she was given the handkerchief. Three years
later I met the young lady again. The handkerchief? I said. She
brought the handkerchief. It lay in its paper, still unwashed; I saw it myself.

Edvarda glanced up at me.

Yes? What happened then?

No, there was no more, I said. But I thought it was a
lovely gesture.

Pause.

Where is that lady now?

Abroad.

23 — Hamsun: II
We spoke no more about it. But when she was going home, she said:

Good night, then. Do not go on thinking about that lady, will you?
I think of no one but you.

I believed her; I saw that she meant what she said, and it was enough
for me for all eternity if only she thought of me. I followed her.

Thank you, Edvarda, I said. Later I added with all my heart: You
are far too good for me, but I am grateful that you want me;
God will reward you for it. I may not be as splendid as
many others you could have; but I am so entirely yours, so violently
yours, by my immortal soul. What are you thinking about? There are
tears in your eyes.

It was nothing, she answered. It sounded so strange that
God would reward me for it. You say such things as.... I
love you so much!

She suddenly threw her arms around my neck right in the middle of the road
and kissed me passionately.

When she had gone, I turned aside and slipped into the forest to hide
and be alone with my joy. And, deeply moved, I ran back
to the road again and looked to see whether anyone might have noticed that
I went in there. But I saw no one.

XIII

Summer nights and still water and endlessly still forests. No
cry, no footstep from the roads; my heart was full as though with
dark wine.

Moths and hawk moths come flying soundlessly in through my
window, lured here by the glow from the hearth and by the smell of my
roasted bird. They strike the ceiling with a dull sound, whir
past my ears so that a chill passes through me, and settle
on my white powder horn on the wall. I observe them; they sit
trembling and look at me; they are spinners, borers, and moths. I
think some of them are like flying pansies.

I step outside the hut and listen. Nothing, no mountain farm,
everything sleeps. The air glows with flying insects, with myriads of
whirring wings. Over at the edge of the forest stand ferns and monkshood;
the bearberry is in bloom, and I love its little flowers. Thank
You, my God, for every heather blossom I have seen; they have been like little
roses on my path, and I weep for love of them. Somewhere
nearby there are wild pinks; I do not see them, but I
sense their fragrance.

But now, in the hours of night, great white flowers have suddenly
unfolded in the forest; their stigmas stand open, they breathe. And shaggy
hawk moths descend into their petals and make the whole
plant tremble. I go from one flower to another;
they are intoxicated, they are sexually intoxicated flowers, and I see
how they become intoxicated.

Light footsteps, a human being’s breath, a cheerful good evening.

I answer and throw myself down on the road and embrace the two knees
and the poor dress.

Good evening, Edvarda! I say once again, exhausted with happiness.

How you love me! she whispers.

How grateful I can be! I answer. You are mine, and
all day my heart lies still within me and thinks of you. You
are the most beautiful girl on this earth, and I have kissed you.
Often I blush with joy merely when I remember that I have
kissed you.

Why have you come to love me so much this very evening? she asks.

And I had for countless reasons; I had only needed
to think of her for it to happen. That gaze beneath the arched eyebrows
high upon her forehead, and that dark, lovely skin!

Should I not love you! I say. I go about thanking
every tree because you are well and in good health. Once, at a ball,
there was a young lady who sat out dance after dance, and everyone left
her sitting. I did not know her, but her face made
an impression on me, and I bowed to her. Well? No, she shook
her head. Does the young lady not dance? I said. Can You understand it,
she answered; my father was so handsome and my mother was a perfect
beauty, and my father swept my mother off her feet. But I
became lame.

Edvarda looked at me.

Let us sit down, she said.

We sat down in the heather.

Do you know what my friend says about you? she began. You
have the eyes of an animal, she says, and when you look at her you drive her
mad. It is as though you were touching her, she says.

Jeg rodde ut til min fiskegrund. Veiret var blit trykkende,

Da jeg kom til bryggen stod smeden der. Han stod i arbeide.
Det farer en tanke gjennem mig, jeg spør ham:

Får jeg følge hjem?
Nei, svarer han, hr. Mack har git mig arbeide like til midnat.

Jeg nikket og tænkte ved mig selv at det var godt.

Jeg tok min fangst med og gik, jeg la veien om smedens hus.
Eva var alene hjemme.

Jeg længtet så hjærtelig efter dig, sa jeg til hende. Og jeg
blev bevæget ved synet av hende, hun kunde knapt se på mig

Nei, svarte hun forfærdet.

Jeg ropte på Edvarda, jomfru Edvarda, men jeg mente dig.
Jeg vaknet av det. Jo jeg mente dig, jeg var undskyldt, jeg for-

En glæde som jeg endnu aldrig har set hos hende fløi over
hendes ansigt; hun vil vende sig bort, men betænker sig og slår
den ene arm om min hals.

En tid går. Vi taler sammen, sitter hele tiden på en lang
bænk og taler til hverandre om mange ting. Jeg sa:

Vil du tro det, jomfru Edvarda har ikke lært å tale endnu,
hun taler som et barn, hun sier «mere lykkeligere», jeg har selv
hørt det. Synes du at hun har en vakker pande? Det synes ikke
jeg. Hun har en djævelsk pande. Hun vasker heller ikke sine
hænder.

Vi skulde jo ikke snakke mere om hende?

Rigtig. Jeg glemte det bare.

En tid går igjen. Jeg tænker på noget, jeg tier.

Hvorfor blir dine øine våte? spør Eva.

Hun har forresten en vakker pande, sier jeg, og hendes hæn-
der er altid rene. Det var bare en tilfældighet at de var skitne
engang. Jeg mente ikke å si andet. — Men nu fortsætter jeg
hidsig og med sammenbitte tænder: Jeg sitter uavlatelig og
tænker på dig, Eva; men det falder mig ind at du kanske ikke
har hørt hvad jeg nu vil fortælle dig. Den første gang Edvarda
så Æsop sa hun: Æsop, det var jo en vismand, han var frygier.
Er det ikke naragtig? Hun hadde læst det i en bok den samme
dag, det er jeg sikker på.

Ja, sier Eva, men hvad så?

Såvidt jeg mindes talte hun også om at Æsop hadde hat
Xanthus til lærer. Hahaha.

Jaså.
Hvad satan er nu det å fortælle en forsamling at Æsop har
hat Xanthus til lærer? Jeg spør bare. Ak du er ikke oplagt
idag, Eva, ellers vilde du le dig syk av det.

Jo jeg synes også at det er morsomt, sier Eva og begynder
å le anstrængt og forundret. Men jeg forstår det ikke så godt
som du.

Jeg tier og tænker, tier og tænker.

Vil du at vi helst skal sitte stille og ikke si noget? spør Eva
sagte. Godheten lyste ut av hendes øine, hun tok mig over
håret med sin hånd.

Du gode, gode sjæl! utbryter jeg og trykker hende hæftig ind

jeg elsker dig mere og mere, tilslut blir du med mig når jeg
reiser. Du skal bare se. Kunde du følge med mig

Ja, svarer hun.

Jeg hører næsten ikke dette ja, men jeg føler det av hendes
pust, jeg mærker det på hende, vi holder vildt om hverandre
og hun gir sig så sanseløst bort.

En times tid efter kysser jeg Eva til avsked og går. Jeg
møter hr. Mack 1 døren.

Hr. Mack selv.

Han rykker til og stirrer ind i stuen, blir stående der på dør-
stokken og stirre. Nå! sier han og kan ikke få sagt mere, han
er som slåt fortumlet.

De hadde ikke ventet å finde mig her? sier jeg og hilser.

Eva rører sig ikke.

Hr. Mack fatter sig, en mærkværdig sikkerhet lægger sig over
ham, han svarer:

De tar feil, det er netop Dem jeg søker. Jeg vil gjøre Dem
opmærksom på at fra første april til femtende august er det
forbudt å løse skudd inden en ottendedels mil fra æg- og dun-
vær. De har idag skutt to fugler ved øen, der er folk som har
set Dem.

Jeg skjøt to alker, sa jeg slagen. Det gik op for mig på stedet
at manden var i sin ret.

To alker eller to edderfugler, det er like meget. De har været
indenfor fredlyst område.

Jeg erkjender det, sa jeg. Det har ikke faldt mig ind før nu.

Men det burde ha faldt Dem ind før nu.

Jeg har også i mai måned skutt av begge mine løp omtrent
på samme sted. Det var på en øtur. Det skedde på Deres
egen anmodning.

Det er en anden sak, sa hr. Mack kort.
Men så for djævelen, så vet De vel hvad De har å gjøre?

Såre vel, svarte han.

Eva holdt sig i beredskap; da jeg gik ut fulgte hun efter, hun
hadde tat et tørklæ på og gik bort fra huset, jeg så hende
ta veien ned til bryggerne. Hr. Mack vandret hjem.

Jeg tænkte over det. For en smidighet i å finde på en utveil
hvor hans øine stak! Et skudd, to skudd, et par alker, en mulkt,
en utbetaling. Og så var alt, alt opgjort med hr. Mack og hans
hus. Alt gik i grunden så overmåte smukt og hurtig ....

Det begyndte allerede å regne med store, bløte dråper.
Skjorene fløi langsmed jorden og da jeg kom hjem og slap Æsop
løs åt den græs. Vinden begyndte å suse.

XXIII

En mil nedenunder mig ser jeg havet. Det regner og jeg er
tilfjælds, en berghammer beskytter mig mot regnet. Jeg røker
på min snadde, røker den ene pipe efter den andre, og hver
gang jeg tænder kravler tobakken op som glødende småormer
av asken. Således myldrer også tankerne i mit hode. Foran
mig på marken ligger en bundt tørre kvister av et ruineret

Jeg husker hver minste bagatel av denne og den næste dags

Jeg sitter her tilfjælds og havet og luften suser, det koker

translation.text:
I rowed out to my fishing ground. The weather had turned oppressive, the mosquitoes gathered in swarms, and I had to smoke tobacco the whole time to save myself. The haddock were biting; I hauled in the two-hook line; I made a good catch. On the way home I shot two auks.

When I reached the pier, the smith was standing there. He was at work. A thought passes through me, and I ask him:

May I go home with you?
No, he answers, Mr. Mack has given me work until midnight.

I nodded and thought to myself that this was good.

I took my catch with me and went, taking the road past the smith’s house. Eva was home alone.

I have longed for you so dearly, I said to her. And I was moved at the sight of her; she could scarcely look at me for astonishment. I love your youth and your good eyes, I said. Punish me today because I have thought more of another than of you. Listen, I come to you only to look at you; you do me good, I am in love with you. Did you hear me calling for you last night?

No, she answered in alarm.

I called for Edvarda, Miss Edvarda, but I meant you. It woke me. Yes, I meant you; I was excused—I misspoke when I said Edvarda. But let us speak no more of her. God, how you are my dearest girl, Eva! Your mouth is so red today. You have prettier feet than Edvarda; just look for yourself. — I lifted her dress and showed her her own legs.

A joy I had never yet seen in her flew across her face; she is about to turn away, but thinks better of it and puts one arm around my neck.

Some time passes. We talk together, sit all the while on a long bench, and talk to each other about many things. I said:

Would you believe it, Miss Edvarda has not yet learned to speak; she talks like a child, she says “more happier”; I have heard it myself. Do you think she has a beautiful forehead? I do not. She has a devilish forehead. Nor does she wash her hands.

Were we not supposed to speak no more of her?

Quite right. I merely forgot.

Some time passes again. I am thinking of something; I am silent.

Why are your eyes growing wet? Eva asks.

She has a beautiful forehead, by the way, I say, and her hands are always clean. It was only by chance that they were dirty once. I did not mean to say otherwise. — But now I continue heatedly and through clenched teeth: I sit constantly thinking of you, Eva; but it occurs to me that perhaps you have not heard what I am about to tell you. The first time Edvarda saw Aesop, she said: Aesop, why, he was a wise man; he was a Phrygian. Is that not ridiculous? She had read it in a book that same day, I am certain of it.

Yes, says Eva, but what of it?

As far as I remember, she also spoke of Aesop having had Xanthus as his teacher. Hahaha.

I see.
What the devil is the point of telling a gathering that Aesop had Xanthus as his teacher? I am merely asking. Ah, you are not in the mood today, Eva, otherwise you would laugh yourself sick over it.

Yes, I think it is amusing too, says Eva, and begins to laugh with effort and astonishment. But I do not understand it as well as you do.

I am silent and think, silent and thinking.

Would you rather that we sit quietly and say nothing? Eva asks softly. Goodness shone from her eyes; she stroked my hair with her hand.

You good, good soul! I exclaim, pressing her fiercely to me. I am certain I shall perish from love for you; I love you more and more; in the end you will come with me when I leave. You will see. Could you come with me?

Yes, she answers.

I scarcely hear this yes, but I feel it in her breath, I sense it in her; we hold each other wildly, and she gives herself to me so senselessly.

An hour later I kiss Eva farewell and leave. I meet Mr. Mack in the doorway.

Mr. Mack himself.

He starts and stares into the room, remains standing there on the threshold and staring. Well! he says, and cannot manage to say more; he is as though struck senseless.

You had not expected to find me here? I say, greeting him.

Eva does not move.

Mr. Mack collects himself; a remarkable assurance settles over him, and he answers:

You are mistaken; it is precisely you I am looking for. I wish to make you aware that from the first of April until the fifteenth of August, it is forbidden to fire shots within one eighth of a mile of an egg-and-down nesting ground. Today you shot two birds by the island; there are people who saw you.

I shot two auks, I said, stricken. It dawned on me on the spot that the man was within his rights.

Two auks or two eider ducks, it is all the same. You were within the protected area.

I acknowledge it, I said. It had not occurred to me until now.

But it ought to have occurred to you before now.

I also fired both barrels in roughly the same place in the month of May. It was on an island excursion. It happened at your own request.

That is another matter, Mr. Mack said curtly.
But then, for the devil’s sake, you surely know what you have to do?

Very well indeed, he answered.

Eva had held herself in readiness; when I went out, she followed, having put on a kerchief, and walked away from the house; I saw her take the road down to the piers. Mr. Mack walked home.

I thought it over. What agility in contriving a way out—how his eyes stabbed! One shot, two shots, a couple of auks, a fine, a payment. And then everything, everything was settled with Mr. Mack and his house. Fundamentally, it all went so exceedingly smoothly and quickly....

It had already begun to rain in large, soft drops. The magpies flew close to the ground, and when I came home and let Aesop loose, it ate grass. The wind began to sigh.

XXIII

A mile below me I see the sea. It is raining, and I am up in the mountains; a rock overhang shelters me from the rain. I smoke my short pipe, smoke one pipe after another, and each time I light it, the tobacco crawls upward like tiny glowing worms out of the ash. Thus, too, the thoughts swarm in my head. Before me on the ground lies a bundle of dry twigs from a ruined bird’s nest. And as this bird’s nest is, so too is my soul.

I remember every smallest trifle of the experiences of this day and the next. Hoho, how badly I was mauled....

I sit here up in the mountains, and the sea and the air roar; wind and weather seethe and lament horribly in my ears. Freighters and yachts can be seen far out with reefed sails; there are people aboard, they must be going somewhere, and God knows where all these lives are going, I think. The sea rises foaming into the air and tumbles, tumbles; it is as though peopled by great, raging figures that fling out their limbs and roar at one another—no, it is a revel among ten thousand shrieking devils who duck their heads between their shoulders and wheel around, whipping the sea white with the tips of their wings. Far, far out lies a submerged reef; from this reef a white merman rises and shakes his head after a leaking square-rigger running before the wind out to sea—hoho, out to sea, out into the desolate sea....

Og ganske som en liten skjælvende sang lød hendes røst i
skogen.

Og løvet gulner end mere, det lier mot høsten, det er kommet
nogen flere stjærner på himlen og månen ser fra nu av ut
som en skygge av sølv som er dyppet i guld. Det var ingen
kulde, ingenting, bare en sval stilhet og et strømmende liv i
skogen. Hvert træ stod og tænkte. Bærene var modne.

Så kom den to og tyvende august og de tre jærnnætter.

XXVI
Den første jærnnat.
Klokken ni går solen ned. Det lægger sig et mat mørke over
jorden, et par stjærner ses, to timer efter ses et skjær av månen.
Jeg vandrer tilskogs med min børse og min hund, jeg gjør en
nying op og lyset fra mit bål skinner ind mellem furustam-
merne. Det er ingen frost.

Den første jærnnat, sier jeg. Og en forvirrende hæftig glæde
over tiden og stedet gjennemryster mig sælsomt ....

En skål, I mennesker og dyr og fugler, for den ensomme nat
i skoger, i skoger! En skål for mørket og Guds mumlen mellem
trærne, for taushetens søte, enfoldige vellyd mot mine ører,
for grønt løv og gult løv! En skål for den livets lyd jeg hører,
en snøftende snute mot græsset, en hund som snuser henover
jorden! En stormende skål for den vildkat som ligger på stru-
pen og sigter og bereder sig til spranget på en spurv i mørke,
i mørke! En skål for den miskundelige stilhet på jorderik, for
stjærnene og for halvmånen, ja for dem og den! .

Jeg reiser mig op og lytter. Ingen har hørt mig. Jeg sætter
mig igjen.

En tak for den ensomme nat, for bergene, mørkets og havets
sus, det suser gjennem mit hjærte! En tak for mit liv, for mit
åndepust, for den nåde å leve inat, det takker jeg for av mit
hjærte! Hør i øst og hør i vest, nei hør! Det er den evige Gud!
Denne stilhet som mumler mot mit øre er alnaturens blod som
syder, Gud som gjennemvæver verden og mig. Jeg ser en blank
spindeltråd i skinnet av min nying, jeg hører en roende båt på
havnen, et nordlys glir opover himlen i nord. Å, ved min udøde-
lige sjæl, jeg takker også meget fordi det er mig som sitter her!

Stilhet. En furukongle falder dumpt til jorden. En furukongle
faldt! tænker jeg. Månen er høit oppe, ilden flakker på de halv-
brændte brande og vil gå ut. Og i den sene nat vandrer jeg
hjem.

Den anden jærnnat, den samme stilhet og det milde veir.
Min sjæl grubler. Jeg går mekanisk bort til et træ, trækker
luen dypt ned i panden og læner mig med ryggen til dette
træ, med hænderne foldet bak min nakke. Jeg stirrer og tænker,
flammen fra min nying blænder mine øine og jeg føler det ikke.
Jeg står i denne meningsløse stilling en god stund og ser på
ilden; mine ben svigter først og blir trætte, ganske stivbenet
sætter jeg mig ned. Først nu tænker jeg over hvad jeg har
gjort. Hvorfor dog stirre så længe på ilden?

Æsop reiser hodet og lytter, den hører trin, Eva viser sig
mellem trærne.

Jeg er såre tankefuld og bedrøvet iaften, sier jeg.

Og hun svarer av medfølelse intet.

Jeg elsker tre ting, sier jeg så. Jeg elsker en kjærlighetsdrøm
jeg hadde engang. jeg elsker dig og jeg elsker denne plet jord.
Og hvad elsker du mest?

Drømmen.

Det blir atter stille. Æsop kjender Eva og lægger hodet på
siden og ser på hende. Jeg mumler:

Jeg så en pike på veien idag, hun gik arm i arm med sin
elsker. Piken pekte på mig med sine øine og kunde vanskelig
bare sig for latter da jeg kom forbi.

Hvad lo hun av?

Det vet jeg ikke. Hun lo vel av mig. Hvorfor spør du om det?

Kjendte du hende?

Ja. Jeg hilste.

Og kjendte ikke hun dig?

Nei, hun lot som hun ikke kjendte mig .... Men hvorfor
sitter du og utfritter mig? Det er stygt av dig. Du får mig
ikke til å si hendes navn.

Pause.

Jeg mumler igjen:

Hvad lo hun av? Hun er en flane; men hvad lo hun av?
I Jesu Kristi navn, hvad har jeg da gjort hende?

Eva svarer:

Det var stygt av hende å le av dig.

Nei det var ikke stygt av hende! skriker jeg. Du skal ikke
sitte her og laste hende, hun gjør intet stygt, det var rigtig av
hende å le av mig. Ti stille for satan og lat mig i fred,
hører du!

Og Eva later mig forskræmt i fred. Jeg ser på hende og
angrer i samme stund mine hårde ord, jeg falder ned for hende
og vrir mine hænder.

Gå hjem, Eva. Det er dig jeg elsker mest; hvordan kunde jeg
elske en drøm? Det var bare en spøk, det er dig jeg elsker. Men
gå nu hjem, jeg skal komme til dig imorgen; husk på jeg er
din, ja glem det ikke. Godnat.

Og Eva går hjem.

Den tredje jærnnat, en nat i den ytterste spænding. Var det
endda litt frost! Istedenfor frosten stillestående varme efter
dagens sol, natten var som et lunkent morads. Jeg gjorde min
nying op +....

Eva, det kan undertiden være nogen nytelse å bli trukket
efter håret. Så forvendt kan et menneskes sind bli. Man kan
bli trukket efter håret nedover dale og opover berg, og hvis
nogen spør hvad det da er som foregår så kan man svare aldeles
henrykt: Jeg trækkes efter håret! Og hvis det spørres: Men skal
jeg ikke hjælpe dig, befri dig? så svarer man: Nei. Og hvis
det spørres: Men holder du det ut? så svarer man: Ja jeg holder
det ut, for jeg elsker den hånd som trækker mig .... Vet du,
Eva, hvad det er å håpe?

Ja jeg tror det.

Ser du, Eva, det å håpe det er noget underlig, ja noget meget
besynderlig. Man kan gå en morgen på en vei og håpe å træffe
på den vei et menneske som man har kjær. Og træffer man
dette menneske? Nei. Hvorfor ikke? Fordi mennesket er optat
for den morgen og er ganske andre steder henne .... Jeg lærte
å kjende en gammel blind lap tilfjælds. I otte og femti år hadde
han intet set og nu var han over sytti. Det forekom ham at
han så bedre og bedre tid for tid, det gik jævnt fremover,
syntes han. Kom ikke noget iveien vilde han kunne skimte
solen om nogen år. Han hadde endnu sort hår, men hans øine
var ganske hvite. Når vi sat sammen i hans gamme og røkte
fortalte han om alt han hadde set før han blev blind. Han
var hård og sund, uten følelse, uopslitelig, og sit håp bevarte
han. Når jeg skulde gå fulgte han mig ut og begyndte å peke
i forskjellige retninger. Der er syd, sa han, og der er nord. Nu
går du først i den retning og når du er kommet et stykke ned
i fjældet svinger du om i den retning, sa han. Ganske rigtig]!
svarte jeg. Og da lo lappen tilfreds og sa: Se det visste jeg ikke
for en firti femti år siden så jeg ser da bedre nu end dengang,
det går stadig fremover. Så dukket han sig og krøp ind i gam-
men igjen, den evige gamme, hans hjem på jorden. Og han
satte sig foran ilden igjen som før fuld av håp om at om nogen
år kunde han nok skimte solen .... Eva, det er såre mærk-
værdig med håpet. Jeg går for eksempel nu og håper å glemme
det menneske som jeg ikke traf på veien imorges.

translation.text:
But that does not matter. Nothing matters now.

And quite like a little trembling song, her voice sounded in the forest.

And the foliage turns even yellower, autumn is drawing on, a few more stars have appeared in the sky, and from now on the moon looks like a shadow of silver dipped in gold. There was no cold, nothing, only a cool stillness and a streaming life in the forest. Every tree stood thinking. The berries were ripe.

Then came the twenty-second of August and the three iron nights.

XXVI
The first iron night.
At nine o’clock the sun goes down. A dim darkness settles over the earth, a couple of stars can be seen; two hours later, a gleam of the moon can be seen. I wander into the forest with my gun and my dog, I kindle a campfire, and the light from my fire shines in among the pine trunks. There is no frost.

The first iron night, I say. And a bewilderingly fierce joy in the time and the place thrills through me strangely....

A toast, you men and beasts and birds, to the solitary night in forests, in forests! A toast to the darkness and God’s murmuring among the trees, to the sweet, simple harmony of the silence against my ears, to green foliage and yellow foliage! A toast to the sound of life I hear, a snuffling muzzle against the grass, a dog sniffing across the ground! A tempestuous toast to the wildcat lying flat on its throat, taking aim and preparing to spring upon a sparrow in the dark, in the dark! A toast to the merciful stillness on earth, to the stars and to the half-moon, yes, to them and to it!

I rise and listen. No one has heard me. I sit down again.

Thanks for the solitary night, for the mountains, for the sighing of the darkness and the sea; it sighs through my heart! Thanks for my life, for my breath, for the grace of being alive tonight; for that I give thanks from my heart! Listen in the east and listen in the west—no, listen! It is the eternal God! This stillness murmuring against my ear is the blood of all nature seething, God interweaving the world and me. I see a gleaming spider’s thread in the light of my campfire, I hear a boat being rowed in the harbor, an aurora glides up across the sky in the north. Oh, by my immortal soul, I also give great thanks that it is I who am sitting here!

Silence. A pine cone falls dully to the ground. A pine cone fell! I think. The moon is high, the fire flickers on the half-burned firebrands and is about to go out. And late in the night I wander home.

The second iron night, the same stillness and the mild weather.
My soul broods. I walk mechanically over to a tree, pull my cap low over my forehead, and lean with my back against this tree, my hands clasped behind my neck. I stare and think; the flame from my campfire dazzles my eyes, and I do not feel it. I stand in this senseless position for a good while, looking at the fire; my legs are the first to give way and grow tired, and quite stiff-legged I sit down. Only now do I reflect upon what I have done. Why stare at the fire for so long?

Aesop raises his head and listens; he hears footsteps; Eva appears among the trees.

I am exceedingly pensive and sorrowful tonight, I say.

And out of compassion she makes no reply.

I love three things, I then say. I love a dream of love I once had. I love you, and I love this patch of earth. And which do you love most?

The dream.

It grows quiet again. Aesop knows Eva and tilts his head to one side and looks at her. I murmur:

I saw a girl on the road today; she was walking arm in arm with her lover. The girl pointed me out with her eyes and could hardly keep from laughing when I passed.

What was she laughing at?

I do not know. I suppose she was laughing at me. Why do you ask about it?

Did you know her?

Yes. I bowed to her.

And did she not know you?

No, she pretended not to know me.... But why are you sitting there cross-questioning me? It is ugly of you. You will not get me to say her name.

Pause.

I murmur again:

What was she laughing at? She is a flighty creature; but what was she laughing at? In the name of Jesus Christ, what have I ever done to her?

Eva replies:

It was ugly of her to laugh at you.

No, it was not ugly of her! I scream. You are not to sit here and censure her; she does nothing ugly; it was right of her to laugh at me. For Satan’s sake, be quiet and leave me alone, do you hear!

And Eva, frightened, leaves me alone. I look at her and at that very moment regret my harsh words; I fall down before her and wring my hands.

Go home, Eva. It is you I love most; how could I love a dream? It was only a joke; it is you I love. But go home now; I shall come to you tomorrow. Remember that I am yours, yes, do not forget it. Good night.

And Eva goes home.

The third iron night, a night of the utmost tension. If only there had been a little frost! Instead of frost, stagnant warmth after the day’s sun; the night was like a lukewarm morass. I kindled my campfire....

Eva, at times there can be a certain pleasure in being dragged by the hair. So perverse can a human mind become. One may be dragged by the hair down valleys and up mountains, and if someone asks what is going on, one may answer in utter rapture: I am being dragged by the hair! And if one is asked: But shall I not help you, free you? then one answers: No. And if one is asked: But can you endure it? then one answers: Yes, I can endure it, for I love the hand that is dragging me.... Do you know, Eva, what it is to hope?

Yes, I think so.

You see, Eva, to hope is something strange, yes, something very peculiar. One may walk along a road one morning and hope to meet upon that road a person one holds dear. And does one meet this person? No. Why not? Because the person is occupied that morning and is somewhere else altogether.... I came to know an old blind Lapp up in the mountains. For fifty-eight years he had seen nothing, and now he was over seventy. It seemed to him that he saw better and better as time went on; there was steady improvement, he thought. If nothing intervened, he would be able to glimpse the sun in a few years. His hair was still black, but his eyes were quite white. When we sat together in his hut and smoked, he told me about everything he had seen before he became blind. He was hardy and healthy, without feeling, indefatigable, and he preserved his hope. When I was about to leave, he followed me out and began pointing in different directions. There is south, he said, and there is north. First you go in that direction, and when you have gone some way down the mountain, you turn in that direction, he said. Quite right! I answered. And then the Lapp laughed contentedly and said: See, I did not know that forty or fifty years ago, so I do see better now than I did then; it is steadily improving. Then he ducked down and crept back into the hut, the eternal hut, his home on earth. And he sat down before the fire again, as before, full of hope that in a few years he would surely be able to glimpse the sun.... Eva, hope is exceedingly remarkable. I, for example, am now going about hoping to forget the person whom I did not meet on the road this morning.

wide.text:
Men ta nu De doktoren som jeg sier. Lyd en vens råd; den
prins er jo en halvgammel nar. — Og jeg løi på ham i min
ophidselse, overdrev hans alder, sa at han var skaldet, at han
var næsten aldeles blind; jeg påstod også at han gik med den
krone i sine skjorteknapper ene og alene for å blære sig av sin
adel. — Jeg har forøvrig ikke giddet lære ham å kjende, sa jeg.
Det er intet i ham som markerer noget, han mangler hoved-
linjerne, han er ikke noget.

Men han er noget, han er noget! skrek hun og hendes røst
klikket av sinne. Han er meget mere end du tror, dit skog-
menneske! Men vent du bare, å, han vil tale med dig, jeg skal
be ham om det. Du tror ikke at jeg elsker ham, men du skal
se at du tar feil. Jeg vil gifte mig med ham, jeg skal tænke på
ham nat og dag. Husk på at jeg sier: jeg elsker ham. Lat bare
Eva komme, håhå Gud i himlen, lat hende bare komme, det
er mig så usigelig likegyldig. Ja jeg må se å komme bort herfra
+++. Hun begyndte å gå nedover stien fra hytten, hun gjorde
nogen små, ivrige skridt, vendte sig om endnu likblek i ansigtet
og stønnet: Og kom aldrig for mine øine mere.

XXV

Løvet gulner, potetgræsset var vokset høit op og stod i blomst,
jagttiden kom igjen, jeg skjøt ryper, årfugl og harer, jeg skjøt
en ørn en dag. Stille, høi himmel, svale nætter, mange klare
klange og skjære lyder i skog og mark. Stor og fredelig hvilte
verden ....

Jeg har intet videre hørt fra hr. Mack angående de to alker
jeg skjøt, sa jeg til doktoren.

Det kan De takke Edvarda for, svarte han. Jeg vet det, jeg
hørte at hun motsatte sig det.

Jeg takker hende ikke, sa jeg ....

Indian summer, indian summer. Stierne lå som bælter ind
gjennem den gulnende skog, en ny stjærne kom hver dag, månen
skimtedes som en skygge, en skygge av guld dyppet i sølv ....

Gud hjælpe dig, du er jo gift, Eva?

Visste du det ikke?

Nei jeg visste det ikke.

Hun knuget taus min hånd.

Gud hjælpe dig, barn, hvad skal vi gjøre nu?

Hvad du vil. Du reiser kanske ikke endnu, jeg vil være glad
sålænge du er her.

Nei, Eva.

Jo jo, bare sålænge du er her!

Hun ser forlatt ut og knuger hele tiden min hånd.

Nei, Eva, gå! Aldrig mere!

Og nætter forløper og dager kommer. Det er allerede den tredje
dag siden denne samtale. Eva går på veien med en bør. Hvor-
meget ved har dog dette barn båret hjem fra skogen i sommer!
Læg børen ned, Eva, og lat mig se om dine øine er like blå.

Hendes øine var røde.

Nei smil igjen, Eva! Jeg motstår dig ikke længer, jeg er din,
jeg er din ....

Kvæld. Eva synger, jeg hører hendes sang og det går en hete
gjennem mig.

Du synger ikvæld, Eva?

Ja jeg er glad.

Og da hun er mindre end jeg hopper hun litt op for å række
mig om halsen.

Men Eva, du har revet dine hænder? Herregud, gid du ikke
hadde revet dem!

Det gjør ingenting.

Hendes ansigt stråler så vidunderlig.

Eva, har du talt med hr. Mack?

En gang.

Hvad sa han og hvad sa du?

Han er blit meget hård mot os, han later min mand arbeide
nat og dag på bryggen, mig sætter han også til alslags arbeide.
Han har befalet mig å gjøre mandfolkarbeide.

Hvorfor gjør han det?

Eva ser ned.

Hvorfor gjør han det, Eva?

Fordi jeg elsker dig.

Men hvordan kan han vite det?

Jeg har sagt ham det.

Pause.

Gud gi at han ikke var så hård mot dig, Eval

Men det gjør ingenting. Ingenting gjør det nu.

Og ganske som en liten skjælvende sang lød hendes røst i
skogen.

Og løvet gulner end mere, det lier mot høsten, det er kommet
nogen flere stjærner på himlen og månen ser fra nu av ut
som en skygge av sølv som er dyppet i guld. Det var ingen
kulde, ingenting, bare en sval stilhet og et strømmende liv i
skogen. Hvert træ stod og tænkte. Bærene var modne.

Så kom den to og tyvende august og de tre jærnnætter.

XXVI
Den første jærnnat.
Klokken ni går solen ned. Det lægger sig et mat mørke over
jorden, et par stjærner ses, to timer efter ses et skjær av månen.
Jeg vandrer tilskogs med min børse og min hund, jeg gjør en
nying op og lyset fra mit bål skinner ind mellem furustam-
merne. Det er ingen frost.

Den første jærnnat, sier jeg. Og en forvirrende hæftig glæde
over tiden og stedet gjennemryster mig sælsomt ....

En skål, I mennesker og dyr og fugler, for den ensomme nat
i skoger, i skoger! En skål for mørket og Guds mumlen mellem
trærne, for taushetens søte, enfoldige vellyd mot mine ører,
for grønt løv og gult løv! En skål for den livets lyd jeg hører,
en snøftende snute mot græsset, en hund som snuser henover
jorden! En stormende skål for den vildkat som ligger på stru-
pen og sigter og bereder sig til spranget på en spurv i mørke,
i mørke! En skål for den miskundelige stilhet på jorderik, for
stjærnene og for halvmånen, ja for dem og den! .

Jeg reiser mig op og lytter. Ingen har hørt mig. Jeg sætter
mig igjen.

En tak for den ensomme nat, for bergene, mørkets og havets
sus, det suser gjennem mit hjærte! En tak for mit liv, for mit
åndepust, for den nåde å leve inat, det takker jeg for av mit
hjærte! Hør i øst og hør i vest, nei hør! Det er den evige Gud!
Denne stilhet som mumler mot mit øre er alnaturens blod som
syder, Gud som gjennemvæver verden og mig. Jeg ser en blank
spindeltråd i skinnet av min nying, jeg hører en roende båt på
havnen, et nordlys glir opover himlen i nord. Å, ved min udøde-
lige sjæl, jeg takker også meget fordi det er mig som sitter her!

Stilhet. En furukongle falder dumpt til jorden. En furukongle
faldt! tænker jeg. Månen er høit oppe, ilden flakker på de halv-
brændte brande og vil gå ut. Og i den sene nat vandrer jeg
hjem.

Den anden jærnnat, den samme stilhet og det milde veir.
Min sjæl grubler. Jeg går mekanisk bort til et træ, trækker
luen dypt ned i panden og læner mig med ryggen til dette
træ, med hænderne foldet bak min nakke. Jeg stirrer og tænker,
flammen fra min nying blænder mine øine og jeg føler det ikke.
Jeg står i denne meningsløse stilling en god stund og ser på
ilden; mine ben svigter først og blir trætte, ganske stivbenet
sætter jeg mig ned. Først nu tænker jeg over hvad jeg har
gjort. Hvorfor dog stirre så længe på ilden?

Æsop reiser hodet og lytter, den hører trin, Eva viser sig
mellem trærne.

Jeg er såre tankefuld og bedrøvet iaften, sier jeg.

translation.text:
But now take the doctor, as I tell you. Heed a friend’s advice; that prince is, after all, a half-old fool. — And in my agitation I lied about him, exaggerated his age, said that he was bald, that he was almost completely blind; I also claimed that he wore that crown on his shirt buttons solely and entirely to flaunt his nobility. — Besides, I have not bothered to get to know him, I said. There is nothing in him that marks him out in any way, he lacks the main lines, he is nothing.

But he is something, he is something! she screamed, and her voice cracked with anger. He is much more than you think, you forest creature! But just you wait, oh, he will speak to you, I shall ask him to. You do not believe that I love him, but you shall see that you are wrong. I will marry him, I shall think of him night and day. Remember that I say: I love him. Just let Eva come, ha-ha, God in heaven, just let her come, it is so unspeakably indifferent to me. Yes, I must see about getting away from here +++. She began to walk down the path from the hut, she took a few small, eager steps, turned around, still deathly pale in the face, and groaned: And never come before my eyes again.

XXV

The leaves are turning yellow, the potato tops had grown tall and were in bloom, hunting season came again, I shot ptarmigan, black grouse, and hares; one day I shot an eagle. Still, high sky, cool nights, many clear notes and piercing sounds in forest and field. Great and peaceful, the world rested ....

I have heard nothing further from Mr. Mack concerning the two auks I shot, I said to the doctor.

You may thank Edvarda for that, he replied. I know it; I heard that she opposed it.

I do not thank her, I said ....

Indian summer, Indian summer. The paths lay like belts through the yellowing forest, a new star appeared each day, the moon could be glimpsed like a shadow, a shadow of gold dipped in silver ....

God help you, you are married, Eva?

Did you not know?

No, I did not know.

Silently, she clasped my hand.

God help you, child, what are we to do now?

Whatever you wish. Perhaps you are not leaving yet; I will be happy as long as you are here.

No, Eva.

Yes, yes, only as long as you are here!

She looks forsaken and keeps clasping my hand.

No, Eva, go! Never again!

And nights pass and days come. It is already the third day since this conversation. Eva walks along the road carrying a load. How much firewood this child has carried home from the forest this summer! Put down your load, Eva, and let me see whether your eyes are still as blue.

Her eyes were red.

No, smile again, Eva! I resist you no longer, I am yours, I am yours ....

Evening. Eva sings; I hear her song, and a heat passes through me.

You are singing tonight, Eva?

Yes, I am happy.

And because she is shorter than I am, she jumps up a little to put her arms around my neck.

But Eva, you have torn your hands? Dear God, if only you had not torn them!

It does not matter.

Her face shines so wondrously.

Eva, have you spoken with Mr. Mack?

Once.

What did he say, and what did you say?

He has become very harsh toward us; he makes my husband work night and day on the wharf, and he sets me to all kinds of work as well. He has ordered me to do men’s work.

Why does he do that?

Eva looks down.

Why does he do that, Eva?

Because I love you.

But how can he know that?

I have told him.

Pause.

God grant that he were not so harsh toward you, Eva!

But it does not matter. Nothing matters now.

And her voice sounded in the forest exactly like a little trembling song.

And the leaves turn yellower still, it is drawing toward autumn, a few more stars have appeared in the sky, and from now on the moon looks like a shadow of silver dipped in gold. There was no cold, nothing, only a cool stillness and a streaming life in the forest. Every tree stood thinking. The berries were ripe.

Then came the twenty-second of August and the three iron nights.

XXVI

The first iron night.

At nine o’clock the sun goes down. A dim darkness settles over the earth, a couple of stars can be seen; two hours later, a gleam of the moon can be seen. I wander into the forest with my gun and my dog, I make a fire, and the light from my fire shines in among the pine trunks. There is no frost.

The first iron night, I say. And a bewilderingly intense joy at the time and the place strangely shakes me through and through ....

A toast, you human beings and animals and birds, to the solitary night in forests, in forests! A toast to the darkness and God’s murmuring among the trees, to the sweet, simple harmony of silence against my ears, to green leaves and yellow leaves! A toast to the sound of life that I hear, a snuffling muzzle against the grass, a dog sniffing over the ground! A resounding toast to the wildcat that lies with its throat to the ground, taking aim and preparing to spring upon a sparrow in the dark, in the dark! A toast to the merciful stillness on earth, to the stars and to the half-moon, yes, to them and to it! .

I rise and listen. No one has heard me. I sit down again.

Thanks for the solitary night, for the mountains, for the soughing of the darkness and the sea; it soughs through my heart! Thanks for my life, for my breath, for the grace of being alive tonight; for that I give thanks from my heart! Listen in the east and listen in the west, no, listen! It is the eternal God! This stillness that murmurs against my ear is the blood of all Nature seething, God weaving through the world and me. I see a shining strand of spiderweb in the light of my fire, I hear a boat being rowed in the harbor, a northern light glides upward across the sky in the north. Oh, by my immortal soul, I also give much thanks because it is I who am sitting here!

Silence. A pinecone falls dully to the ground. A pinecone fell! I think. The moon is high, the fire flickers on the half-burned brands and is about to go out. And late in the night I walk home.

The second iron night, the same stillness and the mild weather.

My soul broods. I walk mechanically over to a tree, pull my cap low over my forehead, and lean with my back against this tree, my hands clasped behind my neck. I stare and think; the flame from my fire dazzles my eyes, and I do not feel it. I stand in this senseless posture for quite some time and look at the fire; my legs are the first to fail and grow tired, and quite stiff-legged I sit down. Only now do I think about what I have done. Why stare at the fire for so long?

Aesop raises his head and listens; he hears footsteps, and Eva appears among the trees.

I am deeply pensive and sorrowful tonight, I say.

Johannes så fortumlet på manden, på sin port, om han
skulde gå ind gjennem den eller bli stående, på manden igjen,
på hans lange frak, hans hat; han smilte forvirret og sårt som
en nødlidende.

Den gamle huslærer fortsatte truende:

Atter et eksempel; kan De fragå det? Heller ikke hun fik
den hun skulde ha, hendes kjæreste like fra barneårene, en
ung, herlig Iøitnant. Han gik på jagt en kvæld, et skudd træffer
ham midt i panden og slår hans hode i to. Der lå han nu, et
offer for den lille dikkedar som Gud vilde lage med ham.
Victoria, hans brud, begynder å skrante, en orm åt hende,
hullet hendes hjærte op som et sold; vi, hendes venner, så det.
Så gik hun for nogen dager siden i et selskap hos en familje
Seier; hun fortalte mig forøvrig at også De skulde ha været
der, men kom ikke. Noksagt, i dette selskap bevæger hun sig
over ævne, minderne om hendes elskede stormer ind på hende
og gjør hende livlig på trods, hun danser, danser hele kvælden,
danser som et rasende menneske. Så falder hun om, gulvet
blir rødt under hende; man løfter hende op, bærer hende ut,
kjører hende hjem. Hun gjorde det ikke længe.

Huslæreren går tæt ind til Johannes og sier hårdt:

Victoria er død.

Ganske som en blind begyndte Johannes å værge for sig med
hænderne.

Død? Når døde hun? Jaså, er Victoria død?

Hun er død, svarer huslæreren. Hun døde imorges, nu i for-
middag. Han stak hånden ned i sin lomme og drog op et tykt
brev. Og dette brev betrodde hun mig å levere Dem. Her er
det. Efter min død, sa hun. Hun er død. Jeg leverer Dem brevet.
Min mission er endt.

Og uten å hilse, uten å si mere, vendte huslæreren sig om
og drev langsomt nedover gaten og forsvandt.

Johannes stod tilbake med brevet i sin hånd. Victoria var
død. Han nævnte gang på gang hendes navn høit og han
hadde en følesløs, næsten forhærdet stemme. Han så ned på
brevet og kjendte skriften; der var store og små bokstaver,
linjerne rette, og hun som hadde skrevet dem var død!

Så begir han sig ind gjennem sin port, op trappen, finder
den rigtige nøkkel å stikke i dørlåset og åpner. Hans værelse
var koldt og mørkt. Han sætter sig bort til vinduet og læser i
den siste rest av dagslys Victorias brev.

Kjære Johannes! skrev hun. Når De læser dette brev da er
jeg død! Alting er så underlig for mig nu, jeg skammer mig ikke
for Dem mere og skriver til Dem igjen, likesom det ikke var
nogen ting iveien herfor. Før, mens jeg var fuldstændig i le-
vende live, vilde jeg heller ha lidt nat og dag end skrevet til
Dem igjen; men nu er jeg begyndt å avsjæles og jeg tænker
ikke således længer. Fremmede har set mig blø, doktoren har
undersøkt mig og set at jeg har bare en rest av en lunge til-
bake, hvad skal jeg da undse mig for mere?

Jeg har ligget her på sengen og tænkt over de siste ord
jeg sa til Dem. Det var i skogen den kvæld. Dengang tænkte
jeg ikke at det skulde være mine siste ord, for så vilde jeg ha
sagt farvel til Dem med det samme og takket Dem. Nu får
jeg ikke se Dem mere, så jeg angrer nu på at jeg ikke fik kastet
mig ned for Dem og kysset Deres sko og jorden som De gik
på, og fik vist Dem hvor usigelig jeg har elsket Dem. Jeg har
ligget her og ønsket både igår og idag at jeg ikke var sykere
end at jeg kunde komme mig hjem igjen og gå i skogen og
finde den plass vi sat på da De holdt begge mine hænder;
for så kunde jeg lægge mig ned der og se om jeg ikke fandt
sporet efter Dem og kysse al lyngen deromkring. Men jeg kan
ikke komme hjem nu hvis jeg ikke muligens blir litt bedre
som mama tror.

Kjære Johannes! Det er mærkelig å tænke på at jeg ikke
har fåt nogen anden ting gjort end å komme på jorden og
elske Dem og nu si farvel til livet. De kan tro det er underlig
å ligge her og vente på dagen og timen. Jeg fjærner mig skridt
for skridt fra livet og menneskene på gaten og vognramme-
len; våren kommer jeg vel heller aldrig til å se mere og disse
huser og gaterne og trærne i parken vil være tilbake efter mig.
Jeg fik sitte i sengen idag og se litt ut av vinduet. Nede på
hjørnet var det to som traf hverandre, de hilste og grep hver-
andres hænder og lo av det de sa; men da var det så underlig
for mig at jeg som lå og så på dette skulde dø. Jeg kom
til å tænke: de to dernede vet ikke at jeg ligger her og venter
på min time; men om de visste det så vilde de vel allikevel hilse
på hverandre og tale med hverandre likesom nu. Igår nat da
det var mørkt tænkte jeg at det skulde være min siste stund,
mit hjærte begyndte å stå stille og det var likesom jeg allerede
hørte evigheten bruse imot mig langt ute. Men i næste øieblik
vendte jeg tilbake langt borte fra og begyndte å puste igjen.
Det var en aldeles ubeskrivelig følelse. Men mama tror at det
kanske bare var elven og fossen derhjemme som jeg husket.

Du gode Gud, De skulde vite hvor jeg har elsket Dem,
Johannes. Jeg har ikke fåt vise Dem det, det har lagt sig
så meget iveien for mig, og først og fremst min egen natur.
Papa var også således ond mot sig selv og jeg er hans datter.
Men nu når jeg skal dø og altsammen er forsent da skriver
jeg til Dem endnu en gang og sier Dem det. Jeg spør mig
selv hvorfor jeg gjør det da det dog er likegyldig for Dem, især
når jeg ikke engang skal være ilive mere; men jeg vilde gjærne
være nær hos Dem til det siste så jeg ikke følte mig mere
forlatt end før ialfald. Når De læser dette da er det likesom
jeg ser Deres aksler og hænder og ser alle Deres bevægelser
med brevet når De holder det foran Dem og læser det. Så er
vi ikke så langt fra hverandre, tænker jeg. Jeg kan ikke sende
bud efter Dem, dertil har jeg ingen ret. Mama vilde sende bud
efter Dem allerede for to dager siden, men jeg vilde heller
skrive. Jeg vilde også helst at De skulde huske mig således som
jeg engang var da jeg endnu ikke hadde været syk. Jeg husker
at De .... (Her er nogen ord uteglemt) .... mine øine og
øienbryn; men heller ikke de er mere som før. Også av den
grund vilde jeg ikke at De skulde komme. Og jeg vil også be
Dem om ikke å se mig i kisten. Jeg er vistnok omtrent som
da jeg levet, bare noget blekere, og jeg ligger i gul kjole; men
allikevel vilde De angre på det hvis De kom og så mig.

Nu har jeg skrevet mange ganger på dette brev idag og
allikevel har jeg ikke fåt sagt Dem en tusendel av det jeg
vilde si. Det er så forfærdelig for mig å dø, jeg vil det ikke,
jeg håper endnu så inderlig til Gud at jeg kanske kunde
bli litt bedre, om ikke længer end til våren. Da er dagene
lyse og det er løv på trærne. Hvis jeg blev frisk igjen nu så
skulde jeg nok aldrig være ond mot Dem mere, Johannes.
Hvor jeg har grått og tænkt på det! Å jeg vilde gå ut og klappe
alle gatestenene og stanse og takke hvert trin i trapperne som
jeg kom forbi og være god mot alle. Det var det samme hvor
ondt jeg fik det hvis jeg bare fik leve. Jeg skulde aldrig klage
mere over nogen ting, nei jeg skulde smile til den som over-
faldt og slog mig og takke og love Gud hvis jeg fik leve. Mit
liv er så ulevet, intet har jeg fåt gjort for nogen og dette feil-
slagne liv skal ende nu. Hvis De visste hvor nødig jeg vilde dø
så kanske De vilde gjøre noget, gjøre alt som stod i Deres magt.
De kan vistnok ikke gjøre noget; men jeg tænkte at hvis De og
hele verden bad for mig og ikke vilde slippe mig så vilde Gud
skjænke mig livet. Å hvor jeg vilde være taknemmelig da og
aldrig gjøre ondt mot nogen mere, men smile til alt som ble
mig beskikket bare jeg fik lov til å leve.

translation.text:
Johannes looked bewilderedly at the man, at his gate, wondering whether he should go in through it or remain standing there, then at the man again, at his long coat, his hat; he smiled in confusion and pain, like someone in distress.

The old tutor continued threateningly:

Another example; can you deny it? Nor did she get the man she was to have, her beloved since childhood, a young, splendid lieutenant. He went hunting one evening, a shot struck him squarely in the forehead and split his head in two. There he lay, a victim of the little caprice God wished to indulge in with him. Victoria, his bride, began to waste away; a worm ate at her, riddled her heart like a sieve; we, her friends, saw it. Then, a few days ago, she went to a gathering at the home of a family named Seier; incidentally, she told me that you too were to have been there, but did not come. In short, at this gathering she exerts herself beyond her strength; memories of her beloved come storming in upon her and make her lively out of defiance; she dances, dances all evening, dances like a mad person. Then she collapses, the floor turns red beneath her; they lift her up, carry her out, drive her home. She did not last long.

The tutor stepped close to Johannes and said harshly:

Victoria is dead.

Just like a blind man, Johannes began to fend the words off with his hands.

Dead? When did she die? Oh, so Victoria is dead?

She is dead, the tutor replied. She died this morning, this very forenoon. He thrust his hand into his pocket and drew out a thick letter. And she entrusted this letter to me to deliver to you. Here it is. After my death, she said. She is dead. I am delivering the letter to you. My mission is ended.

And without a greeting, without saying anything more, the tutor turned around and drifted slowly down the street and disappeared.

Johannes remained standing with the letter in his hand. Victoria was dead. Again and again he spoke her name aloud, and his voice was numb, almost hardened. He looked down at the letter and recognized the handwriting; there were capital and lowercase letters, the lines were straight, and she who had written them was dead!

Then he went in through his gate, up the stairs, found the right key to insert into the door lock, and opened it. His room was cold and dark. He sat down by the window and read Victoria’s letter in the last remnant of daylight.

Dear Johannes! she wrote. When you read this letter, I shall be dead! Everything is so strange to me now; I am no longer ashamed before you, and I am writing to you again, as though there were nothing to prevent it. Before, while I was still fully alive, I would rather have suffered night and day than written to you again; but now my soul has begun to leave my body, and I no longer think that way. Strangers have seen me bleed, the doctor has examined me and seen that I have only a remnant of one lung left; what more have I to be bashful about?

I have lain here in bed thinking over the last words I said to you. It was in the woods that evening. At the time I did not think they would be my last words, for then I would have said farewell to you at once and thanked you. Now I shall never see you again, so now I regret that I did not throw myself down before you and kiss your shoes and the ground you walked on, and show you how inexpressibly I have loved you. I have lain here, both yesterday and today, wishing that I were not too ill to make my way home again and go into the woods and find the place where we sat when you held both my hands; for then I could lie down there and see whether I could find some trace of you and kiss all the heather around it. But I cannot come home now unless perhaps I get a little better, as Mama believes.

Dear Johannes! It is strange to think that I have done nothing but come to earth and love you, and now say farewell to life. You may believe that it is strange to lie here and wait for the day and the hour. Step by step I am moving away from life and the people in the street and the clatter of carriages; I suppose I shall never see spring again either, and these houses and the streets and the trees in the park will remain after me. Today I was allowed to sit up in bed and look out of the window for a little while. Down on the corner there were two people who met; they greeted each other and took each other’s hands and laughed at what they said; but then it was so strange to me that I, who lay watching this, was to die. I found myself thinking: those two down there do not know that I am lying here waiting for my hour; but if they knew it, they would surely still greet each other and speak to each other just as they do now. Last night, when it was dark, I thought it was to be my final moment; my heart began to stand still, and it was as though I could already hear eternity rushing toward me from far away. But the next moment I returned from far away and began to breathe again. It was an utterly indescribable feeling. But Mama thinks that perhaps it was only the river and the waterfall back home that I remembered.

Good God, if only you knew how I have loved you, Johannes. I have not been able to show you; so much has placed itself in my way, first and foremost my own nature. Papa too was so cruel to himself, and I am his daughter. But now, when I am going to die and everything is too late, I write to you once more and tell you so. I ask myself why I do it, since it is of no consequence to you, especially when I shall not even be alive anymore; but I wanted so much to be close to you until the end, so that at least I would not feel more forsaken than before. When you read this, it is as though I can see your shoulders and hands and see all your movements with the letter as you hold it before you and read it. Then we are not so far apart, I think. I cannot send for you; I have no right to do so. Mama wanted to send for you as early as two days ago, but I preferred to write. I would also prefer you to remember me as I once was, when I had not yet been ill. I remember that you .... (Here some words have been omitted) .... my eyes and eyebrows; but they too are no longer as they were. For that reason as well, I did not want you to come. And I also want to ask you not to see me in my coffin. I am probably much as I was when I lived, only somewhat paler, and I am lying in a yellow dress; but even so, you would regret it if you came and saw me.

Now I have written on this letter many times today, and still I have not managed to tell you one thousandth of what I wanted to say. It is so terrible for me to die; I do not want to; I still hope so fervently in God that perhaps I might get a little better, if only until spring. Then the days are bright and there are leaves on the trees. If I were to recover now, I would certainly never be cruel to you again, Johannes. How I have wept and thought about it! Oh, I would go out and pat all the paving stones and stop and thank every stair I passed, and be good to everyone. It would not matter how badly I suffered, if only I were allowed to live. I would never complain about anything again; no, I would smile at whoever attacked and struck me, and thank and praise God if I were allowed to live. My life is so unlived; I have done nothing for anyone, and this failed life is to end now. If you knew how unwilling I am to die, then perhaps you would do something, do everything in your power. You probably cannot do anything; but I thought that if you and the whole world prayed for me and would not let me go, then God would grant me life. Oh, how grateful I would be then, and never again do harm to anyone, but smile at everything ordained for me, if only I were allowed to live.

Dersom det kan være Dem til nogen fornøielse så skal jeg

Vil De det?

Ja jeg takker Dem for Deres venlighet.

Da han var kommet ned i skogen vendte han sig om og

set på hendes hånd hvor ringen engang sat, — hun hadde

Det går en time. Dunsterne av skogen og marken omsvævet

Så hadde han igjen oplevet det! Da hun steg op til ham

Han reiste sig hæftig og blev stående. Victoria kom tilbake,

De fandt ingen blomster? spurte han fraværende.

Nei jeg opgav det. Jeg søkte ikke heller, jeg bare sat der.

Han sa:

Med det samme jeg husker det: De skal aldeles ikke gå
og mene at De har gjort noget ondt imot mig. De har intet

Ikke det, svarte hun overrumplet. Hun tænkte videre over
det, så på ham og grundet. Ikke det. Jeg trodde at den gang
«+++ Jeg vilde ikke at De hele tiden skulde gå og bære nag

Nei jeg bærer ikke nag til Dem.

Hun tænker endnu en stund. Pludselig kneiser hun.

Så er det godt, sier hun. Nei det burde jeg jo ha visst. Så

om det.

Nei lat os ikke det. Mine indtryk er Dem likegyldige nu
som før.

Adjø, sa hun. Adjø sålænge.

Adjø, svarte han. |

Victoria! ropte han.

Hun hørte det, hun rykket til og vendte sig om, men ved-

Det forløp nogen dager. Johannes gik i den høieste uro og
arbeidet ikke, sov ikke, han tilbragte næsten hele dagen i sko-

En besynderlig spænding grep ham. Det skulde komme frem-

Eftermiddagen var stille og varm; elven løp som en puls

Skibet la til, herrer og damer steg iland og tok plass i vog-

Javel det skulde være fest på Slottet; de fremmede blev mot-
tat med flaging og salut. I vognene sat nogen militære; kanske

Johannes steg ned fra haugen og begav sig hjemover. Han
blev indhentet av en mand fra Slottet som stanset ham. Man-
den bar et brev i luen, han var sendt av frøken Victoria og
skulde ha svar.

Johannes læste brevet med bankende hjærte. Victoria ind-

budet.

En underlig og uventet glæde var vederfaret ham, blodet
steg ham til hodet og han svarte manden at han vilde komme, ja
tak han vilde komme straks.

Værsågod!

Han rakte et latterlig stort pengestykke til budet og ilet
hjem for å klæ sig.

VIII

For første gang i sit liv trådte han ind gjennem Slottets
port og begav sig op trappen til anden etage. Det summet
ham røster imøte indefra, hans hjærte slog stærkt, han banket
på og steg ind.

Den endnu unge slotsfrue kom ham imøte og hilste venlig

stor mand .... Og det var som om slotsfruen vilde ha sagt
noget mere, hun holdt hans hånd længe og så forskende på
ham.

Også slotsherren kom tilstede og rakte ham hånden. Som
hans hustru hadde sagt, en stor mand, i mere end en betyd-
ning. En berømt mand. Glædet ham meget ...

Han blev præsenteret for herrer og damer, for kammerherren
som hadde sine ordener på, for fru kammerherreinden, for en
godseier fra nabobygden, for Otto, løitnanten. Victoria så
han ikke.

Det gik en rum tid. Victoria trådte ind, blek, endog usikker;
hun ledte en ung pike ved hånden. De gik en runde gjen-
nem salen, hilste på alle, talte litt med hver. De stanset ved
Johannes.

9— Hamsun: III
Victoria smilte og sa:

Se, her er Camilla, er ikke det en overraskelse? I kjender
hverandre.

Hun stod litt og så på dem begge, så gik hun ut av salen.

Johannes blev i det første øieblik stående stiv og fortumlet
på pletten. Her var overraskelsen; Victoria hadde venligst skaf-
fet en anden i sit sted. Hør her, gå nu hen og ha hverandre,
I mennesker! Våren står i flor, solen skinner; slå vinduerne op
om I så vil, for det er duft i haven og det leker også stærer
i bjørketopperne derute. Hvorfor taler I ikke til hverandre.
Men så le nul!

translation.text:
I once did you a wrong, Johannes; I wanted to make amends for it, put it right. I really have a surprise that I think ... that is to say, that I hope you will be pleased by. I cannot say any more. But this time I will ask you to be present.

If it can give you any pleasure, then I shall come.

Will you?

Yes, I thank you for your kindness.

When he had gone down into the forest, he turned around and looked back. She had seated herself; the basket stood beside her. He did not go home, but continued wandering along the road and back again. A thousand thoughts struggled within him. A surprise? She had said it just now, only a moment ago; her voice had trembled. A hot and nervous joy arose within him, made his heart pound violently, and he felt himself lifted from the road on which he walked. And was it merely chance that she was dressed in yellow today as well? He had looked at her hand where the ring had once been—she wore no ring.

An hour passed. The vapors of the forest and the fields surrounded him, entered into his breath, into his heart. He sat down, lay back with his hands clasped beneath his neck, and listened for a time to the cuckoo’s piping on the other side of the inlet. Passionate birdsong quivered in the air around him.

So he had experienced it again! When she came up to him in the quarry in her yellow dress and with her blood-red hat, she looked like a wandering butterfly stepping from stone to stone and stopping before him. I did not want to disturb you, she had said, smiling; her smile was red, her whole face lit up, she scattered stars. Some fine blue veins had appeared on her neck, and the few freckles beneath her eyes gave her a warm color. She was in her twentieth summer.

A surprise? What was her intention? Did she perhaps mean to show him his books, to lay out those two or three volumes and please him by telling him that she had bought them all and cut open their pages? There you are, one tiny little token of attention and gentle consolation! Do not disdain my modest contribution!

He rose abruptly and remained standing. Victoria came back; her basket was empty.

You found no flowers? he asked absently.

No, I gave it up. Nor did I look; I merely sat there.

He said:

While I remember it: you must not go about thinking that you have done me any wrong. You have nothing to make amends for with any kind of gentle consolation.

No? she answered, taken aback. She thought further about it, looked at him, and pondered. No? I thought that at the time
«+++ I did not want you to go on bearing a grudge against me all the time for what happened.

No, I bear you no grudge.

She thought for another moment. Suddenly she drew herself up.

Then that is well, she said. No, I ought to have known that. It did not leave so great an impression. Well, well, then we shall speak no more of it.

No, let us not. My impressions are as immaterial to you now as they were before.

Goodbye, she said. Goodbye for now.

Goodbye, he answered. |

They went their separate ways. He stopped and turned around. There she went now. He stretched out his hands and whispered, speaking tender words to himself: I bear you no grudge, no, no, I do not; I still love you, love you ....

Victoria! he called.

She heard it, started, and turned around, but continued walking.

Several days passed. Johannes went about in the greatest agitation and did not work, did not sleep; he spent almost the whole day in the forest. He climbed onto the great mound of pinewood where the Castle’s flagpole stood; there was a flag on the pole. A flag had also been raised on the Castle’s round tower.

A strange excitement seized him. Guests were to come to the Castle; there was to be a celebration.

The afternoon was still and warm; the river ran like a pulse through the hot landscape. A steamship glided in toward land and left a fan of white streaks spreading across the inlet. Now four carriages drove out from the Castle courtyard and took the road down to the landing.

The ship docked; gentlemen and ladies came ashore and took their places in the carriages. Then a succession of shots began to crack from the Castle; two men stood atop the round tower and loaded and fired, loaded and fired hunting guns. When they had discharged twenty-one shots, the carriages rolled in through the Castle gate and the shooting ceased.

Indeed, there was to be a celebration at the Castle; the guests were received with flags and a salute. Several military men sat in the carriages; perhaps Otto, the lieutenant, was among them.

Johannes descended from the mound and set off for home. He was overtaken by a man from the Castle, who stopped him. The man carried a letter in his cap; he had been sent by Miss Victoria and was to have an answer.

Johannes read the letter with a pounding heart. Victoria invited him after all, wrote to him in heartfelt words, and asked him to come. This time she would ask him. Reply by the messenger.

A strange and unexpected joy had befallen him; the blood rose to his head, and he answered the man that he would come—yes, thank you, he would come at once.

There you are!

He handed the messenger a ridiculously large coin and hurried home to dress.

VIII

For the first time in his life, he passed through the Castle gate and went up the stairs to the second floor. The murmur of voices came toward him from within; his heart beat hard; he knocked and entered.

The still-young lady of the Castle came toward him and greeted him kindly, pressing his hand. She was pleased to see him; she remembered him from the time when he had been no taller than this; now he was a great man .... And it was as though the lady of the Castle had meant to say something more; she held his hand for a long time and looked at him searchingly.

The lord of the Castle also came forward and offered him his hand. As his wife had said, a great man, in more than one sense. A famous man. He was very pleased ...

He was introduced to gentlemen and ladies, to the chamberlain, who wore his decorations, to the chamberlain’s wife, to a landowner from the neighboring district, to Otto, the lieutenant. He did not see Victoria.

A considerable time passed. Victoria entered, pale, even uncertain; she was leading a young girl by the hand. They made a circuit of the drawing room, greeted everyone, and spoke a little with each person. They stopped beside Johannes.

9—Hamsun: III
Victoria smiled and said:

Look, here is Camilla; is that not a surprise? You know each other.

She stood for a little while and looked at them both, then left the drawing room.

For the first moment Johannes remained standing rigid and bewildered on the spot. Here was the surprise; Victoria had most kindly provided someone else in her place. Listen here, go now and have each other, you people! Spring is in bloom, the sun is shining; throw open the windows if you wish, for there is fragrance in the garden, and starlings are also playing in the tops of the birches out there. Why do you not speak to each other? But then laugh now!

I det samme reiste han sig.

Da åpnet løitnanten ilsomt døren og trådte utenfor.

Jeg mener det! skrek han tilbake. Jeg mener det, øk!

Så slog han døren i med et skrald.

Johannes satte sig igjen.

Victoria stod endnu omtrent midt på gulvet. Hun så på ham
og var blek som et lik.

Støtte han Dem? spurte Camilla i høieste forundring.

Av vanvare. Han traf mig 1 øiet. Vil De se.

Gud, det er jo rødt, der er blod. Nei gnid det ikke, lat mig
hælde vand på. Deres lommetørklæde er så grovt, se her, ta
det igjen; jeg bruker mit eget. Har man set maken, like i øiet!

Victoria rakte også sit lommetørklæde ut. Hun sa intet. Derpå
gik hun ganske langsomt til glasdøren, hvor hun blev stående
med ryggen til stuen og se ut. Hun rev sit lommetørklæde op
