translation.text:
Besides, money had never been spared at the Castle; the sums were always large there. What, for example, did a dinner like that not cost! But now it was to look empty everywhere, even in the lady of the Castle’s familiar jewel case, and therefore the son-in-law’s money was to restore the splendour.

How much does he have, one wonders?

Oh, fie, he has such an unfathomable amount of money.

Johannes rose again and went down into the garden. The lilacs were in bloom; streams of fragrance from auriculas and narcissi, jasmines and lilies of the valley met him. He sought out a corner down by the wall and sat on a stone; a thicket concealed him from all the world. He was exhausted by emotion, weary as a slave, his reason darkened; he thought of getting up and going home, but remained sitting there, dull and listless. Then he heard murmuring farther along the gravel path; someone was coming, and he recognized Victoria’s voice. He held his breath and waited a little; then the lieutenant’s uniform also flashed through the foliage. The betrothed couple were walking together.

I do not think, he said, that this quite adds up. You listen to what he says, you sit there concerning yourself with his speech and cry out. What did that really mean?

She stopped and stood tall before him.

Do you want to know? she said.

Yes.

She was silent.

It is all the same to me if it meant nothing, he continued. Then you need not say it.

She subsided again.

No, it meant nothing, she replied.

They began walking again. The lieutenant nervously shrugged his epaulettes and said loudly:

He ought to watch himself a little. Otherwise an officer’s hand might box his ears.

They took the path to the summerhouse.

Johannes remained sitting on the stone for a while, dull and tormented as before. Everything was beginning to be a matter of indifference to him. The lieutenant had grown suspicious of him, and his fiancée had given an account of herself on the spot. She said what had to be said, set the officer’s heart at rest, and walked on with him. And the starlings chattered in the branches above their heads. Indeed. May God grant them a long life.... He had spoken on her behalf at dinner and torn out his heart; it had cost him dearly to put right and cover over her insolent interruption, and she had not thanked him for it. She had seized her glass and drunk. Cheers, look at me, how prettily I drink.... For that matter, look at a woman from the side when she drinks. Let her drink from a cup, from a glass, from anything at all, but look at her from the side. She puts on such airs that it is dreadful. She purses her mouth and dips its outermost rim into the drink, and she is in despair if, while she does so, anyone notices her hand. On the whole, do not look at a woman’s hand. She cannot bear it; she capitulates. At once she begins drawing her hand back, placing it in an ever more beautiful position, all to conceal a wrinkle, a crookedness in the fingers, or a less well-shaped nail. In the end she can bear it no longer, but asks, beside herself: what are you looking at?.... She had once kissed him, once, one summer. It was so long ago; God knows whether it had even been true. How was it—had they not been sitting on a bench? They talked together for a long time, and when they left he came so very close to her that he touched her arm. Outside an entrance she kissed him. I love you! she said.... Now they had passed by; perhaps they were still sitting in the summerhouse. The lieutenant would box his ears, he had said. He had heard it perfectly well; he was not asleep, but neither did he rise and step forward. An officer’s hand, he had said. Indeed, it was a matter of indifference to him....

He rose from the stone and followed them to the summerhouse. It was empty. Up by the veranda of the main building, Camilla stood calling to him; would he please come, there was coffee in the garden room. He followed her. The betrothed couple were sitting in the garden room; several others were present as well. He was given his coffee, stepped back, and found himself a place.

Camilla began talking to him. Her face was so bright, and she looked at him with open eyes; he could not resist her, he joined in the conversation, answered her questions, and laughed. Where had he been? In the garden? That was not true at all; she had searched in the garden and had not found him. Far from it, he had not been in the garden.

Was he in the garden, Victoria? she asked.

Victoria replied:

No, I did not see him.

The lieutenant cast her an embittered glance and, to give his fiancée a warning, said unnecessarily loudly across to the landowner:

Was it the case that you wished to take me woodcock shooting at your estate?

Yes indeed, the landowner replied. You are welcome.

The lieutenant looked at Victoria. She said nothing and remained sitting as before, making no effort whatever to dissuade him from this woodcock shoot at the landowner’s estate. His face grew darker and darker; he stroked his moustache with nervous movements.

Camilla addressed another question to Victoria.

Then the lieutenant rose with a sudden movement and said to the landowner:

Very well, then I shall go with you tonight, at once.

With that he left the room.

The landowner and some others followed.

There was a brief pause.

Suddenly the door opened and the lieutenant entered again. He was in a state of extreme agitation.

Have you forgotten something? Victoria asked, rising.

He took a few bounding steps by the door, as though unable to stand still, and went straight over to Johannes, whom, as if in passing, he struck with his hand. Then he ran back to the door and continued hopping about.

Take care, man, you struck me in the eye, Johannes said, laughing hollowly.

You are mistaken, the lieutenant replied. I boxed your ear. Do you understand? Do you understand?

Johannes reached for his handkerchief, wiped his eye, and said:

You do not mean that. You know I can fold you double and put you in my pocket.

At that same moment he rose.

Then the lieutenant hastily opened the door and stepped outside.

I do mean it! he shouted back. I mean it, you nag!

Then he slammed the door with a crash.

Johannes sat down again.

Victoria was still standing approximately in the middle of the floor. She looked at him and was pale as a corpse.

Did he strike you? Camilla asked in the greatest astonishment.

By accident. He caught me in the eye. Would you like to see?

God, it is red; there is blood. No, do not rub it; let me pour water on it. Your handkerchief is so coarse—here, take it back; I shall use my own. Did anyone ever see the like, right in the eye!

Victoria also held out her handkerchief. She said nothing. Then she walked very slowly to the glass door, where she remained standing with her back to the room, looking out. She tore her handkerchief into small strips. A few minutes later she opened the door and left the garden room, silent and mute.

Så gik han ut i byen. Hun var kanske å træffe, å opdage,
hun sat kanske i en vogn. Han vandret om til om aftenen.
Utenfor teatret så han hende, han hilste, smilte og hilste, og
hun besvarte hans hilsen. Han vilde træde frem til hende, det
var nogen skridt, — da ser han at hun ikke er alene, hun har
Otto med sig, kammerherrens søn. Han var i Iøitnants uniform.

Johannes tænkte: nu gir hun mig kanske et vink, et lite tegn
med øinene? Hun skyndte sig ind i teatret, rød, med lutende
hode, som om hun vilde gjæmme sig.

Kanske kunde han se hende derinde? Han fik billet og
gik ind.

Han visste av kammerherrens loge, javel, disse rike mennes-
ker de hadde loge. Der sat hun i al sin herlighet og så sig
omkring. Så hun på ham? Aldrig!

Da akten var ute passet han hende op ute på gangen. Han
hilste igjen; hun så på ham litt forundret og nikket.

Det er her inde du kan få vand, sa Otto og pekte fremover.

De gik forbi.

Johannes så efter dem. En underlig dæmring la sig for hans
øine. Alle disse mennesker var ærgerlige på ham og puffet
ham; han bad mekanisk om forlatelse og blev stående. Der for-
svandt hun.

Da hun kom tilbake bukket han dypt for hende og sa:

Undskyld, frøken .

Otto svarte og så mysende på ham.

Det er Johannes, sa hun præsenterende. Kjender du ham
igjen?

De vil formodentlig vite hvorledes det står til hjemme, ved-
blev hun og hendes ansigt var skjønt og rolig. Jeg vet virkelig
ikke, men det er visst godt. Utmærket. Jeg skal hilse møllerens.

Tak. Reiser frøkenen snart?

En av dagene. Joda, jeg skal hilse.

Hun nikket og gik.

Johannes så igjen efter hende til hun var forsvundet, så begav
han sig ut. En evig vandring, en tung og trist gang gate op
og gate ned slog tiden ihjæl. Klokken ti stod han utenfor
kammerherrens og ventet. Nu sluttet teatrene snart, nu kom
hun. Han kunde kanske åpne vogndøren, ta hatten av, åpne
vogndøren og bøle sig til jorden.

Endelig en halv time senere kom hun. Kunde han bli stående
der ved porten og igjen bringe sig i erindring? Han ilet op-
over gaten og så sig ikke om. Han hørte at porten hos kam-
merherrens gik op, at vognen kjørte ind og at porten atter sloges
i. Da vendte han om.

Nu vedblev han å drive frem og tilbake foran huset i en
time. Han ventet ikke på nogen og hadde intet ærend. Plud-
selig åpnes porten indenfra og Victoria stiger igjen ut på gaten.
Hun har ikke hat på og har bare kastet et sjal over akslerne.
Hun smiler halvt rædd, halvt forlegen og spør til en
begyndelse:

Går De her og tænker?

Nei, svarer han. Om jeg tænker? Nei jeg går her bare.

Jeg så Dem gå op og ned her utenfor og så vilde jeg ....
jeg så Dem fra mit vindu. Jeg må ind igjen straks.

Tak fordi De kom, Victoria. Jeg var så fortvilet for litt siden
og nu er det over. Undskyld at jeg hilste på Dem i teatret; jeg
har desværre også spurt efter Dem her hos kammerherrens,
jeg vilde træffe Dem og få vite hvad De mente, hvad Deres
mening er.

Ja, sa hun, det vet De jo. Jeg sa så meget iforgårs at det
kunde De ikke misforstå.

Jeg er endnu like uviss på alt.

Lat os ikke snakke mere om det. Jeg har sagt nok, jeg har
sagt meget formeget og jeg gjør dem ondt nu. Jeg elsker Dem,
Jeg løi ikke iforgårs og lyver ikke nu; men det er så meget
som skiller os. Jeg holder meget av Dem, taler gjærne med
Dem, heller med Dem end nogen anden, men.... Ja jeg tør
ikke stå her længer, de kan se os fra vinduerne. Johannes, det
er så mange grunde som De ikke kjender, så De skal ikke be
mig mere om å si hvad jeg mener. Jeg har tænkt på det nat og
dag; jeg mener hvad jeg har sagt. Men det blir umulig.

Hvad blir umulig?

Det hele. Altsammen. Hør, Johannes, lat mig slippe å være
stolt for os begge.

Javel. Godt, det skal De slippe! Men altså narret De mig
iforgårs. Det gik således til at De traf mig på gaten og så var
De i god stemning og så ....

Hun vendte sig og vilde gå ind.

Har jeg gjort noget galt? spurte han. Hans ansigt var blekt
og ukjendelig. Jeg mener, hvormed har jeg forspildt Deres ....?
Har jeg på disse to dager og to nætter forbrutt noget?

Nei. Det er ikke det. Jeg har bare tænkt det over; har ikke
De det? Det har hele tiden været umulig, vet De. Jeg holder
av Dem, sætter pris på Dem ....

Og agter Dem.
Hun ser på ham, hans smil krænker hende og hun fortsætter
hæftigere:

Herregud, forstår De ikke selv at papa vilde nægte Dem
det? Hvorfor tvinger De mig til å si det? De skjønner det selv.
Hvad skulde det ha blit til? Har jeg ikke ret?

Pause.
Jo, svarer han.
Desuten, vedblir hun, det er så mange grunde .... Nei De

må virkelig ikke komme efter mig til teatret mere, jeg blev
rædd for Dem. Det må De aldrig mere.

Nei, sier han.

Hun tar hans hånd.

Kan De ikke komme hjem en tur? Jeg vilde glæde mig meget
til det. Hvor Deres hånd er varm; jeg fryser. Nei nu må jeg
gå. Godnat.

Godnat, svarer han.

Gaten lå kold og grå opover byen, den så ut som et bælte

en bitte liten femkrone i guld, en gave, og gik videre. Kort

ti år sitter stille og ser på; han har gamle blå øine som følger
leken, hule kinder og en firkantet hake og på hodet bar han
en lue av lærred. Det var foret av en lue. Dette barn brukte
paryk, en hårsykdom hadde vansiret dette hode for bestandig.
Hans sjæl var kanske også aldeles vissen.

Alt dette la han mærke til skjønt han ikke hadde nogen klar
forestilling om på hvilken kant av byen han befandt sig eller
hvorhen han gik. Det begyndte også å regne, han kjendte det
ikke og slog ikke sin paraply op skjønt han hadde båret den
med sig den hele dag.

Da han omsider kom til en plass hvor det stod bænker gik
han hen og satte sig. Det regnet mere og mere, han slog ube-
visst paraplyen op og blev sittende. Efter kort tid overfaldt ham
en uovervindelig døsighet, hans hjærne lå i tåke, han lukket
øinene og begyndte å nikke og sove.

En stund efter våknet han ved at nogen forbigående talte
høit. Han reiste sig og drev videre. Hans hjærne var blit kla-
rere, han husket hvad som var foregåt, alle hændelser, endog
gutten som han gav fem kroner for en rose. Han forestilte sig
den lille herres henrykkelse når han opdaget denne forunderlige
mynt blandt sine skillinger, at det ikke var en femogtyve øre,
men en femkrone i guld. Gå med Gud!

Then he went out into the city. Perhaps she was to be met, to be discovered; perhaps she was sitting in a carriage. He wandered about until evening.

Outside the theatre he saw her; he bowed, smiled and bowed, and she returned his greeting. He was about to step forward to her—it was only a few paces—when he sees that she is not alone; she has Otto with her, the chamberlain’s son. He was in a lieutenant’s uniform.

Johannes thought: perhaps now she will give me a hint, a little sign with her eyes? She hurried into the theatre, red, with bowed head, as though she wished to hide.

Perhaps he could see her in there? He obtained a ticket and went in.

He knew about the chamberlain’s box; yes indeed, these rich people had a box. There she sat in all her splendour and looked about her. Did she look at him? Never!

When the act was over, he waited for her out in the corridor. He bowed again; she looked at him with a little surprise and nodded.

It is in here that you can get water, said Otto, pointing ahead.

They went past.

Johannes looked after them. A strange dimness settled before his eyes. All these people were angry with him and jostled him; he mechanically begged their pardon and remained standing. There she disappeared.

When she came back, he bowed deeply to her and said:

Excuse me, miss.

Otto answered and looked at him through narrowed eyes.

This is Johannes, she said by way of introduction. Do you remember him?

You presumably wish to know how things are at home, she continued, and her face was beautiful and calm. I really do not know, but I am sure all is well. Excellent. I shall give the miller’s family your regards.

Thank you. Will you be leaving soon, miss?

One of these days. Yes, I shall give them your regards.

She nodded and left.

Johannes again looked after her until she had disappeared, then went outside. An endless wandering, a heavy and sorrowful tramping up one street and down another, killed the time. At ten o’clock he stood outside the chamberlain’s house and waited. The theatres would soon be letting out; now she would come. Perhaps he could open the carriage door, take off his hat, open the carriage door and bow himself to the ground.

At last, half an hour later, she came. Could he remain standing there by the gate and once more bring himself to her notice? He hurried up the street and did not look back. He heard the gate at the chamberlain’s house open, the carriage drive in and the gate slam shut again. Then he turned around.

Now he continued pacing back and forth in front of the house for an hour. He was waiting for no one and had no errand. Suddenly the gate opens from within and Victoria steps out into the street again. She has no hat on and has merely thrown a shawl over her shoulders. She smiles, half frightened, half embarrassed, and begins by asking:

Are you walking here thinking?

No, he answers. Am I thinking? No, I am only walking here.

I saw you walking up and down out here, and so I wanted to.... I saw you from my window. I must go back in at once.

Thank you for coming, Victoria. I was so desperate a little while ago, and now it is over. Forgive me for greeting you at the theatre; unfortunately I have also asked for you here at the chamberlain’s house. I wanted to meet you and learn what you meant, what your opinion is.

Yes, she said, you already know that. I said so much the day before yesterday that you could not have misunderstood it.

I am still just as uncertain about everything.

Let us not speak of it any more. I have said enough; I have said far too much, and I am hurting you now. I love you. I did not lie the day before yesterday and I am not lying now; but there is so much that separates us. I am very fond of you, I like speaking with you, with you rather than with anyone else, but.... Yes, I dare not stand here any longer; they can see us from the windows. Johannes, there are so many reasons that you do not know, so you must not ask me any more to say what I mean. I have thought about it night and day; I mean what I have said. But it will be impossible.

What will be impossible?

The whole thing. All of it. Listen, Johannes, spare me from having to be proud for both of us.

Very well. Good, you shall be spared that! But then you deceived me the day before yesterday. What happened was that you met me in the street and then you were in good spirits and then....

She turned and was about to go inside.

Have I done something wrong? he asked. His face was pale and unrecognisable. I mean, by what have I forfeited your....? During these two days and two nights, have I committed some offence?

No. That is not it. I have merely thought it over; have you not? It has been impossible all along, you know. I am fond of you, esteem you....

And respect me.

She looks at him; his smile wounds her, and she continues more vehemently:

My God, do you not understand for yourself that Papa would refuse you that? Why do you force me to say it? You understand it yourself. What could it have come to? Am I not right?

A pause.

Yes, he answers.

Besides, she continues, there are so many reasons.... No, you really must not follow me to the theatre any more; I became frightened of you. You must never do that again.

No, he says.

She takes his hand.

Could you not come home for a visit? I should be very glad of it. How warm your hand is; I am freezing. No, now I must go. Good night.

Good night, he answers.

The street lay cold and grey uphill through the city; it looked like a belt of sand, an endless road to walk. He came upon a boy selling old, ruined roses; he called to him, took a rose, gave the boy a tiny five-kroner gold coin as a gift, and walked on. Shortly afterward he saw a cluster of children playing by a gate. A ten-year-old boy sits quietly watching; he has old blue eyes that follow the game, hollow cheeks and a square chin, and on his head he wore a cap of canvas. It was the lining of a cap. This child wore a wig; a disease of the hair had disfigured this head for good. Perhaps his soul too was utterly withered.

He noticed all this although he had no clear notion of which part of the city he was in or where he was going. It began to rain as well; he did not notice it and did not put up his umbrella, although he had carried it with him all day.

When at last he came to a square where there were benches, he went over and sat down. It rained more and more; unconsciously he put up the umbrella and remained sitting. After a short while an irresistible drowsiness came over him; his brain lay in a fog, he closed his eyes and began to nod and sleep.

After a while he awoke when some passers-by spoke loudly. He rose and drifted onward. His brain had grown clearer; he remembered what had happened, every event, even the boy to whom he had given five kroner for a rose. He imagined the little gentleman’s delight when he discovered this remarkable coin among his small change, that it was not a twenty-five-øre piece, but a five-kroner gold coin. Go with God!

wide.text:
Det går uker og måneder igjen og våren kom. Sneen var
allerede borte, det bruste langt ute i rummet som av løste
vande fra solen til månen. Svalerne var kommet og i skogen
utenfor byen våknet et spillende liv av alle slags hoppende dyr
og fugler med fremmede tungemål. En fersk og søtlig lukt
svævet op fra jorden.

Hans arbeide har varet den ganske vinter. Som en opsang
hadde poplernes tørre grener knirket mot husvæggen nat og
dag; nu var våren kommet, stormene var forbi og stampeværket
hadde knaket istå.

Han åpner vinduet og ser ut, gaten er allerede rolig skjønt
det ikke er midnat, stjærnerne blinker på en himmel uten
skyer, det tegner til en varm og lys dag den dag imorgen. Han
hører buldret fra byen som blander sig med det evige brus i det
fjærne. Pludselig skingrer en jærnbanepipe, det er nattogets
signal; det lyder som et enkelt hanegal i den stille nat. Nu er
tiden til arbeide inde, denne togfløite har været som et bud
til ham i hele vinter.

Og han lukker vinduet og sætter sig ved bordet igjen. Han
kaster de bøker han har læst i tilside og finder papirerne frem.
Han griper pennen.

Nu er hans store arbeide næsten færdig, det mangler bare
et slutningskapitel, en hilsen som fra et bortseilende skib, og
han har det allerede i hodet:

Det sitter en herre i et gjæstgiversted ved veien, han er på
gjennemreise og skal langt, langt ut i verden. Han er grå i hår
og skjæg og det er gåt mange år hen over ham; men han er
stor og stærk endnu og han er næppe så gammel som han ser
ut. Utenfor står hans vogn, hestene hviler, kusken er glad og
fornøiet; for han har fåt vin og mat av den fremmede. Da
herren har indskrevet sit navn kjender værten ham og bøier sig
for ham og viser ham megen ære. Hvem lever på Slottet nu?
spør herren. Værten svarer: Kapteinen, han er meget rik; fruen
er god mot alle. Mot alle? spør herren sig selv og smiler sælsomt,
også mot mig? Og herren sætter sig til å skrive på et papir
og da det er utskrevet læser han det over, det er et dikt, tungt
og rolig, men med mange bitre ord. Men bakefter river han
papiret istykker og han vedblir å sitte der og rive papiret endnu
mere istykker. Da banker det på hans dør og en gulklædt
kvinde træder ind. Hun slår sløret op, det er slotsfruen, fru
Victoria. Hun er som en majestæt. Herren reiser sig brat, hans
mørke sjæl blir som beskinnet av en lystre-ild i samme nu. De
er så god mot alle, sier han bitter, De kommer også til mig. Hun
svarer ikke, hun står bare og ser på ham og hendes ansigt blir
dunkelt rødt. Hvad vil De? spør han like så bittert som før: er
De kommet for å minde mig om det forbigangne? for så er det
siste gang, nådige frue, nu reiser jeg for altid. Og fremdeles
svarer ikke den unge slotsfrue, men hendes mund bæver. Han
sier: Er det Dem ikke nok at jeg har erkjendt min dårskap én
gang, så hør, jeg gjør det igjen: min hu stod til Dem, jeg var
Dem ikke værdig, — er De nu tilfreds? Han fortsætter med sti-
gende hæftighet: De svarte mig nei, De tok en anden; jeg var
en bonde, en bjørn, en barbar som i min ungdom var tumlet
ind på en kongelig vildtbane! Men da kaster herren sig på
en stol og hulker og ber: Å, gål tilgiv mig, gå Deres veil Nu er
al rødme veket fra slotsfruens ansigt. Så sier hun og hun uttaler
ordene så langsomt og vel: Jeg elsker Dem; misforstå mig ikke
mere, det er Dem jeg elsker; farvel! Og det var sig den unge slots-
frue, hun la hænderne for ansigtet og gik hurtig ut av døren ....

Han lægger pennen ned og læner sig tilbake. Javel, punktum,
ende. Der lå boken, alle de beskrevne blade, ni måneders ar-
beide. En varm tilfredshet risler gjennem ham fordi hans værk
er ført tilende. Og mens han sitter der og ser mot vinduet
hvorigjennem dagen gryr summer og banker det i hans hode og
hans ånd arbeider videre. Han er fuld av stemning, hans hjærne
ligger som en uhøstet vild have hvor det damper av jorden:

Han er på en hemmelighetsfuld måte kommet ind i en dyp,
utdødd dal hvor intet levende findes. Langt borte, alene og
efterglemt står et orgel og spiller. Han går det nærmere, han
undersøker det, orglet blør, det rinder blod ut av dets ene side
mens det spiller. Længer fremme kommer han til et torv. Der
er alt øde, intet træ ses og ingen lyd høres, det er bare et øde
torv. Men på sandet er det mærker efter folks sko og i luften
står likesom endnu de siste ord som var uttalt på stedet, så nylig
var det forlatt. En sælsom fornemmelse opfylder ham, disse
ord som står igjen i luften over torvet ængster ham, kommer
ham nærmere, trykker ham. Han slår dem bort fra sig og de
kommer igjen, det er ikke ord, det er oldinger, en gruppe
oldinger som danser; han ser dem nu. Hvorfor danser de og
hvorfor er de ikke det minste glade når de danser? Det står
et koldt gust ut fra dette selskap av gamle, de ser ham ikke,
de er blinde, og da han roper til dem hører de ham ikke,
de er døde. Han vandrer mot østen, mot solen, han kommer til
et berg. En røst roper: Er du ved et berg? Ja, svarer han, jeg
står ved et berg. Da sier røsten: Det berg du står ved er min
fot; jeg ligger bundet i det ytterste land, kom og løs mig!
Så begir han sig avsted til det ytterste land. Ved en bro står
en mand og passer ham op, han samler skygger ind; manden
er av moskus. En isnende rædsel griper ham ved synet av denne
mand som vil ta hans skygge. Han spytter imot ham og truer
ham med knyttede hænder, men manden står urørlig og venter
på ham. Vend om! roper en røst bak ham. Han vender sig og
ser et hode som triller avsted på veien og viser ham retningen.
Hodet er et menneskes hode og nu og da ler det stille og tyst.
Han følger det. Det triller i dager og nætter og han følger det;
ved havbredden smutter det ned i jorden og gjæmmer sig. Han
vader ut i havet og dukker. Han står ved en vældig port og
han møter en stor, gjøende fisk. Den har faks på halsen og den
gjør imot ham som en hund. Bak fisken står Victoria. Han
strækker hænderne ut mot hende, hun har ingen klær på, hun
ler imot ham og det blåser en storm gjennem hendes hår. Da
roper han til hende, han hører selv sit skrik — og våkner.

Johannes reiser sig og går til vinduet. Det er blit næsten lyst
og i det lille speil på vindusposten ser han at hans tindinger
er røde. Han slukker lampen og læser endnu en gang i det grå
lys av dagen den siste side i sin bok. Så lægger han sig.
Ut på eftermiddagen den samme dag hadde Johannes betalt
sit værelse, leveret sit manuskript og forlatt byen. Han var
reist utenlands, ingen visste hvorhen.

translation.text:
Weeks and months pass again, and spring came. The snow was already gone; far out in space there was a roaring as of waters released from the sun to the moon. The swallows had come, and in the forest outside the town a lively life awoke, of all kinds of leaping animals and birds with foreign tongues. A fresh, sweetish smell drifted up from the earth.

His work has lasted the whole winter. Like a work song, the poplars’ dry branches had creaked against the wall of the house night and day; now spring had come, the storms were past, and the stamping mill had creaked to a halt.

He opens the window and looks out; the street is already quiet although it is not midnight, the stars twinkle in a cloudless sky, and tomorrow promises to be a warm and bright day. He hears the rumble from the town mingling with the eternal roar in the distance. Suddenly a railway whistle shrills; it is the night train’s signal; it sounds like a single cockcrow in the still night. Now the time for work has come; this train whistle has been like a summons to him all winter.

And he closes the window and sits down at the table again. He throws aside the books he has been reading and brings out the papers. He takes up the pen.

Now his great work is almost finished; it lacks only a final chapter, a greeting as though from a ship sailing away, and he already has it in his head:

A gentleman is sitting in an inn by the road; he is passing through and is going far, far out into the world. His hair and beard are gray, and many years have passed over him; but he is still big and strong, and he is hardly as old as he looks. Outside stands his carriage, the horses are resting, the coachman is happy and content; for the stranger has given him wine and food. When the gentleman has entered his name, the innkeeper recognizes him and bows to him and shows him great honor. Who lives at the Castle now? the gentleman asks. The innkeeper answers: The Captain; he is very rich; his wife is good to everyone. To everyone? the gentleman asks himself and smiles strangely, to me as well? And the gentleman sits down to write on a piece of paper, and when it is filled he reads it over; it is a poem, grave and calm, but with many bitter words. But afterward he tears the paper to pieces, and he continues to sit there and tear the paper into still smaller pieces. Then there is a knock at his door, and a woman clad in yellow enters. She lifts her veil; it is the lady of the Castle, Mrs. Victoria. She is like a majesty. The gentleman rises abruptly; his dark soul is as though lit by a flash of lightning at that very moment. You are so good to everyone, he says bitterly; You come to me as well. She does not answer; she merely stands and looks at him, and her face turns a dusky red. What do You want? he asks, just as bitterly as before: have You come to remind me of what is past? For then it is for the last time, gracious lady; now I am leaving forever. And still the young lady of the Castle does not answer, but her mouth trembles. He says: Is it not enough for You that I have acknowledged my folly once? Then hear me, I do so again: my heart was set on You, I was not worthy of You—are You satisfied now? He continues with mounting vehemence: You answered me no, You took another; I was a peasant, a bear, a barbarian who in his youth had blundered into a royal game preserve! But then the gentleman throws himself onto a chair and sobs and begs: Oh, go! Forgive me, go Your way! Now all the flush has left the lady of the Castle’s face. Then she says, pronouncing the words so slowly and distinctly: I love You; misunderstand me no longer, it is You whom I love; farewell! And the young lady of the Castle turned away; she put her hands over her face and went quickly out of the door....

He puts down the pen and leans back. Yes, full stop, the end. There lay the book, all the written pages, nine months’ work. A warm satisfaction ripples through him because his work has been brought to completion. And while he sits there looking toward the window through which day is dawning, it hums and pounds in his head, and his spirit continues to work. He is full of feeling; his brain lies like an unharvested wild garden from whose earth steam rises:

In some mysterious way he has entered a deep, extinct valley where no living thing is to be found. Far away, alone and forgotten, an organ stands playing. He goes nearer to it, he examines it; the organ is bleeding, blood runs from one of its sides while it plays. Farther on he comes to a square. Everything there is deserted; no tree can be seen and no sound can be heard; it is merely an empty square. But in the sand are marks left by people’s shoes, and the last words spoken in the place seem still to remain in the air, so recently was it abandoned. A strange sensation fills him; these words remaining in the air above the square distress him, come nearer to him, press upon him. He strikes them away from himself and they return; they are not words, they are old men, a group of old men dancing; he sees them now. Why are they dancing, and why are they not in the least happy when they dance? A cold, ghastly air emanates from this company of old men; they do not see him, they are blind, and when he calls to them they do not hear him, they are dead. He wanders toward the east, toward the sun; he comes to a mountain. A voice calls: Are you beside a mountain? Yes, he answers, I am standing beside a mountain. Then the voice says: The mountain beside which you stand is my foot; I lie bound in the outermost land; come and free me!

Then he sets out for the outermost land. By a bridge a man stands lying in wait for him; he collects shadows; the man is made of musk. An icy terror grips him at the sight of this man who means to take his shadow. He spits at him and threatens him with clenched fists, but the man stands motionless and waits for him. Turn back! a voice calls behind him. He turns and sees a head rolling along the road and showing him the direction. The head is a human head, and now and then it laughs softly and soundlessly. He follows it. It rolls for days and nights, and he follows it; at the seashore it slips down into the earth and hides. He wades out into the sea and dives. He stands before a mighty gate and encounters a large, barking fish. It has a mane on its neck and barks at him like a dog. Behind the fish stands Victoria. He stretches his hands out toward her; she has no clothes on, she laughs toward him, and a storm blows through her hair. Then he calls out to her, he himself hears his scream—and wakes.

Johannes rises and goes to the window. It has grown almost light, and in the little mirror on the window jamb he sees that his temples are red. He puts out the lamp and, once more, in the gray light of day, reads the last page of his book. Then he lies down.

By the afternoon of that same day Johannes had paid for his room, delivered his manuscript, and left the town. He had gone abroad; no one knew where.

wide.text:
Men efter å ha talt om mange slags kjærlighet fortæller
munken Vendt om endnu en slags og sier:

For så berusende er en egen slags kjærlighet!

Det unge herskap er just kommet hjem, deres lange bryllups-
reise er tilende og de begir sig til ro.

Et stjærneskudd brændte av over deres tak.

Om sommeren spaserte det unge herskap sammen og vek
ikke fra hverandres side. De plukket gule, røde og blå blomster
som de gav hverandre, de så græsset bevæge sig i vinden og
hørte fuglene synge i skogene og hvert ord de talte var som
kjærtegn. Om vinteren kjørte de med bjælder på hestene og
himlen var blå og høit oppe suset stjærnerne avsted på de
evige sletter.

Således gik mange, mange år. Det unge herskap fik tre børn
og deres hjærter elsket hverandre som den første dag under det
første kyss.

Da får den stolte herre sin sykdom, denne sykdom som læn-
ket ham til sengen så længe og satte hans hustrus tålmodighet
på så hård prøve. Den dag han blev frisk og stod op av sengen
kjendte han ikke sig selv igjen; sykdommen hadde vansiret
ham og tat hans hår.

Han led og grublet. En morgen så sa han:

Nu elsker du mig vel ikke mere?

Men hans hustru slog rødmende sine armer om ham og kys-
set ham så lidenskapelig som i ungdommens vår og svarte:

Jeg, jeg elsker, elsker dig bestandig. Jeg glemmer aldrig at det
var mig og ingen anden som du tok og som blev så lyk-
kelig.

Og hun gik ind i sit kammers og klippet alt sit gule hår av
hodet for å være lik sin mand som hun elsket.

Og det gik atter mange, mange år, det unge herskap blev
gammelt og deres børn var voksne. Hver lykke delte de som
før; om sommeren gik de endnu på markerne og så græsset
bølge og om vinteren hyllet de sig i sine pelser og kjørte under
stjærnehimlen. Og deres hjærter vedblev å være varme og
glade som av forunderlig vin.

Da blev fruen lam. Den gamle frue kunde ikke gå på sine
føtter, hun måtte trækkes i en stol med hjul og herren selv
trak hende. Men fruen led så usigelig ved sin ulykke og hendes
ansigt fik dype furer av sorg.

Da sa hun en dag:

Nu vilde jeg gjærne dø. Jeg er så lam og hæslig og dit ansigt
er så skjønt, du kan ikke kysse mig mere og du kan ikke elske
mig som før.

Men herren omfavner hende rød av bevægelse og svarer:

Jeg, jeg elsker dig mere, mere end mit liv, du kjære, elsker
dig som den første dag, den første stund da du gav mig rosen.
Husker du det? Du rakte mig rosen og så på mig med dine
skjønne øine; rosen duftet som du, du rødmet som den og jeg
blev beruset i alle mine sanser. Men endnu mere elsker jeg dig
nu, du er skjønnere end i din ungdom og mit hjærte takker og
velsigner dig for hver dag du har været min.

Herren går ind i sit kammers, slår syre i sit ansigt for å
vanskape det og sier til sin hustru:

Jeg hadde det uheld å få syre i mit ansigt, mine kinder er
fulde av brandsår og du elsker mig vel ikke mere?

O, du min brudgom, min elskede! stammer den gamle kvinde
og kysser hans hænder. Du er skjønnere end nogen mand på
jorden, din røst gjør mig endnu den dag idag het i hjærtet
og jeg elsker dig til døden.

XIII

Johannes træffer Camilla på gaten; hun er sammen med sin
mor, sin far og ung Richmond; de stanser sin vogn og taler
venlig med ham.

Camilla griper hans arm og sier:

Du kom ikke til os. Vi hadde stor fest, kan du tro; vi ventet
på dig til det siste, men du kom ikke.

Jeg var forhindret, svarte han.

Undskyld at jeg ikke har været oppe hos dig siden, vedblev
hun. Nu kommer jeg en av dagene, ganske sikkert, når Rich-
mond er reist. Å for en fest vi hadde! Victoria blev syk, hun blev
kjørt hjem, har du hørt det? Nu går jeg snart op til hende.
Hun er visst meget bedre, kanske aldeles frisk igjen. Jeg har
foræret Richmond en medaljon næsten maken til din. Hør, Jo-
hannes, du skal love mig å passe din ovn; når du skriver glem-
mer du alt og det blir iskoldt hos dig. Da skal du ringe på
piken.
Ja jeg skal ringe på piken, svarte han.

Også fru Seier talte til ham, spurte om hans arbeide, om
stykket om Slægten; hvordan gik det? Hun ventet med længsel
det næste fra ham.

Johannes gav de nødvendige svar, hilste meget dypt og så
vognen kjøre. Hvor lite det hele vedkom ham, denne vogn,
disse mennesker, denne snak! En tom og kold stemning drog
ind i ham og fulgte ham på hele hjemveien. Ved hans port
gik en mand og drev frem og tilbake på gaten, en gammel
bekjendt, den forhenværende huslærer på Slottet.

Johannes hilste til ham.

Han var klædt i en lang, varm frak som var omhyggelig
børstet og han hadde en kjæk og bestemt mine.

De ser her Deres ven og kollega, sa han. Ræk mig Deres
hånd, unge mand. Gud har ført mine veier vidunderlig siden
sist, jeg er gift, jeg har et hjem, en liten have, en hustru. Det
sker endnu mirakler i livet. Har De noget å bemærke til min
siste ytring?

ohannes ser forundret på ham.

Altså vedtat. Jo ser De, jeg læste med hendes søn. Hun har
en søn, poden er fra første ægteskap; hun har naturligvis været
gift før, hun var enke. Jeg giftet mig altså med en enke. De
kan indvende at dette ikke var sunget ved min vugge; men jeg
giftet mig altså med en enke. Poden hadde hun fra før. Jeg
går nemlig der og ser på haven og på enken og lever en tid-
lang med intense tanker desangående. Pludselig har jeg det
og jeg sier til mig selv: vel nok, det er ikke sunget ved din
vugge, og så videre; men jeg gjør det allikevel, jeg slår til, for
det er rimeligvis skrevet i stjærnerne. Se, således gik det til.

Gratulerer! sa Johannes.

Stop! ikke et ord mere! Jeg vet hvad De vil si. Og hun
den første, vil De nemlig si, har De glemt Deres ungdoms evige
kjærlighet? Akkurat dette vil De si. Tør da jeg på min side
spørre Dem, høistærede, hvor min første, eneste og evige kjær-
lighet blev av? Tok hun ikke en kaptein i artilleriet? Forøvrig
gjør jeg Dem et lite spørsmål til: har De nogensinde, nogen-
sinde set at en mand har fåt den han skulde ha? Ikke jeg. Det
går et sagn om en mand som Gud bønhørte i så måte, han
fik sin første og eneste kjærlighet. Men det blev ikke til nogen
videre herlighet for ham. Hvorfor ikke? vil De atter spørre,
og se, jeg svarer Dem: Nei av den lille grund at hun døde
straks efter — straks efter, hører De, ha-ha-ha, øieblikkelig efter.
Således er det altid. Naturligvis får man ikke den kvinde man
skulde ha; men hænder det en eneste gang av pur forbandet
ret og rimelighet så dør hun altså straks efter. Dikkedarer blir
det altid. Så er da manden henvist til å forhverve sig en anden
kjærlighet av bedst mulig sort og han behøver ikke å dø
av denne forandring. Jeg sier Dem, det er så viselig indrettet
av naturen at han utmærket holder det ut. Se bare til mig.

translation.text:
But after speaking of many kinds of love, the monk Vendt tells of yet another kind and says:

For so intoxicating is a peculiar kind of love!

The young master and mistress have just come home, their long honeymoon is over, and they retire for the night.

A shooting star flared above their roof.

In summer the young master and mistress walked together and never left each other’s side. They picked yellow, red, and blue flowers, which they gave to one another; they watched the grass move in the wind and heard the birds singing in the forests, and every word they spoke was like a caress. In winter they drove with bells on the horses, and the sky was blue, and high above, the stars rushed across the eternal plains.

Thus many, many years passed. The young master and mistress had three children, and their hearts loved one another as on the first day beneath the first kiss.

Then the proud master contracted his illness, the illness that chained him to his bed for so long and put his wife’s patience to so severe a test. The day he recovered and rose from his bed, he did not recognize himself; the illness had disfigured him and taken his hair.

He suffered and brooded. Then one morning he said:

Now you surely do not love me anymore?

But his wife, blushing, threw her arms around him and kissed him as passionately as in the springtime of youth, and answered:

I, I love, love you always. I never forget that it was me and no one else whom you chose, and who became so happy.

And she went into her chamber and cut all the yellow hair from her head so as to resemble her husband, whom she loved.

And again many, many years passed; the young master and mistress grew old, and their children were grown. They shared every happiness as before; in summer they still walked in the fields and watched the grass ripple, and in winter they wrapped themselves in their furs and drove beneath the starry sky. And their hearts continued to be warm and glad, as if from wondrous wine.

Then the mistress became paralyzed. The old mistress could not walk on her feet; she had to be pulled in a wheeled chair, and the master himself pulled her. But the mistress suffered so unspeakably in her misfortune, and her face acquired deep furrows of sorrow.

Then one day she said:

Now I should like to die. I am so paralyzed and hideous, and your face is so handsome; you can no longer kiss me, and you cannot love me as before.

But the master embraces her, red with emotion, and answers:

I, I love you more, more than my life, my dear; I love you as on the first day, the first moment when you gave me the rose. Do you remember? You held out the rose to me and looked at me with your beautiful eyes; the rose was fragrant like you, you blushed like it, and I became intoxicated in all my senses. But I love you even more now; you are more beautiful than in your youth, and my heart thanks and blesses you for every day you have been mine.

The master goes into his chamber, pours acid on his face to disfigure it, and says to his wife:

I had the misfortune of getting acid on my face; my cheeks are covered with burns, and surely you do not love me anymore?

Oh, you, my bridegroom, my beloved! stammers the old woman, and kisses his hands. You are more handsome than any man on earth; your voice still makes my heart burn even today, and I love you unto death.

XIII

Johannes meets Camilla in the street; she is with her mother, her father, and young Richmond; they stop their carriage and speak kindly with him.

Camilla takes hold of his arm and says:

You did not come to see us. We had a grand celebration, you may be sure; we waited for you until the very end, but you did not come.

I was prevented, he answered.

Forgive me for not having come up to see you since then, she continued. I shall come one of these days, quite certainly, when Richmond has left. Oh, what a celebration we had! Victoria became ill; she was driven home—have you heard? I shall soon go up to see her. She is surely much better, perhaps entirely well again. I have given Richmond a medallion almost like yours. Listen, Johannes, you must promise me to tend your stove; when you write, you forget everything, and it becomes ice-cold at your place. Then you must ring for the maid.

Yes, I shall ring for the maid, he answered.

Mrs. Seier also spoke to him, asking about his work, about the piece on The Family; how was it going? She was waiting eagerly for the next thing from him.

Johannes gave the necessary answers, bowed very deeply, and watched the carriage drive away. How little the whole thing concerned him—this carriage, these people, this talk! An empty, cold mood entered him and accompanied him all the way home. By his gate, a man was loitering back and forth in the street, an old acquaintance, the former private tutor at the Castle.

Johannes greeted him.

He was dressed in a long, warm coat that had been carefully brushed, and he wore a bold and resolute expression.

You see before You Your friend and colleague, he said. Give me Your hand, young man. God has guided my paths wondrously since last we met; I am married, I have a home, a little garden, a wife. Miracles still happen in life. Have You any comment to make on my last utterance?

ohannes looks at him in astonishment.

Then it is settled. You see, I tutored her son. She has a son; the brat is from her first marriage. Naturally, she had been married before; she was a widow. Thus I married a widow. She already had the brat. I go about there, you see, looking at the garden and the widow, and for some time I entertain intense thoughts on the subject. Suddenly it comes to me, and I say to myself: very well, it was not sung over your cradle, and so forth; but I do it all the same, I take the plunge, for it is probably written in the stars. See, that is how it happened.

Congratulations! said Johannes.

Stop! Not another word! I know what You mean to say. And the first one, You mean to say—have You forgotten the eternal love of Your youth? That is precisely what You mean to say. Then may I, for my part, ask You, most honored sir, what became of my first, only, and eternal love? Did she not take an artillery captain? Moreover, I shall ask You one more little question: have You ever, ever seen a man get the woman he was meant to have? I have not. There is a legend of a man whose prayer God answered in that respect: he got his first and only love. But it brought him no particular glory. Why not? You will ask again, and see, I answer You: No, for the simple reason that she died immediately afterward—immediately afterward, do You hear, ha-ha-ha, at once afterward. That is always how it is. Naturally, a man does not get the woman he was meant to have; but if, for once, it happens by sheer damned right and reason, then she dies immediately afterward. There are always complications. Thus the man is obliged to acquire another love of the best possible kind, and he need not die from this change. I tell You, nature has arranged it so wisely that he endures it splendidly. Just look at me.

sig drukken i lykke.

nogen har banket på hos ham. Han roper: Kom! En mand
træder ind.

Godmorgen! sier han imot den indtrædende.
Det er en ældre mand, han er blek og rasende og han bærer

og sang litt.

forstår De. Og endnu er det midt på natten.

også en gang til i nattens løp og gik nogen ganger rundt på
gulvet. Jeg var så glad.

Yes, he said, I wrote that. It was so long ago; it was one night, the poplars outside my window were rustling so when I wrote it. No, are you really putting it away again? Thank you! You put it away again. Oh! he exclaimed, enraptured, and his voice was quite low, just think that you are sitting no farther away than this. I feel your arm against mine; a warmth radiates from you. Many a time, when I was alone and thought of you, I froze with emotion; but now I am warm. The last time I was home you were lovely then too; but you are lovelier now. It is the eyes and the eyebrows, your smile—no, I do not know, it is everything, everything about you.

She smiled and looked at him with half-closed eyes; beneath the long lashes there was a dark blue shadow. She had a warm glow. She seemed to be prey to the highest joy and reached toward him with her hand in an unconscious movement.

Thank you! she said.

No, Victoria, do not thank me, he answered. His whole soul streamed toward her, and he wanted to say more, say more; it became confused outbursts, he was as though intoxicated. Yes, but Victoria, if you are a little fond of me.... I do not know, but say that you are, even if it is not so. Please. Oh, I should promise you to become something, become a great deal, almost an unheard-of amount. You have no idea what I could become; I ponder it sometimes and know that I am utterly full of deeds not yet done. Many a time it pours out of me; at night I pace up and down the floor of my room because I am full of visions. There is a man in the room next door; he cannot sleep, he knocks on the wall. When morning dawns he comes in to me and is furious. It does not matter, I do not care about him; for by then I have thought of you for so long that I feel you are with me. I go to the window and sing; it is beginning to grow a little light, the poplars rustle outside. Good night! I say to the day. It is meant for you. Now she is sleeping, I think, good night, God bless her! Then I lie down. So it goes, evening after evening. But I never believed that you were as lovely as you are. Now I will remember you like this when you leave; as you are now. I will remember you so clearly....

Are you not coming home?

No. I am not finished. Yes, I am coming. I am leaving now. I am not finished, but I will do all manner of things. Do you sometimes wander in the garden at home now? Do you ever go out in the evening? I could see you, I could perhaps have the chance to greet you; it is not for anything else. But if you are a little fond of me, if you can tolerate me, endure me, then say.... Grant me that joy.... Do you know, there is a palm that blossoms only once in its life, and yet it lives to be seventy years old, the talipot palm. But it blossoms only once. I am blossoming now. Yes, I will get some money and go home. I shall sell what I have written; you see, I am writing a large book, and I shall sell it now, at once tomorrow, everything I have finished. I shall get a good deal for it. Would you then want me to come home?

Thank you, thank you! Forgive me if I hope too much, believe too much; it is so lovely to believe an extraordinary amount. This is the happiest day I have lived....

He took off his hat and laid it beside him.

Victoria looked around; a lady was coming down the street, and farther up there was a woman with a basket. Victoria grew uneasy; she reached for her watch.

They walked on.

People say that you are going to marry the little girl, the girl, the one you rescued; what is her name?

Camilla, do you mean?

Camilla Seier. People say that you are going to marry her.

Is that so. Why do you ask? She is not grown up. I have been to her home; it is so large and rich, a palace like your own; I have been there many times. No, she is not grown up.

She is fifteen years old. I have met her; we have spent time together. I became very fond of her. How lovely she is!

I am not going to marry her, he said.

Oh, you are not.

He looked at her. A twitch passed over his face.

But why are you saying this now? Do you wish to direct my attention to someone else?

She walked on with rapid steps and did not answer. They were outside the chamberlain’s house. She took his hand and pulled him through the gateway and up the stairs.

I am not going in, he said, half astonished.

She pressed the bell; she turned toward him, and her breast heaved.

I love you, she said. Do you understand that? It is you I love.

Suddenly she pulled him quickly down the stairs again, three, four steps, threw her arms around him, and kissed him. She trembled against him.

It is you I love, she said.

The entrance door opened above. She tore herself free and hurried up the stairs.

IV

It is drawing toward morning; day is dawning, a bluish, trembling September morning.

The poplars in the garden murmur softly. A window opens; a man leans out of it and hums. He has no coat on; he looks out into the world like an undressed madman who tonight has drunk himself drunk on happiness.

He suddenly turns away from the window and looks toward his door; someone has knocked. He calls: Come in! A man enters.

Good morning! he says to the man entering.
He is an elderly man; he is pale and furious, and he carries a lamp because it is not yet quite light.

Once again I must ask you, Mr. Møller, Mr. Johannes Møller, whether you consider this reasonable, the man stammers bitterly.

No, Johannes answers, you are right. I have written something; it came to me so readily; look, I have written all this, I have been fortunate tonight. But now I am finished. I opened the window and sang a little.

You bellowed, the man says. It is the loudest singing I have ever heard, do you understand? And it is still the middle of the night.

Johannes grabs at his papers on the table and takes a handful of large and small sheets.

Look here! he cries. I tell you, it has never gone so well for me. It was like one long flash of lightning. I once saw a bolt of lightning that followed a telegraph wire; God help you, it looked like a sheet of fire. That is how it has poured through me tonight. What am I to do? I do not think you will hold anything against me any longer when you hear how matters stand. I sat here and wrote, do you hear, I did not move; I remembered you and kept quiet. Then comes the moment when I no longer remember it; my chest was about to burst; perhaps I rose then, perhaps I also rose once more in the course of the night and walked around the floor a few times. I was so happy.

But after speaking of many kinds of love, the
monk Vendt tells of yet another kind and says:

For so intoxicating is a particular kind of love!

The young master and mistress have just come home, their long wedding
journey is at an end, and they retire for the night.

A shooting star burned out above their roof.

In summer the young master and mistress walked together and did
not leave each other’s side. They picked yellow, red, and blue flowers
which they gave to each other; they watched the grass move in the wind and
heard the birds singing in the forests, and every word they spoke was like
a caress. In winter they drove with bells on the horses, and
the sky was blue, and high above, the stars rushed away across the
eternal plains.

Thus many, many years passed. The young master and mistress had three children,
and their hearts loved each other as on the first day beneath the
first kiss.

Then the proud gentleman was stricken with his illness, the illness that
chained him to his bed for so long and put his wife’s patience
to so hard a test. On the day he recovered and rose from the bed,
he did not recognize himself; the illness had disfigured
him and taken his hair.

He suffered and brooded. Then one morning he said:

Now you no longer love me, do you?

But his wife, blushing, threw her arms around him and kissed
him as passionately as in the springtime of youth, and answered:

I, I love, love you always. I never forget that it
was I and no other whom you took, and who became so
happy.

And she went into her chamber and cut all the yellow hair from
her head so as to resemble her husband, whom she loved.

And again many, many years passed; the young master and mistress grew
old, and their children were grown. They shared every happiness as
before; in summer they still walked in the fields and watched the grass
wave, and in winter they wrapped themselves in their furs and drove beneath
the starry sky. And their hearts continued to be warm and
glad, as though from wondrous wine.

Then the lady became paralyzed. The old lady could not walk on her
feet; she had to be pulled in a wheeled chair, and the gentleman himself
pulled her. But the lady suffered so unspeakably from her misfortune, and her
face acquired deep furrows of sorrow.

Then one day she said:

Now I should like to die. I am so paralyzed and ugly, and your face
is so beautiful; you cannot kiss me anymore, and you cannot love
me as before.

But the gentleman embraces her, red with emotion, and answers:

I, I love you more, more than my life, my dear one; I love
you as on the first day, the first moment when you gave me the rose.
Do you remember it? You held out the rose to me and looked at me with your
beautiful eyes; the rose was fragrant like you, you blushed like it, and I
became intoxicated in all my senses. But I love you even more
now; you are more beautiful than in your youth, and my heart thanks and
blesses you for every day you have been mine.

The gentleman goes into his chamber, dashes acid into his face to
disfigure it, and says to his wife:

I had the misfortune to get acid in my face; my cheeks are
covered with burns, and you no longer love me, do you?

Oh, you my bridegroom, my beloved! stammers the old woman
and kisses his hands. You are more beautiful than any man on
earth; your voice makes my heart hot even to this very day,
and I love you unto death.

XIII

Johannes meets Camilla in the street; she is with her
mother, her father, and young Richmond; they stop their carriage and speak
kindly to him.

Camilla takes his arm and says:

You did not come to see us. We had a grand celebration, you may be sure;
we waited for you until the very end, but you did not come.

I was prevented, he replied.

Forgive me for not having been up to see you since, she continued.
I shall come one of these days, quite certainly, when Richmond
has left. Oh, what a celebration we had! Victoria became ill; she was
driven home, have you heard? I shall be going up to see her soon.
She is surely much better, perhaps entirely well again. I have
given Richmond a medallion almost identical to yours. Listen, Johannes,
you must promise me to tend your stove; when you write, you forget
everything, and it becomes icy cold at your place. Then you must ring for
the maid.
Yes, I shall ring for the maid, he replied.

Mrs. Seier also spoke to him, asked about his work, about
the play about The Family; how was it going? She awaited his next
one with longing.

Johannes gave the necessary answers, bowed very deeply, and watched
the carriage drive away. How little the whole thing concerned him—this carriage,
these people, this chatter! An empty and cold mood entered
him and followed him all the way home. At his gate
a man was loitering back and forth in the street, an old
acquaintance, the former tutor at the Castle.

Johannes greeted him.

He was dressed in a long, warm coat that had been carefully
brushed, and he wore a bold and resolute expression.

Here You see Your friend and colleague, he said. Give me Your
hand, young man. God has guided my paths wondrously since
last time; I am married, I have a home, a little garden, a wife. Miracles
still happen in life. Have You anything to remark upon my last statement?

Johannes looks at him in astonishment.

Then it is settled. You see, I tutored her son. She has
a son; the brat is from her first marriage; she had naturally been
married before, she was a widow. Thus I married a widow. You
may object that this was not sung at my cradle; but I
did, then, marry a widow. She had the brat already. I walk
about there, you see, looking at the garden and the widow, and live for a while
with intense thoughts on that subject. Suddenly I have it,
and I say to myself: very well, it was not sung at your
cradle, and so forth; but I do it all the same, I take the plunge, for
it is presumably written in the stars. There, that is how it happened.

Nei, Victoria, tak mig ikke, svarte han. Hele hans sjæl strøm-
met imot hende og han vilde si mere, si mere; det blev til for-
virrede utbrudd, han var som beruset. Ja, men Victoria, hvis
De er litt glad i mig .... jeg vet det ikke, men si at De er det
selv om det ikke er så. Vær så snill Å jeg skulde love Dem
å bli noget, bli meget, uhørt meget næsten. De aner ikke hvad
jeg kunde bli til; jeg grubler over det iblandt og vet at jeg er
aldeles fuld av ugjorte gjærninger. Mangen gang strømmer det
ut av mig, om natten går jeg og gynger op og ned på gulvet
i mit værelse fordi jeg er fuld av syner. Det ligger en mand i
værelset ved siden av, han får ikke sove, han banker i væggen.
Når morgningen gryr kommer han ind til mig og er rasende.
Det gjør ikke noget, jeg bryr mig ikke om ham; for da har jeg
tænkt så længe på Dem at jeg synes De er hos mig. Jeg går
til vinduet og synger, det begynder å bli litt lyst, poplerne rasler
utenfor. Godnat! sier jeg imot dagen. Det er til Dem. Nu
sover hun, tænker jeg, godnat, Gud velsigne hende! Så lægger
jeg mig. Således går det kvæld efter kvæld. Men aldrig har jeg
trodd at De var så deilig som De er. Nu vil jeg huske Dem
således når De reiser; således som De er nu. Jeg vil huske Dem
så tydelig ....

Kommer De ikke hjem?

Nei. Jeg er ikke færdig. Jo jeg kommer. Jeg reiser nu. Jeg er
ikke færdig, men alverdens ting vil jeg gjøre. Driver De stund-
om i haven derhjemme nu? Går De nogensinde ut en aften?
Jeg kunde se Dem, jeg kunde få hilse på Dem kanske, det er
ikke for noget andet. Men hvis De er litt glad i mig, hvis
De tåler mig, utstår mig, så si .... Gjør mig den glæde ....
Vet De, det er en palme som blomstrer bare en gang i sit liv
og den blir dog sytti år, talipotpalmen. Men den blomstrer
bare en gang. Nu blomstrer jeg. Jo jeg skaffer mig penger og
reiser hjem. Jeg sælger det jeg har skrevet; jeg skriver nemlig på
en stor bok og den sælger jeg nu, straks imorgen, alt hvad
jeg har færdig. Jeg får en hel del for det. Vilde De da at jeg
skulde komme hjem?

Victoria så sig om, det kom en dame nedover gaten og høiere

Han sænker hodet.

Ikke her, svarte hun. Jeg skal gjøre det dernede.

De gik.

Man sier at De skal gifte Dem med småpiken, piken, hende

Med Camilla, mener De?

Jaså. Hvorfor spør De om det? Hun er ikke voksen. Jeg har

Han så på hende. En rykning gik over hans ansigt.

Hun gik avsted med hurtige skridt og svarte ikke. De be-

ham med ind i porten, opover trappen.

Jeg skal ikke ind, sa han halvt forundret.

Hun trykket på klokken, hun vendte sig mot ham og hendes
bryst bølget.

Jeg elsker Dem, sa hun. Forstår De det? Det er Dem jeg
elsker.

Pludselig trak hun ham hastig nedover trappen igjen, tre,
fire trin, slog sine armer om ham og kysset ham. Hun skalv
imot ham.

Det er Dem jeg elsker, sa hun.

Entrédøren åpnedes ovenpå. Hun rev sig løs og ilet opover
trappen.

IV

Det lier imot morgen, dagen gryr, en blålig, skjælvende sep-
tembermorgen.

Det suser mildt i poplerne i haven. Et vindu går op, en mand
læner sig ut av det og nynner. Han har ingen frak på, han
ser ut i verden som en upåklædt galning som inat har drukket
sig drukken i lykke.

Han vender sig pludselig bort fra vinduet og ser mot sin dør;
nogen har banket på hos ham. Han roper: Kom! En mand
træder ind.

Godmorgen! sier han imot den indtrædende.
Det er en ældre mand, han er blek og rasende og han bærer
en lampe med sig fordi det endnu ikke er ganske lyst.

Jeg vil endnu en gang henstille til Dem, hr. Møller, hr.
Johannes Møller, om De synes at dette er rimelig, stammer man-
den forbitret.

Nei, svarer Johannes, De har ret. Jeg har skrevet noget, det
faldt mig så villig ind, se, alt dette har jeg skrevet, jeg har
været heldig inat. Men nu er jeg færdig. Jeg åpnet vinduet
og sang litt.

De brølte, sier manden. Det er den høieste sang jeg har hørt,
forstår De. Og endnu er det midt på natten.

Johannes griper i sine papirer på bordet, tar en håndfuld
store og små ark.

Se her! roper han. Jeg sier Dem, det har aldrig gåt så godt
for mig. Det var som et langt lyn. Jeg har engang set et lyn
som fulgte en telegraftråd, Gud hjælpe Dem, det så ut som et
laken av ild. Slik har det strømmet hos mig inat. Hvad skal
jeg gjøre? Jeg tror ikke De vil ha noget imot mig mere når
De hører hvorledes det hænger sammen. Jeg sat her og skrev,
hører De, jeg rørte mig ikke; jeg husket på Dem og var stille.
Så kommer det øieblik da jeg ikke husker det længer, mit bryst
vilde sprænges, kanske reiste jeg mig da, kanske reiste jeg mig
også en gang til i nattens løp og gik nogen ganger rundt på
gulvet. Jeg var så glad.

Jeg hørte Dem ikke så meget inat, sier manden. Men det er
aldeles utilgivelig av Dem å åpne vinduet nu på denne tid
av døgnet og skråle slik.

Javel. Jo, det er utilgivelig. Men nu har jeg forklaret Dem
det. Jeg har hat en nat ’uten make, skal De vite. Igår oplevet
Jeg noget. Jeg går på gaten og møter min lykke, å hør mig,
møter min stjærne og min lykke. Vet De og så kysser hun
mig. Hendes mund var så rød og jeg elsker hende, hun kysser
mig og beruser mig. Har De nogensinde skjælvet så stærkt i
munden at De ikke kunde tale? Jeg kunde ikke tale, mit hjærte
rystet min hele krop. Jeg løp hjem og faldt i søvn; jeg sat her
på stolen og sov. Da det blev aften våknet jeg. Min sjæl
gynget op og ned i mig av stemning og jeg begyndte å skrive.
Hvad jeg skrev? Her er det! Jeg var behersket av en sælsom
og herlig tankegang, himlene åpnedes, det var likesom en varm
sommerdag for min sjæl, jeg fik vin av en engel, jeg drak den;
det var berusende vin, jeg drak den av en granatskål. Hørte
jeg om klokken slog? Så jeg at lampen brændte ut? Gud give
De forstod det! Jeg gjennemlevet det hele påny en gang til,
jeg gik igjen med min elskede på gaten og alle vendte sig efter
hende. Vi gik i parken, vi møtte kongen, jeg førte min hat til
jorden for ham av glæde og kongen vendte sig efter hende,
efter min elskede, for hun er så stor og deilig. Vi gik ned i
byen igjen og alle skolebørnene vendte sig efter hende, for
hun er ung og har en lys kjole. Da vi kom til et rødt stenhus
gik vi ind. Jeg fulgte hende opover trappen og vilde knæle for
hende. Da slog hun armene om mig og kysset mig. Dette hændte
mig igåraftes, det er ikke længer siden. Hvis De spurte mig om
hvad jeg har skrevet så er det en eneste ustanselig sang til glæ-
den, til lykken jeg har skrevet. Det var likesom lykken lå naken
foran mig med en lang, leende hals og vilde imot mig.

translation.text:
No, Victoria, do not take me, he answered. His whole soul flowed toward her and he wanted to say more, say more; it turned into confused outbursts, he was as though intoxicated. Yes, but Victoria, if you are a little fond of me .... I do not know, but say that you are, even if it is not so. Please. Oh, I should promise you to become something, become much, almost unheard-of much. You have no idea what I could become; I brood on it sometimes and know that I am utterly full of deeds not yet done. Many a time it streams out of me; at night I walk up and down, rocking, on the floor of my room because I am full of visions. There is a man in the room next door, he cannot sleep, he knocks on the wall. When morning dawns he comes in to me and is furious. It does not matter, I do not care about him; for by then I have thought of you for so long that I feel you are with me. I go to the window and sing, it is beginning to grow a little light, the poplars rustle outside. Good night! I say to the day. It is for you. Now she is asleep, I think, good night, God bless her! Then I lie down. Thus it goes evening after evening. But I have never believed that you were as lovely as you are. Now I shall remember you like this when you go away; as you are now. I shall remember you so clearly ....

Are you not coming home?

No. I am not finished. Yes, I am coming. I am leaving now. I am not finished, but I shall do all manner of things. Do you sometimes wander in the garden at home now? Do you ever go out in the evening? I could see you, I could perhaps be allowed to greet you, it is not for anything else. But if you are a little fond of me, if you can tolerate me, endure me, then say .... Do me that kindness .... Do you know, there is a palm that flowers only once in its life, and yet it grows to be seventy years old, the talipot palm. But it flowers only once. Now I am flowering. Yes, I shall get myself some money and travel home. I shall sell what I have written; I am, in fact, writing a large book, and I shall sell it now, first thing tomorrow, everything I have finished. I shall get quite a lot for it. Would you then want me to come home?

Yes.
Thank you, thank you! Forgive me if I hope too much, believe too much; it is so lovely to believe extraordinarily much. This is the happiest day I have lived ....

He took off his hat and laid it beside him.

Victoria looked around; a lady was coming down the street and, farther up, a woman with a basket. Victoria grew uneasy, she reached for her watch.

Must you go now? he asked. Say something before you go, let me hear your .... I love you and say it now. It will then depend on your answer whether I .... You have such absolute power over me. What is your answer?

A pause.

He lowers his head.
No, do not say it! he begged.

Not here, she answered. I shall do it down there.

They walked on.

They say that you are to marry the little girl, the girl, the one you rescued; what is her name?

Camilla, do you mean?

Camilla Seier. They say that you are to marry her.

Indeed. Why do you ask about that? She is not grown up. I have been in her home, it is so large and rich, a castle like your own; I have been there many times. No, she is not grown up.

She is fifteen years old. I have met her, we have spent time together. I became very taken with her. How charming she is!

I am not going to marry her, he said.

Oh, you are not.

He looked at her. A twitch passed over his face.

But why do you say this now? Do you wish to direct my attention to someone else?

She walked on with rapid steps and did not answer. They found themselves outside the chamberlain’s house. She took his hand and pulled him through the gateway, up the stairs.

I am not going inside, he said, half astonished.

She pressed the bell, turned toward him, and her breast heaved.

I love you, she said. Do you understand that? It is you I love.

Suddenly she pulled him quickly down the stairs again, three, four steps, flung her arms around him, and kissed him. She trembled against him.

It is you I love, she said.

The entrance door opened above. She tore herself free and hurried up the stairs.

IV

It is drawing toward morning, the day is dawning, a bluish, trembling September morning.

The poplars in the garden murmur softly. A window opens, a man leans out of it and hums. He has no coat on, he looks out into the world like an undressed madman who has drunk himself drunk on happiness during the night.

He suddenly turns away from the window and looks toward his door; someone has knocked. He calls: Come in! A man enters.

Good morning! he says to the man entering.
It is an elderly man, he is pale and furious, and he carries a lamp because it is not yet quite light.

Once again I must ask you to consider, Mr. Møller, Mr. Johannes Møller, whether you think this is reasonable, the man stammers bitterly.

No, Johannes answers, you are right. I have written something, it came to me so readily; look, I have written all this, I have been fortunate tonight. But now I am finished. I opened the window and sang a little.

You bellowed, says the man. It is the loudest singing I have heard, do you understand? And it is still the middle of the night.

Johannes seizes his papers on the table, takes a handful of large and small sheets.

Look here! he cries. I tell you, it has never gone so well for me. It was like a long flash of lightning. I once saw a flash of lightning that followed a telegraph wire, God help you, it looked like a sheet of fire. That is how it has streamed within me tonight. What am I to do? I do not think you will hold anything against me any longer when you hear how matters stand. I sat here and wrote, do you hear, I did not move; I remembered you and kept quiet. Then comes the moment when I no longer remember it, my breast was about to burst; perhaps I got up then, perhaps I also got up once more during the night and walked around the floor a few times. I was so happy.

I did not hear you very much tonight, says the man. But it is utterly unforgivable of you to open the window now at this time of day and bawl like that.

Very well. Yes, it is unforgivable. But now I have explained it to you. I have had a night without equal, you should know. Yesterday I experienced something. I am walking along the street and meet my happiness, oh, listen to me, meet my star and my happiness. Do you know, and then she kisses me. Her mouth was so red and I love her, she kisses me and intoxicates me. Have you ever trembled so violently in the mouth that you could not speak? I could not speak, my heart shook my whole body. I ran home and fell asleep; I sat here on the chair and slept. When evening came I awoke. My soul rocked up and down within me with emotion, and I began to write. What did I write? Here it is! I was possessed by a strange and glorious train of thought, the heavens opened, it was like a warm summer’s day for my soul, I received wine from an angel, I drank it; it was intoxicating wine, I drank it from a pomegranate bowl. Did I hear the clock strike? Did I see the lamp burn out? God grant that you understood it! I lived through it all anew, once again; I walked again with my beloved along the street and everyone turned to look after her. We walked in the park, we met the king, I swept my hat to the ground before him for joy, and the king turned to look after her, after my beloved, for she is so noble and lovely. We went down into the town again and all the schoolchildren turned to look after her, for she is young and wears a light-colored dress. When we came to a red stone house we went in. I followed her up the stairs and wanted to kneel before her. Then she put her arms around me and kissed me. This happened to me yesterday evening, it was no longer ago than that. If you asked me what I have written, then it is one single unceasing song to joy, to the happiness I have written. It was as though happiness lay naked before me with a long, laughing neck and desired me.
