wide.text:
Johannes stod tilbake med brevet i sin hånd. Victoria var
død. Han nævnte gang på gang hendes navn høit og han
hadde en følesløs, næsten forhærdet stemme. Han så ned på
brevet og kjendte skriften; der var store og små bokstaver,
linjerne rette, og hun som hadde skrevet dem var død!

Så begir han sig ind gjennem sin port, op trappen, finder
den rigtige nøkkel å stikke i dørlåset og åpner. Hans værelse
var koldt og mørkt. Han sætter sig bort til vinduet og læser i
den siste rest av dagslys Victorias brev.

Kjære Johannes! skrev hun. Når De læser dette brev da er
jeg død! Alting er så underlig for mig nu, jeg skammer mig ikke
for Dem mere og skriver til Dem igjen, likesom det ikke var
nogen ting iveien herfor. Før, mens jeg var fuldstændig i le-
vende live, vilde jeg heller ha lidt nat og dag end skrevet til
Dem igjen; men nu er jeg begyndt å avsjæles og jeg tænker
ikke således længer. Fremmede har set mig blø, doktoren har
undersøkt mig og set at jeg har bare en rest av en lunge til-
bake, hvad skal jeg da undse mig for mere?

Jeg har ligget her på sengen og tænkt over de siste ord
jeg sa til Dem. Det var i skogen den kvæld. Dengang tænkte
jeg ikke at det skulde være mine siste ord, for så vilde jeg ha
sagt farvel til Dem med det samme og takket Dem. Nu får
jeg ikke se Dem mere, så jeg angrer nu på at jeg ikke fik kastet
mig ned for Dem og kysset Deres sko og jorden som De gik
på, og fik vist Dem hvor usigelig jeg har elsket Dem. Jeg har
ligget her og ønsket både igår og idag at jeg ikke var sykere
end at jeg kunde komme mig hjem igjen og gå i skogen og
finde den plass vi sat på da De holdt begge mine hænder;
for så kunde jeg lægge mig ned der og se om jeg ikke fandt
sporet efter Dem og kysse al lyngen deromkring. Men jeg kan
ikke komme hjem nu hvis jeg ikke muligens blir litt bedre
som mama tror.

Kjære Johannes! Det er mærkelig å tænke på at jeg ikke
har fåt nogen anden ting gjort end å komme på jorden og
elske Dem og nu si farvel til livet. De kan tro det er underlig
å ligge her og vente på dagen og timen. Jeg fjærner mig skridt
for skridt fra livet og menneskene på gaten og vognramme-
len; våren kommer jeg vel heller aldrig til å se mere og disse
huser og gaterne og trærne i parken vil være tilbake efter mig.
Jeg fik sitte i sengen idag og se litt ut av vinduet. Nede på
hjørnet var det to som traf hverandre, de hilste og grep hver-
andres hænder og lo av det de sa; men da var det så underlig
for mig at jeg som lå og så på dette skulde dø. Jeg kom
til å tænke: de to dernede vet ikke at jeg ligger her og venter
på min time; men om de visste det så vilde de vel allikevel hilse
på hverandre og tale med hverandre likesom nu. Igår nat da
det var mørkt tænkte jeg at det skulde være min siste stund,
mit hjærte begyndte å stå stille og det var likesom jeg allerede
hørte evigheten bruse imot mig langt ute. Men i næste øieblik
vendte jeg tilbake langt borte fra og begyndte å puste igjen.
Det var en aldeles ubeskrivelig følelse. Men mama tror at det
kanske bare var elven og fossen derhjemme som jeg husket.

Du gode Gud, De skulde vite hvor jeg har elsket Dem,
Johannes. Jeg har ikke fåt vise Dem det, det har lagt sig
så meget iveien for mig, og først og fremst min egen natur.
Papa var også således ond mot sig selv og jeg er hans datter.
Men nu når jeg skal dø og altsammen er forsent da skriver
jeg til Dem endnu en gang og sier Dem det. Jeg spør mig
selv hvorfor jeg gjør det da det dog er likegyldig for Dem, især
når jeg ikke engang skal være ilive mere; men jeg vilde gjærne
være nær hos Dem til det siste så jeg ikke følte mig mere
forlatt end før ialfald. Når De læser dette da er det likesom
jeg ser Deres aksler og hænder og ser alle Deres bevægelser
med brevet når De holder det foran Dem og læser det. Så er
vi ikke så langt fra hverandre, tænker jeg. Jeg kan ikke sende
bud efter Dem, dertil har jeg ingen ret. Mama vilde sende bud
efter Dem allerede for to dager siden, men jeg vilde heller
skrive. Jeg vilde også helst at De skulde huske mig således som
jeg engang var da jeg endnu ikke hadde været syk. Jeg husker
at De .... (Her er nogen ord uteglemt) .... mine øine og
øienbryn; men heller ikke de er mere som før. Også av den
grund vilde jeg ikke at De skulde komme. Og jeg vil også be
Dem om ikke å se mig i kisten. Jeg er vistnok omtrent som
da jeg levet, bare noget blekere, og jeg ligger i gul kjole; men
allikevel vilde De angre på det hvis De kom og så mig.

Nu har jeg skrevet mange ganger på dette brev idag og
allikevel har jeg ikke fåt sagt Dem en tusendel av det jeg
vilde si. Det er så forfærdelig for mig å dø, jeg vil det ikke,
jeg håper endnu så inderlig til Gud at jeg kanske kunde
bli litt bedre, om ikke længer end til våren. Da er dagene
lyse og det er løv på trærne. Hvis jeg blev frisk igjen nu så
skulde jeg nok aldrig være ond mot Dem mere, Johannes.
Hvor jeg har grått og tænkt på det! Å jeg vilde gå ut og klappe
alle gatestenene og stanse og takke hvert trin i trapperne som
jeg kom forbi og være god mot alle. Det var det samme hvor
ondt jeg fik det hvis jeg bare fik leve. Jeg skulde aldrig klage
mere over nogen ting, nei jeg skulde smile til den som over-
faldt og slog mig og takke og love Gud hvis jeg fik leve. Mit
liv er så ulevet, intet har jeg fåt gjort for nogen og dette feil-
slagne liv skal ende nu. Hvis De visste hvor nødig jeg vilde dø
så kanske De vilde gjøre noget, gjøre alt som stod i Deres magt.
De kan vistnok ikke gjøre noget; men jeg tænkte at hvis De og
hele verden bad for mig og ikke vilde slippe mig så vilde Gud
skjænke mig livet. Å hvor jeg vilde være taknemmelig da og
aldrig gjøre ondt mot nogen mere, men smile til alt som ble
mig beskikket bare jeg fik lov til å leve.

Mama sitter her og gråter. Hun sat også her i hele nat og
gråt for mig. Dette gjør mig litt godt, det mildner min avskeds
bitterhet. Idag tænkte jeg også: hvordan mon De vilde synes
om at jeg kom like til Dem på gaten en dag når jeg var pent
klædt og ikke sa noget sårende mere, men gav Dem en rose
som jeg kunde ha kjøpt på forhånd. Så tænkte jeg straks efter
at jeg kan aldrig mere gjøre det jeg vil; for jeg kan vel aldrig
bli frisk igjen før jeg dør. Jeg gråter så ofte, jeg ligger stille og
gråter ustanselig og trøstesløs; det gjør ikke ondt i mit bryst når
jeg ikke hulker. Johannes, kjære, kjære ven, min eneste elskede
på jorden, kom til mig nu og vær her litt når det begynder
å mørkne. Jeg skal ikke gråte da, men smile så godt som jeg
formår, bare av glæde over at De kom.

translation.text:
Johannes remained standing with the letter in his hand. Victoria was
dead. Again and again he spoke her name aloud, and his
voice was numb, almost hardened. He looked down at
the letter and recognized the handwriting; there were capital and lowercase letters,
the lines straight, and she who had written them was dead!

Then he makes his way in through his gate, up the stairs, finds
the right key to put into the lock, and opens the door. His room
was cold and dark. He sits down by the window and, in
the last remnant of daylight, reads Victoria’s letter.

Dear Johannes! she wrote. When you read this letter, I am
dead! Everything is so strange to me now; I am no longer ashamed
before you and am writing to you again, as though there were
nothing to prevent it. Before, while I was fully
alive, I would rather have suffered night and day than have written to
you again; but now my soul has begun to leave me, and I no longer
think that way. Strangers have seen me bleed, the doctor has
examined me and seen that I have only a remnant of one lung
left; what more have I to be ashamed of?

I have lain here on the bed and thought about the last words
I said to you. It was in the woods that evening. At the time I did
not think they would be my last words, for then I would have
said farewell to you at once and thanked you. Now I shall
never see you again, so now I regret that I did not throw
myself down before you and kiss your shoes and the ground you walked
on, and show you how inexpressibly I have loved you. I have
lain here both yesterday and today wishing that I were no sicker
than to be able to make my way home again and walk into the woods and
find the place where we sat when you held both my hands;
for then I could lie down there and see whether I could find
your traces and kiss all the heather around it. But I cannot
come home now unless perhaps I get a little better,
as Mama believes.

Dear Johannes! It is strange to think that I have
done nothing other than come into the world and
love you, and now say farewell to life. You may believe it is strange
to lie here and wait for the day and the hour. Step by step
I am moving away from life and the people in the street and the clatter
of carriages; I shall probably never see spring again either, and these
houses and the streets and the trees in the park will remain after me.
Today I was able to sit up in bed and look out of the window for a while. Down
on the corner there were two people who met; they greeted each other and clasped
each other’s hands and laughed at what they said; but then it was so strange
to me that I, who lay there watching this, was going to die. I found
myself thinking: those two down there do not know that I am lying here waiting
for my hour; but if they knew, they would probably still greet
each other and talk to each other just as they do now. Last night, when
it was dark, I thought it was going to be my final moment;
my heart began to stop, and it was as though I could already
hear eternity roaring toward me from far out. But in the next moment
I returned from far away and began to breathe again.
It was an utterly indescribable sensation. But Mama thinks that
perhaps it was only the river and the waterfall back home that I remembered.

Dear God, if only you knew how I have loved you,
Johannes. I have not been able to show you; so much has
stood in my way, first and foremost my own nature.
Papa too was so cruel to himself, and I am his daughter.
But now, when I am going to die and everything is too late, I am writing
to you once again and telling you so. I ask myself
why I am doing it, since it is nevertheless of no concern to you, especially
when I shall not even be alive anymore; but I should like
to be close to you until the end, so that at least I would not feel
more forsaken than before. When you read this, it is as though
I can see your shoulders and hands and see all your movements
with the letter as you hold it before you and read it. Then we
are not so far apart, I think. I cannot send for
you; I have no right to do so. Mama wanted to send for
you two days ago already, but I preferred to write. I also wanted most of all
for you to remember me as I once was, when I had not yet
been ill. I remember that you .... (Here some words have been omitted) .... my eyes and
eyebrows; but they too are no longer as they were before. For that
reason as well, I did not want you to come. And I shall also ask
you not to see me in my coffin. I shall presumably look much as
I did when I was alive, only somewhat paler, and I shall be lying in a yellow dress; but
nevertheless you would regret it if you came and saw me.

Now I have written on this letter many times today, and
even so I have not managed to tell you a thousandth of what I
wanted to say. It is so terrible for me to die; I do not want to;
I still hope so fervently in God that perhaps I might
get a little better, if only until spring. Then the days
are bright and there are leaves on the trees. If I were to recover now, I would
certainly never be unkind to you again, Johannes.
How I have wept and thought about it! Oh, I would go out and pat
all the paving stones and stop and thank every step in the stairways
I passed and be good to everyone. It would not matter how
much pain I suffered if only I were allowed to live. I would never complain
about anything again; no, I would smile at anyone who attacked
and struck me, and thank and praise God if I were allowed to live. My
life is so unlived; I have done nothing for anyone, and this
failed life is to end now. If you knew how loath I am to die,
then perhaps you would do something, do everything in your power.
You presumably cannot do anything; but I thought that if you and
the whole world prayed for me and would not let me go, then God
would grant me life. Oh, how grateful I would be then, and
never do wrong to anyone again, but smile at everything that was
ordained for me, if only I were allowed to live.

Mama is sitting here and weeping. She also sat here all night and
wept for me. This does me a little good; it softens the bitterness of my
farewell. Today I also thought: I wonder what you would think
if one day I came right up to you in the street, when I was nicely
dressed, and said nothing hurtful anymore, but gave you a rose
that I could have bought beforehand. Then immediately afterward I thought
that I can never again do what I want; for surely I can never
recover before I die. I weep so often; I lie quietly and
weep incessantly and inconsolably; it does not hurt in my chest when
I do not sob. Johannes, dear, dear friend, my only beloved
on earth, come to me now and stay here for a while when it begins
to grow dark. I shall not weep then, but smile as well as I
can, merely from joy that you came.

11 — Hamsun: III
har lidt i lang tid, Johannes, længe før disse siste dager. Da De
var i utlandet led jeg, og siden, efter at jeg kom hit til byen
i vår har jeg bare lidt hver dag. Jeg har aldrig før visst hvor
uendelig lang natten kunde være. Jeg har set Dem to ganger
på gaten i denne tid; den ene gang nynnet De da De gik forbi
mig, men De så mig ikke. Jeg hadde et håp om å få se Dem hos
Seiers; men De kom ikke. Jeg skulde ikke ha talt til Dem eller
gåt like foran Dem, men været taknemmelig for å få se Dem
langt borte fra. Men De kom ikke. Jeg tænkte da at det kan-
ske var for min skyld De ikke kom. Klokken elleve begyndte jeg
å danse fordi jeg ikke holdt ut å vente længer. Ja, Johannes,
jeg har elsket Dem, elsket bare Dem i hele mit liv. Det er
Victoria som skriver dette og Gud læser det over min skulder.
Og nu må jeg si Dem farvel, det er nu blit næsten mørkt
og jeg ser ikke længer. Farvel, Johannes, tak for hver dag.
Når jeg tlyver ut fra jorden skal jeg takke Dem endnu til det
siste og nævne Deres navn hele veien for mig selv. Lev da vel
for hele Deres liv og tilgiv mig det jeg har gjort Dem imot
og at jeg ikke kunde få kaste mig ned for Dem og be Dem
om forlatelse derfor. Jeg gjør det nu i mit hjærte. Lev da vel,
Johannes, og farvel for altid. Og tak endnu en gang for hver
eneste dag og stund. Jeg kan ikke mere.
Deres
VICTORIA.

translation.text:
Oh, good God, if only you knew how I have loved you,
Johannes. I have not been able to show you; so much has stood
in my way, first and foremost my own nature.
Papa was likewise so cruel to himself, and I am his daughter.
But now, when I am going to die and everything is too late, I am
writing to you once more and telling you. I ask myself why I do
it, since after all it is a matter of indifference to you, especially
when I shall no longer even be alive; but I would like to be near
you until the end, so that at least I would not feel more
forsaken than before. When you read this, it is as though
I see your shoulders and hands and see all your movements
with the letter as you hold it before you and read it. Then
we are not so far apart, I think. I cannot send for you; I have
no right to do so. Mama wanted to send for you two days ago,
but I preferred to write. I would also prefer you to remember me
as I once was, when I had not yet been ill. I remember
that you .... (Some words have been omitted here) .... my eyes and
eyebrows; but they too are no longer as they were. For that
reason as well, I did not want you to come. And I will also ask
you not to look at me in my coffin. I shall no doubt look much as
I did when I was alive, only somewhat paler, and I shall be lying
in a yellow dress; but even so, you would regret it if you came
and saw me.

Now I have returned to writing this letter many times today, and
yet I have not managed to tell you one thousandth of what I
wanted to say. It is so terrible for me to die; I do not want to;
I still hope so fervently in God that I might perhaps
get a little better, even if only until spring. Then the days are
bright and there are leaves on the trees. If I were to recover now,
I would certainly never be cruel to you again, Johannes.
How I have wept and thought of it! Oh, I would go out and pat
all the paving stones and stop and thank every step of every
staircase I passed, and be good to everyone. It would not matter
how badly I suffered, if only I were allowed to live. I would
never complain about anything again; no, I would smile at anyone
who attacked and struck me, and thank and praise God if I were
allowed to live. My life is so unlived; I have done nothing for
anyone, and this failed life is to end now. If you knew how
reluctant I am to die, then perhaps you would do something, do
everything in your power. You probably cannot do anything; but
I thought that if you and the whole world prayed for me and
would not let me go, then God would grant me life. Oh, how
grateful I would be then, and never do wrong to anyone again,
but smile at everything that befell me, if only I were allowed
to live.

Mama is sitting here weeping. She sat here all last night as well
and wept for me. This does me a little good; it softens the
bitterness of my farewell. Today I also thought: how would you
like it if I came straight up to you in the street one day, when I
was nicely dressed, and no longer said anything hurtful, but gave
you a rose that I could have bought beforehand? Then I thought
immediately afterward that I can never again do what I want;
for I can surely never recover again before I die. I weep so
often; I lie quietly and weep ceaselessly and inconsolably; my
chest does not hurt when I do not sob. Johannes, dear, dear
friend, my only beloved on earth, come to me now and stay here
for a little while when it begins to grow dark. I shall not weep
then, but smile as well as I am able, simply for joy that you came.

No, what has become of my pride and my courage! I am not my
father’s daughter now; but that is because my strength has left
me. I have

11 — Hamsun: III

suffered for a long time, Johannes, long before these last days.
When you were abroad, I suffered, and since I came here to town
this spring, I have done nothing but suffer every day. Never
before have I known how infinitely long the night could be. I
have seen you twice in the street during this time; on one of
those occasions you were humming as you walked past me, but
you did not see me. I had hoped to see you at the Seiers’; but
you did not come. I would not have spoken to you or walked
straight in front of you, but would have been grateful merely to
see you from far away. But you did not come. I thought then that
perhaps it was because of me that you did not come. At eleven
o’clock I began to dance because I could not bear to wait any
longer. Yes, Johannes, I have loved you, loved only you throughout
my entire life. It is Victoria who is writing this, and God is
reading it over my shoulder.
And now I must bid you farewell; it has now grown almost dark,
and I can no longer see. Farewell, Johannes; thank you for every
day. When I fly away from the earth, I shall continue to thank
you until the very end and repeat your name to myself all the
way. May you fare well, then, all your life, and forgive me for
what I have done against you, and because I could not throw
myself down before you and ask your forgiveness for it. I am
doing so now in my heart. May you fare well, Johannes, and
farewell forever. And thank you once again for every single day
and hour. I can do no more.
Yours,
VICTORIA.

Now I have had the lamp lit, and it is much brighter for me.
I have lain in a stupor and once again been far away from the
earth. Thank God, it was not as frightening for me as before; I
even heard a little music, and above all, it was not dark. I am so
grateful. But now I have no strength left to write.
Farewell, my beloved ....

wide.text:
NORA. Bare for å sy på min drakt. Herregud, hvor urimelig De
er. (setter seg på sofaen.) Vær nu snill, doktor Rank; i morgen skal
De få se hvor smukt jeg skal danse; og da skal De forestille Dem at
jeg gjør det bare for Deres skyld, - ja, og så naturligvis for
Torvalds; - det forstår seg. (tar forskjellige saker ut av esken.)
Doktor Rank; sett Dem her, så skal jeg vise Dem noe.

RANK (setter seg). Hva er det?

NORA. Se her. Se!

RANK. Silkestrømper.

NORA. Kjødfarvede. Er ikke de deilige? Ja, nu er her så
mørkt; men i morgen -. Nei, nei, nei; De får bare se fotbladet. Å jo,
De kan så menn gjerne få se oventil også.

RANK. Hm -

NORA. Hvorfor ser De så kritisk ut? Tror De kanskje ikke de
passer?

RANK. Det kan jeg umulig ha noen begrunnet formening om.

NORA (ser et øyeblikk på ham). Fy skam Dem. (slår ham lett
på øret med strømpene.) Det skal De ha. (pakker dem atter sammen.)

RANK. Og hva er det så for andre herligheter jeg skal få se?

NORA. De får ikke se en smule mer; for De er uskikkelig.

(hun nynner litt og leter mellem sakene.)

RANK (efter en kort taushet). Når jeg sitter her således
ganske fortrolig sammen med Dem, så begriper jeg ikke - nei, jeg fatter
det ikke - hva der skulle blitt av meg hvis jeg aldri var kommet her i
huset.

NORA (smiler). Jo jeg tror nok at De i grunnen hygger Dem
ganske godt hos oss.

RANK (saktere, ser hen for seg). Og så å skulle gå fra det
alt sammen -

NORA. Snikksnakk; De går ikke fra det.

RANK (som før). - og ikke kunne efterlate seg et fattig
takkens tegn en gang; knapt nok et flyktig savn, - ikke annet enn en
ledig plass, som kan utfylles av den første den beste.

NORA. Og hvis jeg nu ba Dem om -? Nei -

RANK. Om hva?

NORA. Om et stort bevis på Deres vennskap -

RANK. Ja, ja?

NORA. Nei jeg mener, - om en umåtelig stor tjeneste -

RANK. Ville De virkelig for én gangs skyld gjøre meg så
lykkelig?

NORA. Å, De vet jo slett ikke hva det er.

RANK. Nu godt; så si det.

NORA. Nei men jeg kan ikke, doktor Rank; det er noe så
urimelig meget, - både et råd og en hjelp og en tjeneste -

RANK. Så meget desto bedre. Det er meg ufattelig hva De kan
mene. Men så tal dog. Har jeg da ikke Deres fortrolighet?

NORA. Jo det har De som ingen annen. De er min troeste og
beste venn, det vet De nok. Derfor vil jeg også si Dem det. Nu vel da,
doktor Rank; der er noe som De må hjelpe meg å forhindre. De vet hvor
inderlig, hvor ubeskrivelig høyt Torvald elsker meg; aldri et øyeblikk
ville han betenke seg på å gi sitt liv hen for min skyld.

RANK (bøyet mot henne). Nora, - tror De da at han er den
eneste -?

NORA (med et lett rykk). Som -?

RANK. Som gladelig ga sitt liv hen for Deres skyld.

NORA (tungt). Ja så.

RANK. Jeg har svoret ved meg selv at De skulle vite det før
jeg gikk bort. En bedre leilighet ville jeg aldri finne. - Ja, Nora,
nu vet De det. Og nu vet De også at til meg kan De betro Dem som til
ingen annen.

NORA (reiser seg; jevnt og rolig). La meg slippe frem.

RANK (gjør plass for henne, men blir sittende). Nora -

NORA (i døren til forstuen). Helene, bring lampen inn. - (går
hen imot ovnen.) Akk, kjære doktor Rank, dette her var virkelig stygt
av Dem.

RANK (reiser seg). At jeg har elsket Dem fullt så inderlig
som noen annen? Var det stygt?

NORA. Nei, men at De går hen og sier meg det. Det var jo
slett ikke nødvendig -

RANK. Hva mener De? Har De da visst -?

(Stuepiken kommer inn med lampen, setter den på
bordet og går ut igjen.)

RANK. Nora, - fru Helmer -, jeg spør Dem, har De visst noe?

NORA. Å hva vet jeg hva jeg har visst eller ikke visst? Jeg
kan virkelig ikke si Dem -. At De kunne være så klosset, doktor Rank!
Nu var all ting så godt.

RANK. Nå, De har iallfall nu visshet for at jeg står Dem til
rådighet med liv og sjel. Og vil De så tale ut.

NORA (ser på ham). Efter dette?

RANK. Jeg ber Dem, la meg få vite hva det er.

NORA. Ingenting kan De få vite nu.

RANK. Jo, jo. Således må De ikke straffe meg. La meg få lov
til å gjøre for Dem hva der står i menneskelig makt.

NORA. Nu kan De ingenting gjøre for meg. - Forresten behøver
jeg visst ikke noen hjelp. De skal se det er bare innbilninger alt
sammen. Ja visst er det så. Naturligvis! (setter seg i gyngestolen,
ser på ham, smiler.) Jo, De er riktignok en nett herre, doktor
Rank. Synes De ikke De skammer Dem nu lampen er kommet inn?

RANK. Nei; egentlig ikke. Men jeg skal kanskje gå - for
stetse?

NORA. Nei, det skal De da riktignok ikke gjøre. De skal
naturligvis komme her som før. De vet jo godt Torvald kan ikke unnvære
Dem.

RANK. Ja, men De?

NORA. Å, jeg synes alltid her blir så uhyre fornøyelig når
De kommer.

RANK. Det er just det som lokket meg inn på et villspor. De
er meg en gåte. Mangen gang har det forekommet meg at De nesten likså
gjerne ville være sammen med meg som med Helmer.

NORA. Ja, ser De, der er jo noen mennesker som man holder
mest av, og andre mennesker som man nesten helst vil være sammen med.

RANK. Å ja, det er noe i det.

NORA. Da jeg var hjemme, holdt jeg naturligvis mest av
pappa. Men jeg syntes alltid det var så umåtelig morsomt når jeg kunne
stjele meg ned i pikekammeret; for de veiledet meg ikke en smule; og
så talte de alltid så meget fornøyelig seg imellem.

RANK. Aha; det er altså dem jeg har avløst.

NORA (springer opp og hen til ham). Å, kjære, snille doktor
Rank, det mente jeg jo slett ikke. Men De kan vel skjønne at det er
med Torvald liksom med pappa -

(Stuepiken kommer fra forstuen.)

STUEPIKEN. Frue! (hvisker og rekker henne et kort.)

NORA (kaster et øye på kortet). Ah! (stikker det i lommen.)

RANK. Noe galt på ferde?

NORA. Nei, nei, på ingen måte; det er bare noe -; det er min
nye drakt -

RANK. Hvorledes? Der ligger jo Deres drakt.

NORA. Å, ja den; men det er en annen; jeg har bestilt den -;
Torvald må ikke vite det -

RANK. Aha, der har vi altså den store hemmelighet.

NORA. Ja visst; gå bare inn til ham; han sitter i det indre
værelse; hold ham opp så lenge -

RANK. Vær rolig; han skal ikke slippe fra meg. (han går inn
i Helmers værelse.)

NORA (til piken). Og han står og venter i kjøkkenet?

STUEPIKEN. Ja, han kom opp baktrappen -

NORA. Men sa du ikke at her var noen?

STUEPIKEN. Jo, men det hjalp ikke.

NORA. Han vil ikke gå igjen?

STUEPIKEN. Nei, han går ikke før han får talt med fruen.

translation.text:
NORA. Only to sew on my costume. Good heavens, how unreasonable you are. (sits down on the sofa.) Now be nice, Doctor Rank; tomorrow you shall see how beautifully I shall dance; and then you must imagine that I am doing it only for your sake—yes, and then, of course, for Torvald’s; that goes without saying. (takes various things out of the box.) Doctor Rank, sit here, and I shall show you something.

RANK (sits down). What is it?

NORA. Look here. Look!

RANK. Silk stockings.

NORA. Flesh-colored. Aren’t they lovely? Yes, it is so dark in here now; but tomorrow—. No, no, no; you may only see the foot. Oh yes, you may indeed see the upper part too, if you like.

RANK. Hm—

NORA. Why do you look so critical? Perhaps you don’t think they will fit?

RANK. I cannot possibly have any well-founded opinion about that.

NORA (looks at him for a moment). Shame on you. (strikes him lightly on the ear with the stockings.) There, you deserve that. (packs them up again.)

RANK. And what other delights am I to be allowed to see?

NORA. You shall not see another scrap, because you are naughty.

(she hums a little and searches among the things.)

RANK (after a short silence). When I sit here like this, quite intimately together with you, I cannot comprehend—no, I cannot grasp—what would have become of me if I had never come into this house.

NORA (smiles). Oh, I think that, deep down, you enjoy yourself quite well with us.

RANK (more softly, staring ahead). And then to have to leave it all—

NORA. Nonsense; you are not leaving it.

RANK (as before). —and not even be able to leave behind one poor token of gratitude; scarcely even a fleeting sense of loss—nothing but an empty place that can be filled by the first person who comes along.

NORA. And if I were now to ask you to—? No—

RANK. To what?

NORA. To give me a great proof of your friendship—

RANK. Yes, yes?

NORA. No, I mean—to do me an immensely great service—

RANK. Would you really, for once, make me so happy?

NORA. Oh, you do not even know what it is.

RANK. Very well, then; say it.

NORA. No, but I cannot, Doctor Rank; it is something so unreasonably great—advice and help and a service as well—

RANK. So much the better. I cannot imagine what you can mean. But do speak. Do I not have your confidence?

NORA. Yes, you do, as no one else does. You are my most faithful and best friend; you know that. That is why I shall tell you. Very well, then, Doctor Rank; there is something you must help me prevent. You know how deeply, how indescribably dearly Torvald loves me; he would never hesitate for a moment to give his life for my sake.

RANK (leaning toward her). Nora—do you think that he is the only one—?

NORA (with a slight start). Who—?

RANK. Who would gladly give his life for your sake.

NORA (heavily). I see.

RANK. I have sworn to myself that you should know it before I went away. I would never find a better opportunity.—Yes, Nora, now you know it. And now you also know that you can confide in me as in no one else.

NORA (rises; evenly and calmly). Let me pass.

RANK (makes way for her, but remains seated). Nora—

NORA (in the doorway to the hall). Helene, bring in the lamp.—(goes over toward the stove.) Oh, dear Doctor Rank, that was really horrid of you.

RANK (rises). That I have loved you just as deeply as anyone else has? Was that horrid?

NORA. No, but that you should go and tell me so. There was no need at all—

RANK. What do you mean? Did you know—?

(The maid enters with the lamp, puts it on the table, and goes out again.)

RANK. Nora—Mrs. Helmer—I ask you, did you know anything?

NORA. Oh, how do I know what I knew or did not know? I truly cannot tell you—. How could you be so clumsy, Doctor Rank! Everything was so good as it was.

RANK. Well, at any rate, you now know for certain that I am at your disposal, body and soul. And will you now speak openly?

NORA (looks at him). After this?

RANK. I beg you, let me know what it is.

NORA. You cannot know anything now.

RANK. Yes, yes. You must not punish me like this. Allow me to do for you whatever lies within human power.

NORA. Now you can do nothing for me.—Besides, I am sure I do not need any help. You will see that it is all merely imagination. Yes, certainly it is. Of course! (sits down in the rocking chair, looks at him, smiles.) You really are a fine gentleman, Doctor Rank. Don’t you think you ought to be ashamed of yourself now that the lamp has been brought in?

RANK. No; not really. But perhaps I should go—for good?

NORA. No, you certainly must not do that. Of course you must come here as before. You know very well that Torvald cannot do without you.

RANK. Yes, but you?

NORA. Oh, I always think it becomes tremendously enjoyable here when you come.

RANK. That is precisely what led me astray. You are a riddle to me. Many times it has seemed to me that you would almost as gladly be with me as with Helmer.

NORA. Yes, you see, there are some people whom one loves most, and other people whom one would almost rather be with.

RANK. Oh yes, there is something in that.

NORA. When I was at home, naturally I loved Papa most. But I always thought it was so immensely amusing when I could steal downstairs to the maids’ room; for they did not guide me in the least, and they always talked about so many amusing things among themselves.

RANK. Aha; so it is they whom I have replaced.

NORA (springs up and goes over to him). Oh, dear, kind Doctor Rank, I did not mean that at all. But surely you can understand that with Torvald it is just as it was with Papa—

(The maid comes in from the hall.)

MAID. Madam! (whispers and hands her a card.)

NORA (glances at the card). Ah! (puts it in her pocket.)

RANK. Is something wrong?

NORA. No, no, not at all; it is only something—it is my new costume—

RANK. What? Your costume is lying right there.

NORA. Oh yes, that one; but this is another; I have ordered it—Torvald must not know—

RANK. Aha, so there we have the great secret.

NORA. Yes, indeed; just go in to him; he is sitting in the inner room; keep him occupied for a while—

RANK. Do not worry; he shall not get away from me. (he goes into Helmer’s room.)

NORA (to the maid). And he is standing waiting in the kitchen?

MAID. Yes, he came up the back stairs—

NORA. But didn’t you tell him that someone was here?

MAID. Yes, but it did no good.

NORA. He will not go away again?

MAID. No, he will not go until he has spoken with Madam.

vært så snill imot meg. Men jeg kan ikke gjøre ved det. Jeg elsker deg
ikke mer.

NORA. Å, det gjør meg så ondt, Torvald; for du har alltid
vært så snill imot meg. Men jeg kan ikke gjøre ved det. Jeg elsker deg
ikke mer.

wide.text:
NORA. I morgen reiser jeg hjem, - jeg mener, til mitt gamle
hjemsted. Der vil det være lettest for meg å komme inn i et eller
annet.

HELMER. Å du forblindede, uerfarne skapning.

NORA. Jeg må se å få erfaring, Torvald.

HELMER. Forlate ditt hjem, din mann og dine børn! Og du
tenker ikke på hva folk vil si.

NORA. Det kan jeg ikke ta noe hensyn til. Jeg vet bare det
blir nødvendig for meg.

HELMER. Å, det er opprørende. Således kan du svikte dine
helligste plikter.

NORA. Hva regner du da for mine helligste plikter?

HELMER. Og det skal jeg behøve å si deg! Er det ikke
pliktene imot din mann og dine børn?

NORA. Jeg har andre likså hellige plikter.

HELMER. Det har du ikke. Hvilke plikter skulle det være.

NORA. Pliktene imot meg selv.

HELMER. Du er først og fremst hustru og mor.

NORA. Det tror jeg ikke lenger på. Jeg tror at jeg er først
og fremst et menneske, jeg, likså vel som du, - eller iallfall at jeg
skal forsøke på å bli det. Jeg vet nok at de fleste gir deg rett,
Torvald, at det står noe slikt i bøkene. Men jeg kan ikke lenger la
meg nøye med hva de fleste sier, og hva der står i bøkene. Jeg må selv
tenke over de ting og se å få rede på dem.

HELMER. Du skulle ikke ha rede på din stilling i ditt eget
hjem? Har du ikke i sånne spørsmål en usvikelig veileder? Har du ikke
religionen?

NORA. Akk, Torvald, jeg vet jo slett ikke riktig hva
religionen er.

HELMER. Hva er det du sier!

NORA. Jeg vet jo ikke annet enn hva presten Hansen sa da jeg
gikk til konfirmasjonen. Han fortale at religionen var det og det. Når
jeg kommer bort fra alt dette her og blir ensom, så vil jeg undersøke
den sak også. Jeg vil se om det var riktig hva presten Hansen sa,
eller iallfall om det er riktig for meg.

HELMER. Å, slikt er dog uhørt av en så ung kvinne! Men kan
ikke religionen rettlede deg, så la meg dog ryste opp i din
samvittighet. For moralsk følelse har du dog? Eller, svar meg, - har
du kanskje ingen?

NORA. Ja, Torvald, det er ikke godt å svare på det. Jeg vet
det jo slett ikke. Jeg er ganske i villrede med de ting. Jeg vet bare
at jeg har en ganske annen mening om slikt noe enn du. Jeg hører også
nu at lovene er annerledes enn jeg tenkte; men at de love skulle være
riktige, det kan jeg umulig få i mitt hode. En kvinne skal altså ikke
ha rett til å skåne sin gamle døende far, eller til å redde sin manns
liv! Slikt tror jeg ikke på.

HELMER. Du taler som et barn. Du forstår ikke det samfunn du
lever i.

NORA. Nei, det gjør jeg ikke. Men nu vil jeg sette meg inn i
det. Jeg må se å komme efter hvem der har rett, samfunnet eller jeg.

HELMER. Du er syk, Nora; du har feber; jeg tror nesten du er
fra sans og samling.

NORA. Jeg har aldri følt meg så klar og sikker som i natt.

HELMER. Og klar og sikker forlater du din mann og dine børn?

NORA. Ja; det gjør jeg.

HELMER. Så er kun én forklaring mulig.

NORA. Hvilken?

HELMER. Du elsker meg ikke mer.

NORA. Nei, det er just tingen.

HELMER. Nora! - Og det sier du!

NORA. Å, det gjør meg så ondt, Torvald; for du har alltid
vært så snill imot meg. Men jeg kan ikke gjøre ved det. Jeg elsker deg
ikke mer.

HELMER (med tilkjempet fatning). Er dette også en klar og
sikker overbevisning?

NORA. Ja, fullkommen klar og sikker. Det er derfor jeg ikke
vil være her lenger.

HELMER. Og vil du også kunne gjøre meg rede for hvorved jeg
har forspilt din kjærlighet?

NORA. Ja, det kan jeg godt. Det var i aften da det
vidunderlige ikke kom; for da så jeg at du ikke var den mann jeg hadde
tenkt meg.

HELMER. Forklar deg nøyere; jeg begriper deg ikke.

NORA. Jeg har ventet så tålmodig nu i åtte år; for Herregud,
jeg innså jo nok at det vidunderlige kommer ikke sånn til hverdags. Så
brøt dette knusende inn over meg; og da var jeg så usvikelig viss på:
nu kommer det vidunderlige. Da Krogstads brev lå der ute, - aldri falt
det meg med en tanke inn at du kunne ville bøye deg under dette
menneskes vilkår. Jeg var så usvikelig viss på at du ville si til ham:
gjør saken bekjent for hele verden. Og når det var skjedd -

HELMER. Ja hva så? Når jeg hadde prisgitt min egen hustru
til skam og skjensel -!

NORA. Når det var skjedd, da tenkte jeg så usvikelig sikkert
at du ville tre frem og ta alt på deg og si: jeg er den skyldige.

HELMER. Nora -!

NORA. Du mener at jeg aldri ville tatt imot et slikt offer
av deg? Nei, det forstår seg. Men hva ville mine forsikringer gjelde
like overfor dine? - Det var det vidunderlige som jeg gikk og håpet på
i redsel. Og for å hindre det, var det at jeg ville ende mitt liv.

HELMER. Jeg skulle gladelig arbeide netter og dage for deg,
Nora, - bære sorg og savn for din skyld. Men der er ingen som ofrer
sin ære for den man elsker.

NORA. Det har hundre tusen kvinner gjort.

HELMER. Å, du både tenker og du taler som et uforstandig
barn.

NORA. La gå. Men du hverken tenker eller taler som den mann
jeg skal kunne slutte meg til. Da din forskrekkelse var over, - ikke
for hva der truet meg, men for hva du selv var utsatt for, og da hele
faren var forbi, - da var det for deg som om slett ingen ting var
skjedd. Jeg var akkurat som før din lille sanglerke, din dukke, som du
herefter skulle bære dobbelt varlig på hendene, siden den var så skjør
og skrøpelig. (reiser seg.) Torvald, - i den stund gikk det opp for
meg at jeg i åtte år hadde levet her sammen med en fremmed mann, og at
jeg hadde fått tre børn -. Å jeg tåler ikke å tenke på det! Jeg kunne
rive meg selv i stumper og stykker.

HELMER (tungt). Jeg ser det; jeg ser det. Der er visselig
kommet en avgrunn imellem oss. - Å, men, Nora, skulle den ikke kunne
utfylles?

NORA. Således som jeg nu er, er jeg ingen hustru for deg.

HELMER. Jeg har kraft til å bli en annen.

NORA. Måskje, - hvis dukken tas fra deg.

HELMER. Å skilles - skilles fra deg! Nei, nei, Nora, jeg kan
ikke fatte den tanke.

NORA (går inn til høyre). Dess vissere må det skje. (hun
kommer tilbake med sitt yttertøy og en liten vadsekk, som hun setter
på stolen ved bordet.)

HELMER. Nora, Nora, ikke nu! Vent til i morgen.

NORA (tar kåpen på). Jeg kan ikke bli liggende natten over i
en fremmed manns værelser.

HELMER. Men kan vi da ikke bo her som bror og søster -?

translation.text:
NORA. Tomorrow I am going home—I mean, to my old hometown. It will be easiest for me there to find something or other to do.

HELMER. Oh, you blind, inexperienced creature.

NORA. I must try to gain experience, Torvald.

HELMER. Leave your home, your husband, and your children! And you do not think about what people will say.

NORA. I cannot take that into consideration. I know only that it will be necessary for me.

HELMER. Oh, it is outrageous. That you can betray your most sacred duties in this way.

NORA. What, then, do you consider my most sacred duties?

HELMER. And should I need to tell you that! Are they not your duties toward your husband and your children?

NORA. I have other duties just as sacred.

HELMER. You do not. What duties could those be?

NORA. My duties toward myself.

HELMER. First and foremost, you are a wife and mother.

NORA. I no longer believe that. I believe that first and foremost I am a human being, I, just as much as you are—or at any rate that I must try to become one. I know very well that most people agree with you, Torvald, and that something of the sort is written in the books. But I can no longer be satisfied with what most people say and what is written in the books. I must think these things over for myself and try to understand them.

HELMER. Should you not understand your position in your own home? Do you not have an infallible guide in such matters? Do you not have religion?

NORA. Oh, Torvald, I really do not properly know what religion is at all.

HELMER. What are you saying!

NORA. I know nothing beyond what Pastor Hansen said when I went to confirmation classes. He explained that religion was this and that. When I get away from all this here and am alone, I shall examine that matter too. I shall see whether what Pastor Hansen said was right, or at any rate whether it is right for me.

HELMER. Oh, such a thing is unheard of from so young a woman! But if religion cannot guide you, then at least let me awaken your conscience. Surely you have some moral sense? Or answer me—perhaps you have none?

NORA. Yes, Torvald, that is not easy to answer. I really do not know at all. I am completely at a loss about such things. I know only that I have a very different opinion of such matters from yours. I now hear, too, that the laws are different from what I thought; but that those laws should be right is something I cannot possibly get into my head. So a woman is not to have the right to spare her old, dying father, or to save her husband’s life! I do not believe in such things.

HELMER. You speak like a child. You do not understand the society in which you live.

NORA. No, I do not. But now I intend to learn about it. I must try to find out who is right, society or I.

HELMER. You are ill, Nora; you have a fever; I almost believe you are out of your mind.

NORA. I have never felt so clear and certain as I do tonight.

HELMER. And clear and certain, you are leaving your husband and your children?

NORA. Yes; I am.

HELMER. Then only one explanation is possible.

NORA. Which one?

HELMER. You no longer love me.

NORA. No, that is precisely it.

HELMER. Nora!—And you say that!

NORA. Oh, it hurts me so much, Torvald; for you have always been so kind to me. But I cannot help it. I no longer love you.

HELMER (with forced composure). Is this also a clear and certain conviction?

NORA. Yes, perfectly clear and certain. That is why I do not wish to remain here any longer.

HELMER. And will you also be able to explain to me how I have forfeited your love?

NORA. Yes, I can readily do that. It was this evening, when the wonderful thing did not happen; for then I saw that you were not the man I had imagined you to be.

HELMER. Explain yourself more fully; I do not understand you.

NORA. I have waited so patiently for eight years now; for, dear God, I understood well enough that the wonderful thing does not happen every day. Then this crushing blow came upon me; and then I was infallibly certain: now the wonderful thing will happen. When Krogstad’s letter lay out there, it never once entered my mind that you might be willing to submit to that man’s terms. I was infallibly certain that you would say to him: make the matter known to the whole world. And when that had happened—

HELMER. Yes, and then what? When I had exposed my own wife to shame and disgrace—!

NORA. When that had happened, I thought with infallible certainty that you would step forward and take everything upon yourself and say: I am the guilty one.

HELMER. Nora—!

NORA. You think I would never have accepted such a sacrifice from you? No, of course not. But what would my assurances have counted for against yours?—That was the wonderful thing for which I went on hoping in terror. And it was to prevent it that I wanted to end my life.

HELMER. I would gladly work nights and days for you, Nora—bear sorrow and privation for your sake. But no one sacrifices his honor for the person he loves.

NORA. A hundred thousand women have done so.

HELMER. Oh, you both think and speak like a foolish child.

NORA. Let that be so. But you neither think nor speak like the man to whom I could bind myself. When your fright was over—not at what threatened me, but at what you yourself were exposed to—and when all the danger was past, then for you it was as though nothing at all had happened. I was exactly as before, your little songbird, your doll, whom from then on you would carry in your hands with twice the care, since it was so fragile and frail. (rises.) Torvald—in that moment it dawned on me that for eight years I had lived here with a strange man, and that I had had three children—. Oh, I cannot bear to think of it! I could tear myself to pieces.

HELMER (heavily). I see it; I see it. An abyss has indeed opened between us.—Oh, but Nora, could it not be filled in?

NORA. As I am now, I am no wife for you.

HELMER. I have the strength to become another man.

NORA. Perhaps—if your doll is taken away from you.

HELMER. Oh, to part—to part from you! No, no, Nora, I cannot grasp that thought.

NORA (goes into the room on the right). Then it is all the more certain that it must happen. (she returns with her outer clothing and a small traveling bag, which she sets on the chair by the table.)

HELMER. Nora, Nora, not now! Wait until tomorrow.

NORA (puts on her coat). I cannot spend the night in a strange man’s rooms.

HELMER. But could we not live here as brother and sister—?

HELMER (med brevene i hånden). Se her. Vil du se hvorledes
det har opphopet seg. (blar imellem.) Hva er det for noe?

NORA (ved vinduet). Brevet! Å nei, nei, Torvald!

HELMER. To visittkort - fra Rank.

NORA. Fra doktor Rank?

HELMER (ser på dem). Doktor medicinæ Rank. De lå øverst; han
må ha stukket dem inn da han gikk.

NORA. Står der noe på den?

HELMER. Der står et sort kors over navnet. Se her. Det er
dog et uhyggelig påfunn. Det er jo nettopp som han meldte sitt eget
dødsfall.

NORA. Det gjør han også.

HELMER. Hva? Vet du noe? Har han sagt deg noe?

NORA. Ja. Når de kort kommer, så har han tatt avskjed med
oss. Han vil lukke seg inne og dø.

HELMER. Min stakkars venn. Jeg visste jo at jeg ikke skulle
få beholde ham lenge. Men så snart -. Og så gjemmer han seg bort som
et såret dyr.

NORA. Når det skal skje, så er det best at det skjer uten
ord. Ikke sant, Torvald?

HELMER (går opp og ned). Han var så sammenvokset med
oss. Jeg synes ikke jeg kan tenke meg ham borte. Han, med sine
lidelser og med sin ensomhet, ga liksom en skyet bakgrunn for vår
sollyse lykke. - Nå, det er kanskje best således. For ham
iallfall. (stanser.) Og måskje også for oss, Nora. Nu er vi to ganske
henvist til hinannen alene. (slår armene om henne.) Å, du min elskede
hustru; jeg synes ikke jeg kan holde deg fast nok. Vet du vel, Nora, -
mangen gang ønsker jeg at en overhengende fare måtte true deg, for at
jeg kunne vove liv og blod og alt, for din skyld.

NORA (river seg løs og sier sterkt og besluttet). Nu skal du
lese dine breve, Torvald.

HELMER. Nei, nei, ikke i natt. Jeg vil være hos deg, min
elskede hustru.

NORA. Med dødstanken på din venn -?

HELMER. Du har rett. Dette har rystet oss begge; der er
kommet uskjønnhet inn imellem oss; tanker om død og oppløsning. Dette
må vi søke frigjørelse for. Inntil da -. Vil vi gå hver til sitt.

NORA (om hans hals). Torvald, - god natt! God natt!

HELMER (kysser henne på pannen). God natt, du min lille
sangfugl. Sov godt, Nora. Nu leser jeg brevene igjennem. (han går med
pakken inn i sitt værelse og lukker døren efter seg.)

NORA (med forvillede øyne, famler omkring, griper Helmers
domino, slår den omkring seg og hvisker hurtig, hest og avbrutt:)
Aldri se ham mer. Aldri. Aldri. (kaster sitt sjal over hodet.) Aldri
se børnene mer heller. Ikke dem heller. Aldri; aldri. - Å, det iskolde
sorte vann. Å, det bunnløse-; dette -. Å, når det bare var over. - Nu
har han det; nu leser han det. Å nei, nei; ikke ennu. Torvald, farvel
du og børnene -

(Hun vil styrte ut gjennem forstuen; i det samme river
Helmer sin dør opp og står der med et åpnet brev i
hånden.)

HELMER. Nora!

NORA (skriker høyt). Ah -!

HELMER. Hva er det? Vet du hva der står i dette brev?

NORA. Ja, jeg vet det. La meg gå! La meg komme ut!

HELMER (holder henne tilbake). Hvor vil du hen?

NORA (prøver å rive seg løs). Du skal ikke redde meg, Torvald!

HELMER (tumler tilbake). Sant! Er det sant hva han skriver?
Forferdelig! Nei, nei; det er jo umulig at dette kan være sant.

NORA. Det er sant. Jeg har elsket deg over alt i verdens
rike.

HELMER. Å kom ikke her med tåpelige utflukter.

NORA (et skritt imot ham). Torvald -!

HELMER. Du ulykksalige, - hva er det du har foretatt deg!

NORA. La meg komme bort. Du skal ikke bære det for min
skyld. Du skal ikke ta det på deg.

HELMER. Ikke noe komediespill. (låser forstuedøren av.) Her
blir du og står meg til regnskap. Forstår du hva du har gjort? Svar
meg! Forstår du det?

NORA (ser ufravendt på ham og sier med et stivnende
uttrykk:) Ja, nu begynner jeg å forstå det til bunns.

HELMER (går omkring på gulvet). Å hvor forferdelig jeg er
våknet opp. I alle disse åtte år, - hun som var min lyst og stolthet,
- en hyklerske, en løgnerske, - verre, verre, -en forbryterske! - Å,
denne bunnløse heslighet, som ligger i alt dette! Fy, fy!

NORA (tier og ser fremdeles ufravendt på ham).

HELMER (stanser foran henne). Jeg burde ha anet at noe slikt
ville skje. Jeg burde ha forutsett det. Alle din fars lettsindige
grunnsetninger. - Ti! Alle din fars lettsindige grunnsetninger har du
tatt i arv. Ingen religion, ingen moral, ingen pliktfølelse -. Å, hvor
jeg er blitt straffet for at jeg så igjennem fingrene med ham. For din
skyld gjorde jeg det; og således lønner du meg.

NORA. Ja, således.

HELMER. Nu har du ødelagt hele min lykke. Hele min fremtid
har du forspilt for meg. Å, det er forferdelig å tenke på. Jeg er i et
samvittighetsløst menneskes vold; han kan gjøre med meg hva han vil,
forlange av meg hva det skal være, byde og befale over meg som det
lyster ham; - jeg tør ikke kny. Og så jammerlig må jeg synke ned og gå
til grunne for en lettsindig kvinnes skyld!

NORA. Når jeg er ute av verden, så er du fri.

HELMER. Å ingen fakter. Slike talemåter hadde din far også
på rede hånd. Hva ville det nytte meg at du var ute av verden, som du
sier? Ikke det ringeste ville det nytte meg. Han kan gjøre saken
bekjent allikevel; og gjør han det, så blir jeg kanskje mistenkt for å
ha vært vitende om din forbryterske handling. Man vil kanskje tro at
jeg har stått bakved, - at det er meg som har tilskyndet deg! Og alt
dette kan jeg takke deg for, deg, som jeg har båret på hendene gjennem
hele vårt ekteskap. Forstår du nu hva du har gjort imot meg?

NORA (med kold ro). Ja.

HELMER. Dette er så utrolig at jeg ikke kan fastholde
det. Men vi må se å komme til rette. Ta sjalet av. Ta det av, sier
jeg! Jeg må se å tilfredsstille ham på en eller annen måte. Saken må
dysses ned for enhver pris. - Og hva deg og meg angår, så må det se ut
som om alt var imellem oss liksom før. Men naturligvis kun for verdens
øyne. Du blir altså fremdeles her i huset; det er en selvfølge. Men
børnene får du ikke lov til å oppdra; dem tør jeg ikke betro deg -. Å,
å måtte si dette til henne som jeg har elsket så høyt, og som jeg ennu
-! Nå, det må være forbi. Her efter dags gjelder det ikke lenger
lykken; det gjelder bare å redde restene, stumpene, skinnet. (det
ringer på entréklokken.)

HELMER (farer sammen). Hva er det? Så sent. Skulle det
forferdeligste -! Skulle han -! Skjul deg, Nora! Si du er syk.

translation.text:
HELMER (with the letters in his hand). Look here. See how they have piled up. (leafing through them.) What is this?

NORA (at the window). The letter! Oh no, no, Torvald!

HELMER. Two calling cards—from Rank.

NORA. From Doctor Rank?

HELMER (looking at them). Doctor of Medicine Rank. They were on top; he must have slipped them in when he left.

NORA. Is there anything written on them?

HELMER. There is a black cross above the name. Look here. It is a rather uncanny idea. It is exactly as though he were announcing his own death.

NORA. That is what he is doing.

HELMER. What? Do you know something? Has he told you anything?

NORA. Yes. When those cards arrive, he has taken leave of us. He intends to shut himself in and die.

HELMER. My poor friend. I knew, of course, that I would not be allowed to keep him for long. But so soon—. And then he hides himself away like a wounded animal.

NORA. When it has to happen, it is best that it happen without words. Is that not so, Torvald?

HELMER (paces up and down). He was so closely bound up with us. I do not think I can imagine him gone. He, with his sufferings and his loneliness, gave, as it were, a clouded background to our sunlit happiness.—Well, perhaps it is best this way. For him, at any rate. (stops.) And perhaps for us too, Nora. Now the two of us are left entirely to each other alone. (puts his arms around her.) Oh, my beloved wife; I do not think I can hold you tightly enough. Do you know, Nora—many a time I wish that some imminent danger might threaten you, so that I could risk life and blood and everything for your sake.

NORA (tears herself free and says loudly and resolutely). Now you shall read your letters, Torvald.

HELMER. No, no, not tonight. I want to be with you, my beloved wife.

NORA. With the thought of your friend’s death—?

HELMER. You are right. This has shaken us both; something ugly has come between us; thoughts of death and dissolution. We must seek release from this. Until then—. We will each go our own way.

NORA (with her arms around his neck). Torvald—good night! Good night!

HELMER (kisses her on the forehead). Good night, my little songbird. Sleep well, Nora. Now I shall read through the letters. (he takes the bundle into his room and closes the door behind him.)

NORA (with wild eyes, gropes about, seizes Helmer’s domino, wraps it around herself, and whispers rapidly, hoarsely, and brokenly:) Never see him again. Never. Never. (throws her shawl over her head.) Never see the children again either. Not them either. Never; never.—Oh, the ice-cold black water. Oh, the bottomless—; this—. Oh, if only it were over.—Now he has it; now he is reading it. Oh no, no; not yet. Torvald, farewell, you and the children—

(She is about to rush out through the hall; at that same moment Helmer tears open his door and stands there with an opened letter in his hand.)

HELMER. Nora!

NORA (screams loudly). Ah—!

HELMER. What is this? Do you know what is written in this letter?

NORA. Yes, I know. Let me go! Let me get out!

HELMER (holds her back). Where are you going?

NORA (tries to tear herself free). You must not save me, Torvald!

HELMER (reels backward). True! Is what he writes true? Terrible! No, no; it is impossible that this can be true.

NORA. It is true. I have loved you above everything in the whole world.

HELMER. Oh, do not come to me with foolish evasions.

NORA (takes a step toward him). Torvald—!

HELMER. You wretched woman—what have you done!

NORA. Let me go away. You must not bear it for my sake. You must not take it upon yourself.

HELMER. No playacting. (locks the hall door.) You will remain here and answer to me. Do you understand what you have done? Answer me! Do you understand it?

NORA (looks steadily at him and says with an expression that is growing rigid:) Yes, now I am beginning to understand it to the very bottom.

HELMER (paces about the floor). Oh, what a terrible awakening this is. During all these eight years—she who was my joy and pride—a hypocrite, a liar—worse, worse—a criminal!—Oh, the bottomless ugliness that lies in all this! Shame, shame!

NORA (remains silent and continues to look steadily at him).

HELMER (stops in front of her). I should have suspected that something like this would happen. I should have foreseen it. All your father’s frivolous principles.—Be silent! You have inherited all your father’s frivolous principles. No religion, no morality, no sense of duty—. Oh, how I have been punished for turning a blind eye to him. I did it for your sake; and this is how you repay me.

NORA. Yes, this is how.

HELMER. Now you have destroyed all my happiness. You have ruined my entire future for me. Oh, it is terrible to think of. I am in the power of an unscrupulous man; he can do with me whatever he pleases, demand anything at all of me, order and command me as he sees fit—and I dare not make a sound. And I must sink so miserably and be ruined because of a frivolous woman!

NORA. When I am no longer in this world, then you will be free.

HELMER. Oh, no theatrics. Your father always had such phrases ready to hand too. What good would it do me if you were no longer in this world, as you say? It would not do me the slightest good. He could still make the matter public; and if he does, I may perhaps be suspected of having known about your criminal act. People may perhaps think that I was behind it—that it was I who urged you on! And I have you to thank for all this—you, whom I have borne upon my hands throughout our entire marriage. Do you understand now what you have done to me?

NORA (with cold calm). Yes.

HELMER. This is so incredible that I cannot grasp it. But we must try to settle matters. Take off the shawl. Take it off, I tell you! I must try to satisfy him in one way or another. The matter must be hushed up at any cost.—And as for you and me, it must appear as though everything between us were just as before. But naturally only in the eyes of the world. You will therefore continue to remain here in the house; that goes without saying. But you will not be allowed to bring up the children; I dare not entrust them to you—. Oh, to have to say this to her whom I have loved so deeply, and whom I still—! Well, it must be over. From this day forward, it is no longer a question of happiness; it is only a question of saving the remains, the fragments, the appearance. (the entrance bell rings.)

HELMER (starts). What is that? So late. Could the most terrible thing—! Could he—! Hide yourself, Nora! Say you are ill.

pouvait rallumer les sentiments que vous aviez eus pour moi, c'était de
vous faire voir que les miens étaient changés; mais de vous le faire
voir en feignant de vous le cacher, et comme si je n'eusse pas eu la
force de vous l'avouer. Je m'arrêtai à cette résolution; mais qu'elle me
fut difficile à prendre, et qu'en vous revoyant elle me parut impossible
à exécuter! Je fus prête cent fois à éclater par mes reproches et par
mes pleurs; l'état où j'étais encore par ma santé me servit à vous
déguiser mon trouble et mon affliction. Je fus soutenue ensuite par le
plaisir de dissimuler avec vous, comme vous dissimuliez avec moi;
néanmoins, je me faisais une si grande violence pour vous dire et pour
vous écrire que je vous aimais, que vous vîtes plus tôt que je n'avais
eu dessein de vous laisser voir, que mes sentiments étaient changés.
Vous en fûtes blessé; vous vous en plaignîtes. Je tâchais de vous
rassurer; mais c'était d'une manière si forcée, que vous en étiez encore
mieux persuadé que je ne vous aimais plus. Enfin, je fis tout ce que
j'avais eu intention de faire. La bizarrerie de votre coeur vous fit
revenir vers moi, à mesure que vous voyiez que je m'éloignais de vous.
J'ai joui de tout le plaisir que peut donner la vengeance; il m'a paru
que vous m'aimiez mieux que vous n'aviez jamais fait, et je vous ai fait
voir que je ne vous aimais plus. J'ai eu lieu de croire que vous aviez
entièrement abandonné celle pour qui vous m'aviez quittée. J'ai eu aussi
des raisons pour être persuadée que vous ne lui aviez jamais parlé de
moi; mais votre retour et votre discrétion n'ont pu réparer votre
légèreté. Votre coeur a été partagé entre moi et une autre, vous m'avez
trompée; cela suffit pour m'ôter le plaisir d'être aimée de vous, comme
je croyais mériter de l'être, et pour me laisser dans cette résolution
que j'ai prise de ne vous voir jamais, et dont vous êtes si surpris.

wide.text:
«Je vous ai trop aimé pour vous laisser croire que le changement qui
vous paraît en moi soit un effet de ma légèreté; je veux vous apprendre
que votre infidélité en est la cause. Vous êtes bien surpris que je vous
parle de votre infidélité; vous me l'aviez cachée avec tant d'adresse,
et j'ai pris tant de soin de vous cacher que je la savais, que vous avez
raison d'être étonné qu'elle me soit connue. Je suis surprise moi-même,
que j'aie pu ne vous en rien faire paraître. Jamais douleur n'a été
pareille à la mienne. Je croyais que vous aviez pour moi une passion
violente; je ne vous cachais plus celle que j'avais pour vous, et dans
le temps que je vous la laissais voir tout entière, j'appris que vous me
trompiez, que vous en aimiez une autre, et que, selon toutes les
apparences, vous me sacrifiez à cette nouvelle maîtresse. Je le sus le
jour de la course de bague; c'est ce qui fit que je n'y allais point. Je
feignis d'être malade pour cacher le désordre de mon esprit; mais je le
devins en effet, et mon corps ne put supporter une si violente
agitation. Quand je commençai à me porter mieux, je feignis encore
d'être fort mal, afin d'avoir un prétexte de ne vous point voir et de ne
vous point écrire. Je voulus avoir du temps pour résoudre de quelle
sorte j'en devais user avec vous; je pris et je quittai vingt fois les
mêmes résolutions; mais enfin je vous trouvai indigne de voir ma
douleur, et je résolus de ne vous la point faire paraître. Je voulus
blesser votre orgueil, en vous faisant voir que ma passion
s'affaiblissait d'elle-même. Je crus diminuer par là le prix du
sacrifice que vous en faisiez; je ne voulus pas que vous eussiez le
plaisir de montrer combien je vous aimais pour en paraître plus aimable.
Je résolus de vous écrire des lettres tièdes et languissantes, pour
jeter dans l'esprit de celle à qui vous les donniez, que l'on cessait de
vous aimer. Je ne voulus pas qu'elle eut le plaisir d'apprendre que je
savais qu'elle triomphait de moi, ni augmenter son triomphe par mon
désespoir et par mes reproches. Je pensais que je ne vous punirais pas
assez en rompant avec vous, et que je ne vous donnerais qu'une légère
douleur si je cessais de vous aimer lorsque vous ne m'aimiez plus. Je
trouvai qu'il fallait que vous m'aimassiez pour sentir le mal de n'être
point aimé, que j'éprouvais si cruellement. Je crus que si quelque chose
pouvait rallumer les sentiments que vous aviez eus pour moi, c'était de
vous faire voir que les miens étaient changés; mais de vous le faire
voir en feignant de vous le cacher, et comme si je n'eusse pas eu la
force de vous l'avouer. Je m'arrêtai à cette résolution; mais qu'elle me
fut difficile à prendre, et qu'en vous revoyant elle me parut impossible
à exécuter! Je fus prête cent fois à éclater par mes reproches et par
mes pleurs; l'état où j'étais encore par ma santé me servit à vous
déguiser mon trouble et mon affliction. Je fus soutenue ensuite par le
plaisir de dissimuler avec vous, comme vous dissimuliez avec moi;
néanmoins, je me faisais une si grande violence pour vous dire et pour
vous écrire que je vous aimais, que vous vîtes plus tôt que je n'avais
eu dessein de vous laisser voir, que mes sentiments étaient changés.
Vous en fûtes blessé; vous vous en plaignîtes. Je tâchais de vous
rassurer; mais c'était d'une manière si forcée, que vous en étiez encore
mieux persuadé que je ne vous aimais plus. Enfin, je fis tout ce que
j'avais eu intention de faire. La bizarrerie de votre coeur vous fit
revenir vers moi, à mesure que vous voyiez que je m'éloignais de vous.
J'ai joui de tout le plaisir que peut donner la vengeance; il m'a paru
que vous m'aimiez mieux que vous n'aviez jamais fait, et je vous ai fait
voir que je ne vous aimais plus. J'ai eu lieu de croire que vous aviez
entièrement abandonné celle pour qui vous m'aviez quittée. J'ai eu aussi
des raisons pour être persuadée que vous ne lui aviez jamais parlé de
moi; mais votre retour et votre discrétion n'ont pu réparer votre
légèreté. Votre coeur a été partagé entre moi et une autre, vous m'avez
trompée; cela suffit pour m'ôter le plaisir d'être aimée de vous, comme
je croyais mériter de l'être, et pour me laisser dans cette résolution
que j'ai prise de ne vous voir jamais, et dont vous êtes si surpris.

Madame de Clèves lut cette lettre et la relut plusieurs fois, sans
savoir néanmoins ce qu'elle avait lu. Elle voyait seulement que monsieur
de Nemours ne l'aimait pas comme elle l'avait pensé, et qu'il en aimait
d'autres qu'il trompait comme elle. Quelle vue et quelle connaissance
pour une personne de son humeur, qui avait une passion violente, qui
venait d'en donner des marques à un homme qu'elle en jugeait indigne, et
à un autre qu'elle maltraitait pour l'amour de lui! Jamais affliction
n'a été si piquante et si vive: il lui semblait que ce qui faisait
l'aigreur de cette affliction était ce qui s'était passé dans cette
journée, et que, si monsieur de Nemours n'eût point eu lieu de croire
qu'elle l'aimait, elle ne se fût pas souciée qu'il en eût aimé une
autre. Mais elle se trompait elle-même; et ce mal qu'elle trouvait si
insupportable était la jalousie avec toutes les horreurs dont elle peut
être accompagnée. Elle voyait par cette lettre que monsieur de Nemours
avait une galanterie depuis longtemps. Elle trouvait que celle qui avait
écrit la lettre avait de l'esprit et du mérite; elle lui paraissait
digne d'être aimée; elle lui trouvait plus de courage qu'elle ne s'en
trouvait à elle-même, et elle enviait la force qu'elle avait eue de
cacher ses sentiments à monsieur de Nemours. Elle voyait, par la fin de
la lettre, que cette personne se croyait aimée; elle pensait que la
discrétion que ce prince lui avait fait paraître, et dont elle avait été
si touchée, n'était peut-être que l'effet de la passion qu'il avait pour
cette autre personne, à qui il craignait de déplaire. Enfin elle
pensait tout ce qui pouvait augmenter son affliction et son désespoir.
Quels retours ne fit-elle point sur elle-même! quelles réflexions sur
les conseils que sa mère lui avait donnés! Combien se repentit-elle de

“I have loved you too much to let you believe that the change you perceive in me is an effect of my fickleness; I want you to know that your unfaithfulness is the cause of it. You are greatly surprised that I speak to you of your unfaithfulness; you had concealed it from me with such skill, and I took such care to conceal from you that I knew of it, that you have reason to be astonished that it is known to me. I am surprised myself that I was able to keep you from seeing any sign of it. Never has any sorrow equaled mine. I believed that you had a violent passion for me; I no longer concealed from you the passion I had for you, and at the very time when I was letting you see it in its entirety, I learned that you were deceiving me, that you loved another woman, and that, to all appearances, you were sacrificing me to this new mistress. I learned it on the day of the running at the ring; that is why I did not go. I pretended to be ill in order to conceal the disorder of my mind; but I truly became ill, and my body could not withstand so violent an agitation. When I began to recover, I still pretended to be very ill, so that I might have a pretext for neither seeing you nor writing to you. I wanted time to decide how I ought to behave toward you; twenty times I adopted and abandoned the same resolutions; but at last I found you unworthy of seeing my sorrow, and I resolved not to let it show. I wanted to wound your pride by making you see that my passion was weakening of its own accord. I believed that I would thereby diminish the value of the sacrifice you were making of it; I did not want you to have the pleasure of showing how much I loved you in order to appear more lovable on that account. I resolved to write you cold and languid letters, so as to put into the mind of the woman to whom you gave them the thought that you were ceasing to be loved. I did not want her to have the pleasure of learning that I knew she was triumphing over me, nor to increase her triumph by my despair and my reproaches. I thought that I would not punish you enough by breaking with you, and that I would cause you only slight pain if I ceased to love you when you no longer loved me. I concluded that you had to love me in order to feel the pain of not being loved, which I was experiencing so cruelly. I believed that if anything could rekindle the feelings you had once had for me, it was to make you see that mine had changed; but to make you see it while pretending to conceal it from you, and as though I had not had the strength to confess it to you. I settled upon this resolution; but how difficult it was for me to make, and, when I saw you again, how impossible it seemed to carry out! A hundred times I was on the verge of bursting forth in reproaches and tears; the state to which my health had still reduced me helped me disguise my distress and affliction from you. I was then sustained by the pleasure of dissembling with you, as you dissembled with me; nevertheless, I did myself such great violence in order to tell you and write to you that I loved you that you saw sooner than I had intended to let you see that my feelings had changed. You were hurt by it; you complained of it. I tried to reassure you; but it was in so forced a manner that you were still more thoroughly convinced that I no longer loved you. At last, I did everything I had intended to do. The capriciousness of your heart made you return to me as you saw me withdrawing from you. I have enjoyed all the pleasure that vengeance can give; it has seemed to me that you loved me more than you had ever done, and I have made you see that I no longer loved you. I have had reason to believe that you had entirely abandoned the woman for whom you had left me. I have also had reasons to be convinced that you had never spoken to her about me; but your return and your discretion have not been able to make amends for your fickleness. Your heart has been divided between me and another woman; you have deceived me. That is enough to deprive me of the pleasure of being loved by you as I believed I deserved to be, and to leave me in the resolution I have made never to see you again, at which you are so surprised.

Madame de Clèves read this letter and reread it several times, without, however, knowing what she had read. She saw only that Monsieur de Nemours did not love her as she had thought, and that he loved other women whom he deceived as he deceived her. What a sight and what knowledge for a person of her disposition, who had a violent passion, who had just given signs of it to a man she judged unworthy of it, and to another man whom she treated badly for his sake! Never had affliction been so piercing and so acute: it seemed to her that what made this affliction so bitter was what had happened that day, and that, if Monsieur de Nemours had had no reason to believe that she loved him, she would not have cared that he had loved another woman. But she was deceiving herself; and the pain she found so unbearable was jealousy, with all the horrors that may accompany it. She saw from this letter that Monsieur de Nemours had long been engaged in a love affair. She found that the woman who had written the letter had intelligence and merit; she seemed to her worthy of being loved; she found in her more courage than she found in herself, and she envied the strength she had shown in concealing her feelings from Monsieur de Nemours. She saw from the end of the letter that this person believed herself loved; she thought that the discretion this prince had shown her, and by which she had been so deeply moved, was perhaps only the effect of the passion he had for that other person, whom he feared to displease. In short, she thought of everything that could increase her affliction and her despair. How she turned her thoughts back upon herself! What reflections she made upon the advice her mother had given her! How she repented of not having persisted in withdrawing from society, despite Monsieur de Clèves, or of not having followed the thought she had had of confessing to him the inclination she had for Monsieur de Nemours! She found that she would have done better to reveal it to a husband whose goodness she knew, and who would have had an interest in concealing it, than to let it be seen by a man who was unworthy of it, who deceived her, who perhaps sacrificed her, and who desired to be loved by her only out of pride and vanity. In short, she found that all the misfortunes that could befall her, and all the extremes to which she might be driven, were less dreadful than having let Monsieur de Nemours see that she loved him and knowing that he loved another woman. All that consoled her was the thought that, after acquiring this knowledge, she at least had nothing more to fear from herself, and that she would be entirely cured of the inclination she had for this prince.”
