faute... et quelle faute pour un jeune prêtre!

local.text:
--Il faut bien que je parte, car je vous aime avec passion; c'est une
faute... et quelle faute pour un jeune prêtre!

wide.text:
Certaine de l'affection de Julien, peut-être sa vertu eût trouvé des
forces contre lui. Tremblante de le perdre à jamais, sa passion l'égara
jusqu'au point de reprendre la main de Julien que, dans sa distraction,
il avait laissée appuyée sur le dossier d'une chaise. Cette action
réveilla ce jeune ambitieux: il eût voulu qu'elle eût pour témoins tous
ces nobles si fiers qui, à table, lorsqu'il était au bas bout avec les
enfants, le regardaient avec un sourire si protecteur. Cette femme ne
peut plus me mépriser: dans ce cas, se dit-il, je dois être sensible à
sa beauté; je me dois à moi-même d'être son amant! Une telle idée ne lui
fût pas venue avant les confidences naïves faites par son ami.

La détermination subite qu'il venait de prendre forma une distraction
agréable. Il se disait: il faut que j'aie une de ces deux femmes, il
s'aperçut qu'il aurait beaucoup mieux aimé faire la cour à Mme Derville;
ce n'est pas qu'elle fût plus agréable, mais toujours elle l'avait vu
précepteur honoré pour sa science, et non pas ouvrier charpentier, avec
une veste de ratine pliée sous le bras, comme il était apparu à Mme de
Rênal.

C'était précisément comme jeune ouvrier, rougissant jusqu'au blanc des
yeux, arrêté à la porte de la maison et n'osant sonner, que Mme de Rênal
se le figurait avec le plus de charme. Cette femme, que les bourgeois du
pays disaient si hautaine, songeait rarement au rang et la moindre
certitude l'emportait de beaucoup dans son esprit sur la promesse de
caractère faite par le rang d'un homme. Un charretier qui eût montré de
la bravoure eût été plus brave dans son esprit qu'un terrible capitaine
de hussards garni de sa moustache et de sa pipe. Elle croyait l'âme de
Julien plus noble que celle de tous ses cousins, tous gentilshommes de
race et plusieurs d'entre eux titrés.

En poursuivant la revue de sa position, Julien vit qu'il ne fallait pas
songer à la conquête de Mme Derville, qui s'apercevait probablement du
goût que Mme de Rênal montrait pour lui. Forcé de revenir à celle-ci:
Que connais-je du caractère de cette femme? se dit Julien. Seulement
ceci: avant mon voyage, je lui prenais la main, elle la retirait;
aujourd'hui je retire ma main, elle la saisit et la serre. Belle
occasion de lui rendre tous les mépris qu'elle a eus pour moi. Dieu sait
combien elle a eu d'amants! elle ne se décide peut-être en ma faveur
qu'à cause de la facilité des entrevues.

Tel est, hélas! le malheur d'une excessive civilisation! A vingt ans,
l'éducation d'un jeune homme, s'il a quelque éducation, est à mille
lieues du laisser-aller, sans lequel l'amour n'est souvent que le plus
ennuyeux des devoirs.

Je me dois d'autant plus, continua la petite vanité de Julien, de
réussir auprès de cette femme, que si jamais je fais fortune et que
quelqu'un me reproche le bas emploi de précepteur, je pourrai faire
entendre que l'amour m'avait jeté à cette place. Julien éloigna de
nouveau sa main de celle de Mme de Rênal, puis il la reprit en la
serrant. Comme on rentrait au salon, vers minuit, Mme de Rênal lui dit à
mi-voix:

--Vous nous quitterez, vous partirez?

Julien répondit en soupirant:

--Il faut bien que je parte, car je vous aime avec passion; c'est une
faute... et quelle faute pour un jeune prêtre!

Mme de Rênal s'appuya sur son bras, et avec tant d'abandon que sa joue
sentit la chaleur de celle de Julien.

Les nuits de ces deux êtres furent bien différentes. Mme de Rênal était
exaltée par les transports de la volupté morale la plus élevée. Une
jeune fille coquette qui aime de bonne heure s'accoutume au trouble de
l'amour; quand elle arrive à l'âge de la vraie passion, le charme de la
nouveauté manque. Comme Mme de Rênal n'avait jamais lu de romans, toutes
les nuances de son bonheur étaient neuves pour elle. Aucune triste
vérité ne venait la glacer, pas même le spectre de l'avenir. Elle se vit
aussi heureuse dans dix ans qu'elle l'était en ce moment. L'idée même de
la vertu et de la fidélité jurée à M. de Rênal, qui l'avait agitée
quelques jours auparavant, se présenta en vain, on la renvoya comme un
hôte importun. Jamais je n'accorderai rien à Julien se dit Mme de Rênal,
nous vivrons à l'avenir comme nous vivons depuis un mois. Ce sera un
ami.




CHAPITRE XIV

LES CISEAUX ANGLAIS

    Une jeune fille de seize ans avait un teint de rose,
    et elle mettait du rouge.

    POLIDORI


Pour Julien, l'offre de Fouqué lui avait en effet enlevé tout bonheur;
il ne pouvait s'arrêter à aucun parti.

Hélas! peut-être manqué-je de caractère, j'eusse été un mauvais soldat
de Napoléon. Du moins, ajouta-t-il, ma petite intrigue avec la maîtresse
du logis va me distraire un moment.

Heureusement pour lui, même dans ce petit incident subalterne,
l'intérieur de son âme répondait mal à son langage cavalier. Il avait
peur de Mme de Rênal à cause de sa robe si jolie. Cette robe était à ses
yeux l'avant-garde de Paris. Son orgueil ne voulut rien laisser au
hasard et à l'inspiration du moment. D'après les confidences de Fouqué
et le peu qu'il avait lu sur l'amour dans sa bible, il se fit un plan de
campagne fort détaillé. Comme, sans se l'avouer, il était fort troublé,
il écrivit ce plan.

Le lendemain matin au salon, Mme de Rênal fut un instant seule avec lui:

--N'avez-vous point d'autre nom que Julien? lui dit-elle.

A cette demande si flatteuse, notre héros ne sut que répondre. Cette
circonstance n'était pas prévue dans son plan. Sans cette sottise de
faire un plan, l'esprit vif de Julien l'eût bien servi, la surprise
n'eût fait qu'ajouter à la vivacité de ses aperçus.

Il fut gauche et s'exagéra sa gaucherie. Mme de Rênal la lui pardonna
bien vite. Elle y vit l'effet d'une candeur charmante. Et ce qui
manquait précisément à ses yeux à cet homme, auquel on trouvait tant de
génie, c'était l'air de la candeur.

--Ton petit précepteur m'inspire beaucoup de méfiance, lui disait
quelquefois Mme Derville. Je lui trouve l'air de penser toujours et de
n'agir qu'avec politique. C'est un sournois.

Julien resta profondément humilié du malheur de n'avoir su que répondre
à Mme de Rênal.

Un homme comme moi se doit de réparer cet échec, et saisissant le moment
où l'on passait d'une pièce à l'autre, il crut de son devoir de donner
un baiser à Mme de Rênal.

translation.text:
Certain of Julien’s affection, perhaps her virtue would have found the strength to resist him. Trembling at the thought of losing him forever, her passion led her astray to the point of taking Julien’s hand again, which, in his distraction, he had left resting on the back of a chair. This action roused the young man’s ambition: he would have liked all those proud nobles to have witnessed it, those who, at table, when he sat at the lower end with the children, looked at him with such a patronizing smile. This woman can no longer despise me: in that case, he told himself, I must be sensitive to her beauty; I owe it to myself to become her lover! Such an idea would not have occurred to him before the guileless confidences his friend had shared with him.

The sudden resolution he had just made provided a pleasant distraction. He told himself: I must have one of these two women; he realized that he would have much preferred to court Mme Derville; not that she was more attractive, but she had always seen him as a tutor honored for his learning, and not as a carpenter’s workman, with a coarse woolen jacket folded under his arm, as he had appeared to Mme de Rênal.

It was precisely as a young workman, blushing up to the whites of his eyes, stopped at the door of the house and not daring to ring, that Mme de Rênal pictured him at his most charming. This woman, whom the local bourgeois called so haughty, rarely thought about rank, and the slightest certainty carried far more weight in her mind than the promise of character afforded by a man’s rank. A carter who had shown bravery would, in her mind, have been braver than a formidable captain of hussars adorned with his mustache and his pipe. She believed Julien’s soul nobler than those of all her cousins, all gentlemen of ancient lineage and several of them titled.

As he continued reviewing his position, Julien saw that he must not think of conquering Mme Derville, who was probably aware of the liking Mme de Rênal showed for him. Forced to return to the latter: What do I know of this woman’s character? Julien asked himself. Only this: before my journey, I took her hand and she withdrew it; today I withdraw my hand, and she seizes it and presses it. A fine opportunity to repay her for all the contempt she has shown me. God knows how many lovers she has had! Perhaps she decides in my favor only because of the ease with which we can meet.

Such, alas, is the misfortune of excessive civilization! At twenty, a young man’s education, if he has any education at all, is a thousand leagues removed from the freedom from constraint without which love is often merely the most tedious of duties.

I owe it all the more to myself, Julien’s petty vanity continued, to succeed with this woman, because if I ever make my fortune and someone reproaches me for the lowly employment of tutor, I shall be able to hint that love had cast me into that position. Julien once again drew his hand away from Mme de Rênal’s, then took hers again, pressing it. As they were returning to the drawing room, around midnight, Mme de Rênal said to him in a low voice:

“You will leave us, you will go away?”

Julien replied with a sigh:

“I really must go, for I love you passionately; it is a sin... and what a sin for a young priest!”

Mme de Rênal leaned upon his arm, and with such abandon that her cheek felt the warmth of Julien’s.

The nights of these two beings were very different. Mme de Rênal was exalted by the transports of the most elevated moral ecstasy. A coquettish young girl who begins loving early grows accustomed to the turmoil of love; when she reaches the age of true passion, the charm of novelty is lacking. As Mme de Rênal had never read novels, every nuance of her happiness was new to her. No sad truth came to chill her, not even the specter of the future. She saw herself as happy ten years hence as she was at that moment. Even the idea of virtue and of the fidelity she had sworn to M. de Rênal, which had troubled her a few days earlier, presented itself in vain; it was sent away like an unwelcome guest. I shall never grant Julien anything, Mme de Rênal told herself; from now on we shall live as we have lived for the past month. He will be a friend.




CHAPTER XIV

THE ENGLISH SCISSORS

    A sixteen-year-old girl had a rosy complexion,
    and she put on rouge.

    POLIDORI


For Julien, Fouqué’s offer had indeed deprived him of all happiness; he could not settle upon any course.

Alas! perhaps I lack character; I would have made a bad soldier of Napoleon. At least, he added, my little intrigue with the lady of the house will distract me for a while.

Fortunately for him, even in this minor, subordinate incident, the depths of his soul corresponded poorly to his cavalier language. He was afraid of Mme de Rênal because of her very pretty dress. In his eyes, that dress was the vanguard of Paris. His pride would leave nothing to chance or to the inspiration of the moment. On the basis of Fouqué’s confidences and the little he had read about love in his Bible, he devised a highly detailed plan of campaign. Since, without admitting it to himself, he was greatly troubled, he wrote this plan down.

The following morning in the drawing room, Mme de Rênal was alone with him for a moment:

“Have you no other name but Julien?” she asked him.

At this most flattering question, our hero did not know how to reply. This circumstance had not been foreseen in his plan. But for the folly of making a plan, Julien’s lively mind would have served him well; surprise would merely have added to the quickness of his perceptions.

He was awkward and exaggerated his awkwardness to himself. Mme de Rênal quickly forgave him for it. She saw in it the effect of a charming innocence. And precisely what she thought lacking in this man, whom everyone considered so gifted, was an air of innocence.

“Your little tutor inspires a great deal of mistrust in me,” Mme Derville sometimes told her. “I think he always has the air of thinking and of acting only with calculation. He is a sly one.”

Julien remained deeply humiliated by the misfortune of not having known how to reply to Mme de Rênal.

A man like me owes it to himself to make good this failure, and, seizing the moment when they were passing from one room to another, he believed it his duty to give Mme de Rênal a kiss.

wide.text:
--Madame, je viens pour la première fois de ma vie à Besançon; je
voudrais bien avoir, en payant, un pain et une tasse de café.

La demoiselle sourit un peu et puis rougit; elle craignait, pour ce joli
jeune homme, l'attention ironique et les plaisanteries des joueurs de
billard. Il serait effrayé et ne reparaîtrait plus.

--Placez-vous ici près de moi, dit-elle en lui montrant une table de
marbre, presque tout à fait cachée par l'énorme comptoir d'acajou qui
s'avance dans la salle.

La demoiselle se pencha en dehors du comptoir, ce qui lui donna
l'occasion de déployer une taille superbe. Julien la remarqua, toutes
ses idées changèrent. La belle demoiselle venait de placer devant lui
une tasse, du sucre et un petit pain. Elle hésitait à appeler un garçon
pour avoir du café, comprenant bien qu'à l'arrivée de ce garçon, son
tête-à-tête avec Julien allait finir.

Julien, pensif, comparait cette beauté blonde et gaie à certains
souvenirs qui l'agitaient souvent. L'idée de la passion dont il avait
été l'objet lui ôta presque toute sa timidité. La belle demoiselle
n'avait qu'un instant; elle lut dans les regards de Julien.

--Cette fumée de pipe vous fait tousser, venez déjeuner demain avant
huit heures du matin; alors, je suis presque seule.

--Quel est votre nom? dit Julien, avec le sourire caressant de la
timidité heureuse.

--Amanda Binet.

--Permettez-vous que je vous envoie, dans une heure, un petit paquet
gros comme celui-ci?

La belle Amanda réfléchit un peu.

--Je suis surveillée: ce que vous me demandez peut me compromettre;
cependant je m'en vais écrire mon adresse sur une carte, que vous
placerez sur votre paquet. Envoyez-le-moi hardiment.

--Je m'appelle Julien Sorel, dit le jeune homme; je n'ai ni parents, ni
connaissance à Besançon.

--Ah! je comprends, dit-elle avec joie, vous venez pour l'école de
droit?

--Hélas! non, répondit Julien; on m'envoie au séminaire.

Le découragement le plus complet éteignit les traits d'Amanda; elle
appela un garçon: elle avait du courage maintenant. Le garçon versa du
café à Julien, sans le regarder.

Amanda recevait de l'argent au comptoir; Julien était fier d'avoir osé
parler: on se disputa à l'un des billards. Les cris et les démentis des
joueurs, retentissant dans cette salle immense, faisaient un tapage qui
étonnait Julien. Amanda était rêveuse et baissait les yeux.

--Si vous voulez mademoiselle, lui dit-il tout à coup avec assurance, je
dirai que je suis votre cousin?

Ce petit air d'autorité plut à Amanda. Ce n'est pas un jeune homme de
rien, pensa-t-elle. Elle lui dit fort vite, sans le regarder, car son
oeil était occupé à voir si quelqu'un s'approchait du comptoir:

--Moi je suis de Genlis, près de Dijon; dites que vous êtes aussi de
Genlis, et cousin de ma mère.

--Je n'y manquerai pas.

--Tous les jeudis à cinq heures en été, MM. les séminaristes passent ici
devant le café.

--Si vous pensez à moi, quand je passerai, ayez un bouquet de violettes
à la main.

Amanda le regarda d'un air étonné; ce regard changea le courage de
Julien en témérité; cependant il rougit beaucoup en lui disant:

--Je sens que je vous aime de l'amour le plus violent.

--Parlez donc plus bas, lui dit-elle d'un air effrayé. Julien songeait à
se rappeler les phrases d'un volume dépareillé de la _Nouvelle Héloïse_,
qu'il avait trouvé à Vergy. Sa mémoire le servit bien; depuis dix
minutes, il récitait la _Nouvelle Héloïse_ à Mlle Amanda, ravie, il
était heureux de sa bravoure, quand tout à coup la belle Franc-comtoise
prit un air glacial. Un de ses amants paraissait à la porte du café.

Il s'approcha du comptoir, en sifflant et marchant des épaules; il
regarda Julien. A l'instant, l'imagination de celui-ci, toujours dans
les extrêmes, ne fut remplie que d'idées de duel. Il pâlit beaucoup,
éloigna sa tasse, prit une mine assurée, et regarda son rival fort
attentivement. Comme ce rival baissait la tête en se versant
familièrement un verre d'eau-de-vie sur le comptoir, d'un regard Amanda
ordonna à Julien de baisser les yeux. Il obéit, et, pendant deux
minutes, se tint immobile à sa place pâle résolu et ne songeant qu'à ce
qui allait arriver; il était vraiment bien en cet instant. Le rival
avait été étonné des yeux de Julien, son verre d'eau-de-vie avalé d'un
trait il dit un mot à Amanda, plaça ses deux mains dans les poches
latérales de sa grosse redingote, et s'approcha d'un billard en
soufflant et regardant Julien. Celui-ci se leva transporté de colères;
mais il ne savait comment s'y prendre pour être insolent. Il posa son
petit paquet, et, de l'air le plus dandinant qu'il put, marcha vers le
billard.

En vain la prudence lui disait: Mais avec un duel dès l'arrivée à
Besançon, la carrière ecclésiastique est perdue.

Qu'importe, il ne sera pas dit que je manque un insolent.

Amanda vit son courage, il faisait un joli contraste avec la naïveté de
ses manières; en un instant, elle le préféra au grand jeune homme en
redingote. Elle se leva, et, tout en avant l'air de suivre de l'oeil
quelqu'un qui passait dans la rue, elle vint se placer rapidement entre
lui et le billard:

--Gardez-vous de regarder de travers ce monsieur, c'est mon beau-frère.

--Que m'importe? il m'a regardé.

--Voulez-vous me rendre malheureuse? Sans doute il vous a regardé,
peut-être même il va venir vous parler. Je lui ai dit que vous êtes un
parent de ma mère, et que vous arrivez de Genlis. Lui est Franc-comtois
et n'a jamais dépassé Dole, sur la route de la Bourgogne; ainsi dites ce
que vous voudrez, ne craignez rien.

Julien hésitait encore, elle ajouta bien vite, son imagination de dame
de comptoir lui fournissant des mensonges en abondance:

--Sans doute il vous a regardé, mais c'est au moment où il me demandait
qui vous êtes; c'est un homme qui est manant avec tout le monde, il n'a
pas voulu vous insulter.

L'oeil de Julien suivait le prétendu beau-frère; il le vit acheter un
numéro à la poule que l'on jouait au plus éloigné des deux billards.
Julien entendit sa grosse voix qui criait, d'un ton menaçant: Je prends
à faire. Il passa vivement derrière Mlle Amanda, et fit un pas vers le
billard. Amanda le saisit par le bras:

translation.text:
“Madame, I have just come to Besançon for the first time in my life; I should very much like to have, and pay for, a piece of bread and a cup of coffee.”

The young lady smiled a little and then blushed; she feared, for this handsome young man, the ironic attention and jests of the billiard players. He would be frightened and would never return.

“Sit here beside me,” she said, showing him a marble table almost entirely hidden by the enormous mahogany counter that projected into the room.

The young lady leaned out from behind the counter, which gave her the opportunity to display a superb figure. Julien noticed it; all his thoughts changed. The beautiful young lady had just placed before him a cup, some sugar, and a small bread roll. She hesitated to call a waiter to bring coffee, fully understanding that when the waiter arrived, her tête-à-tête with Julien would end.

Lost in thought, Julien compared this cheerful blonde beauty with certain memories that often stirred him. The thought of the passion of which he had been the object took away almost all his timidity. The beautiful young lady had only a moment; she read it in Julien’s eyes.

“This pipe smoke is making you cough; come and have breakfast tomorrow before eight in the morning; then I am almost alone.”

“What is your name?” said Julien, with the caressing smile of happy timidity.

“Amanda Binet.”

“Will you allow me to send you, in an hour, a little parcel about this size?”

The beautiful Amanda reflected for a moment.

“I am watched: what you are asking of me may compromise me; nevertheless, I am going to write my address on a card, which you will put on your parcel. Send it to me without fear.”

“My name is Julien Sorel,” said the young man; “I have neither relatives nor acquaintances in Besançon.”

“Ah! I understand,” she said joyfully, “you have come for the law school?”

“Alas, no,” Julien replied; “I am being sent to the seminary.”

The most complete discouragement extinguished the animation in Amanda’s features; she called a waiter: she had courage now. The waiter poured coffee for Julien without looking at him.

Amanda was taking money at the counter; Julien was proud of having dared to speak: a quarrel broke out at one of the billiard tables. The shouts and denials of the players, resounding through that immense room, made a din that astonished Julien. Amanda was pensive and kept her eyes lowered.

“If you wish, Mademoiselle,” he suddenly said to her with assurance, “I shall say that I am your cousin.”

This little air of authority pleased Amanda. He is not an insignificant young man, she thought. She said to him very quickly, without looking at him, for her eye was occupied in seeing whether anyone was approaching the counter:

“I am from Genlis, near Dijon; say that you too are from Genlis, and that you are my mother’s cousin.”

“I shall not fail to do so.”

“Every Thursday at five o’clock in summer, the gentlemen from the seminary pass here in front of the café.”

“If you think of me when I pass, have a bouquet of violets in your hand.”

Amanda looked at him in astonishment; that look changed Julien’s courage into boldness; nevertheless, he blushed deeply as he said to her:

“I feel that I love you with the most violent love.”

“Do speak more softly,” she said to him with a frightened air. Julien was trying to recall the phrases from an odd volume of the New Heloise that he had found at Vergy. His memory served him well; for ten minutes he had been reciting the New Heloise to Mademoiselle Amanda, who was delighted; he was happy in his bravery, when suddenly the beautiful woman from Franche-Comté assumed an icy expression. One of her lovers had appeared at the door of the café.

He approached the counter, whistling and swaggering with his shoulders; he looked at Julien. At once, the latter’s imagination, always running to extremes, was filled with nothing but thoughts of a duel. He turned very pale, pushed his cup away, assumed a confident expression, and looked at his rival very attentively. As this rival lowered his head while familiarly pouring himself a glass of brandy at the counter, Amanda ordered Julien with a glance to lower his eyes. He obeyed and, for two minutes, remained motionless in his place, pale, resolute, and thinking only of what was about to happen; he was truly admirable at that moment. The rival had been astonished by Julien’s eyes; after swallowing his glass of brandy in one draught, he said a word to Amanda, put both hands into the side pockets of his heavy frock coat, and approached a billiard table, puffing and looking at Julien. The latter rose, carried away by anger; but he did not know how to go about being insolent. He put down his little parcel and, with the most swaggering air he could manage, walked toward the billiard table.

In vain prudence told him: But with a duel as soon as you arrive in Besançon, your ecclesiastical career is ruined.

What does it matter? It shall not be said that I let an insolent fellow escape me.

Amanda saw his courage; it made a charming contrast with the naïveté of his manners; in an instant, she preferred him to the tall young man in the frock coat. She rose and, while appearing to follow with her eyes someone passing in the street, quickly came and placed herself between him and the billiard table:

“Take care not to look askance at that gentleman; he is my brother-in-law.”

“What do I care? He looked at me.”

“Do you want to make me unhappy? No doubt he looked at you; perhaps he is even going to come and speak to you. I told him that you are a relative of my mother’s and that you have just arrived from Genlis. He is from Franche-Comté and has never gone beyond Dole on the road to Burgundy; so say whatever you like, and do not be afraid.”

Julien was still hesitating; she added very quickly, her counter-girl’s imagination supplying her with lies in abundance:

“No doubt he looked at you, but it was at the moment when he was asking me who you are; he is a man who is boorish with everyone; he did not mean to insult you.”

Julien’s eye followed the supposed brother-in-law; he saw him buy a number in the pool being played at the farther of the two billiard tables. Julien heard his loud voice shout in a threatening tone, “I’ll take the shot.” He passed swiftly behind Mademoiselle Amanda and took a step toward the billiard table. Amanda seized him by the arm:

Le lendemain matin, on suivait presque l'abbé Pirard dans les rues, et
les marchands venaient sur la porte de leurs boutiques, lorsqu'il alla
solliciter les juges du marquis. Pour la première fois, il en fut reçu
avec politesse. Le sévère janséniste, indigné de tout ce qu'il voyait,
fit un long travail avec les avocats qu'il avait choisis pour le marquis
de La Mole et partit pour Paris. Il eut la faiblesse de dire à deux ou
trois amis de collège, qui l'accompagnaient jusqu'à la calèche dont ils
admirèrent les armoiries, qu'après avoir administré le séminaire pendant
quinze ans, il quittait Besançon avec cinq cent vingt francs d'économie.
Ces amis l'embrassèrent en pleurant, et se dirent entre eux:

--Le bon abbé eût pu s'épargner ce mensonge, il est aussi par trop
ridicule.

Le vulgaire, aveuglé par l'amour de l'argent, n'était pas fait pour
comprendre que c'était dans sa sincérité que l'abbé Pirard avait trouvé
la force nécessaire pour lutter seul pendant six ans contre Marie
Alacoque, le Sacré-Coeur de Jésus, les jésuites et son évêque.




CHAPITRE XXX

UN AMBITIEUX

    Il n'y a plus qu'une seule noblesse, c'est le titre de duc,
    marquis est ridicule, au mot duc on tourne la tête.

    EDINBURGH REVIEW.


L'abbé fut étonné de l'air noble et du ton presque gai du marquis.
Cependant ce futur ministre le recevait sans aucune de ces petites
façons de grand seigneur, si polies, mais si impertinentes pour qui les
comprend. C'eût été du temps perdu, et le marquis était assez avant dans
les grandes affaires pour n'avoir point de temps à perdre.

Depuis six mois, il intriguait pour faire accepter à la fois au roi et à
la nation un certain ministère, qui, par reconnaissance, le ferait duc.

Le marquis demandait en vain, depuis de longues années, à son avocat de
Besançon un travail clair et précis sur ses procès de Franche-Comté.
Comment l'avocat célèbre les lui eût-il expliqués, s'il ne les
comprenait pas lui-même?

Le petit carré de papier, que lui remit l'abbé, expliquait tout.

--Mon cher abbé, lui dit le marquis, après avoir expédié en moins de
cinq minutes toutes les formules de politesse et d'interrogation sur les
choses personnelles, mon cher abbé, au milieu de ma prétendue
prospérité, il me manque du temps pour m'occuper sérieusement de deux
petites choses assez importantes pourtant: ma famille et mes affaires.
Je soigne en grand la fortune de ma maison, je puis la porter loin; je
soigne mes plaisirs, et c'est ce qui doit passer avant tout, du moins à
mes yeux, ajouta-t-il en surprenant de l'étonnement dans ceux de l'abbé
Pirard.

Quoique homme de sens, l'abbé était émerveillé de voir un vieillard
parler si franchement de ses plaisirs.

--Le travail existe sans doute à Paris, continua le grand seigneur, mais
perché au cinquième étage; et dès que je me rapproche d'un homme, il
prend un appartement au second, et la femme prend un jour, par
conséquent plus de travail, plus d'effort que pour être ou paraître un
homme du monde. C'est là leur unique affaire dès qu'ils ont du pain.

Pour mes procès, exactement parlant, et encore pour chaque procès pris à
part, j'ai des avocats qui se tuent; il m'en est mort un de la poitrine,
avant-hier. Mais, pour mes affaires en général, croiriez-vous, monsieur,
que, depuis trois ans, j'ai renoncé à trouver un homme qui, pendant
qu'il écrit pour moi, daigne songer un peu sérieusement à ce qu'il fait?
Au reste, tout ceci n'est qu'une préface.

Je vous estime, et j'oserais ajouter, quoique vous voyant pour la
première fois, je vous aime. Voulez-vous être mon secrétaire, avec huit
mille francs d'appointements ou bien avec le double? J'y gagnerai
encore, je vous jure; et je fais mon affaire de vous conserver votre
belle cure, pour le jour où nous ne nous conviendrons plus.

L'abbé refusa, mais vers la fin de la conversation le véritable embarras
où il voyait le marquis lui suggéra une idée.

--J'ai laissé au fond de mon séminaire, dit-il au marquis, un pauvre
jeune homme, qui, si je ne me trompe, va y être rudement persécuté. S'il
n'était qu'un simple religieux, il serait déjà _in pace_.

Jusqu'ici ce jeune homme ne sait que le latin et l'Écriture sainte; mais
il n'est pas impossible qu'un jour il déploie de grands talents soit
pour la prédication, soit pour la direction des âmes. J'ignore ce qu'il
fera, mais il a le feu sacré, il peut aller loin. Je comptais le donner
à notre évêque, si jamais il nous en était venu un qui eût un peu de
votre manière de voir les hommes et les affaires.

--D'où sort votre jeune homme? dit le marquis.

--On le dit fils d'un charpentier de nos montagnes, mais je le croirais
plutôt fils naturel de quelque homme riche. Je lui ai vu recevoir une
lettre anonyme ou pseudonyme avec une lettre de change de cinq cents
francs.

--Ah! c'est Julien Sorel, dit le marquis.

--D'où savez-vous son nom? dit l'abbé étonné; et comme il rougissait de
sa question:

--C'est ce que je ne vous dirai pas, répondit le marquis.

--Eh bien! reprit l'abbé, vous pourriez essayer d'en faire votre
secrétaire; il a de l'énergie, de la raison; en un mot, c'est un essai à
tenter.

--Pourquoi pas? dit le marquis; mais serait-ce un homme à se laisser
graisser la patte par le préfet de police ou par tout autre pour faire
l'espion chez moi? Voilà toute mon objection.

D'après les assurances favorables de l'abbé Pirard, le marquis prit un
billet de mille francs:

--Envoyez ce viatique à Julien Sorel; faites-le-moi venir.

--L'habitude d'habiter Paris doit, en effet, M. le marquis, produire
cette illusion dans votre esprit; vous ne connaissez pas, parce que vous
êtes dans une position sociale élevée, la tyrannie qui pèse sur nous
autres pauvres provinciaux, et en particulier sur les prêtres non amis
des jésuites. On ne voudra pas laisser partir Julien Sorel, on saura se
couvrir des prétextes les plus habiles on me répondra qu'il est malade,
la poste aura perdu les lettres, etc., etc.

--Je prendrai un de ces jours une lettre du ministre à l'évêque, dit le
marquis.

--J'oubliais une précaution, dit l'abbé: ce jeune homme quoique né bien
bas a le coeur haut, il ne sera d'aucune utilité dans vos affaires si
l'on effarouche son orgueil; vous le rendriez stupide.

--Ceci me plaît, dit le marquis, j'en ferai le camarade de mon fils,
cela suffira-t-il?

Quelque temps après, Julien reçut une lettre d'une écriture inconnue et
portant le timbre de Châlon, il y trouva un mandat sur un marchand de
Besançon, et l'avis de se rendre à Paris sans délai. La lettre était
signée d'un nom supposé, mais en l'ouvrant Julien avait tressailli: une
grosse tache d'encre était tombée au milieu du treizième mot. C'était le
signal dont il était convenu avec l'abbé Pirard.

translation.text:
The next morning, people almost followed Abbé Pirard through the streets, and shopkeepers came to the doors of their shops when he went to petition the judges on the marquis’s behalf. For the first time, he was received politely by them. The stern Jansenist, indignant at everything he saw, worked at length with the lawyers he had chosen for the Marquis de La Mole and left for Paris. He was weak enough to tell two or three friends from the seminary, who accompanied him as far as the carriage whose coat of arms they admired, that after administering the seminary for fifteen years, he was leaving Besançon with five hundred and twenty francs in savings. These friends embraced him in tears, and said among themselves:

“The good abbé could have spared himself that lie; it really is far too ridiculous.”

The common people, blinded by the love of money, were incapable of understanding that it was in his sincerity that Abbé Pirard had found the strength necessary to struggle alone for six years against Marie Alacoque, the Sacred Heart of Jesus, the Jesuits, and his bishop.




CHAPTER XXX

AN AMBITIOUS MAN

    There is now only one true rank of nobility, and that is the title of duke;
    marquis is ridiculous; at the word duke, heads turn.

    EDINBURGH REVIEW.


The abbé was astonished by the marquis’s noble bearing and almost cheerful tone. Yet this future minister received him without any of those little grand-seigneur airs, so polite, but so impertinent to anyone who understands them. That would have been time wasted, and the marquis was sufficiently involved in great affairs to have no time to waste.

For six months, he had been intriguing to have a certain ministry accepted simultaneously by the king and the nation, a ministry that, out of gratitude, would make him a duke.

For many years, the marquis had vainly asked his lawyer in Besançon for a clear and precise report on his lawsuits in Franche-Comté. How could the celebrated lawyer have explained them to him when he did not understand them himself?

The little square sheet of paper the abbé handed him explained everything.

“My dear abbé,” the marquis said to him, after disposing in less than five minutes of all the formulas of politeness and inquiries about personal matters, “my dear abbé, amid my supposed prosperity, I lack the time to attend seriously to two small matters that are nevertheless fairly important: my family and my affairs. I look after the fortune of my house on a grand scale; I can carry it far. I look after my pleasures, and that is what must come before everything else, at least in my eyes,” he added, catching the astonishment in Abbé Pirard’s eyes.

Though a sensible man, the abbé was amazed to see an old man speak so frankly of his pleasures.

“Work undoubtedly exists in Paris,” the great lord continued, “but perched on the fifth floor; and as soon as I draw closer to a man, he takes an apartment on the second floor, and his wife establishes a reception day; consequently, there is no more work, no more effort except to be, or to appear to be, a man of the world. That is their sole concern as soon as they have bread to eat.

“For my lawsuits, strictly speaking, and even for each lawsuit considered separately, I have lawyers who work themselves to death; one of them died of consumption the day before yesterday. But for my affairs in general, would you believe, monsieur, that for three years I have given up trying to find a man who, while writing for me, deigns to think a little seriously about what he is doing? Besides, all this is merely a preface.

“I esteem you, and I would venture to add, although I am seeing you for the first time, I love you. Will you be my secretary, at a salary of eight thousand francs, or even twice that? I shall still gain by it, I swear to you; and I shall make it my business to preserve your fine parish for you, for the day when we no longer suit one another.”

The abbé refused, but toward the end of the conversation, the genuine predicament in which he saw the marquis suggested an idea to him.

“I left behind, in the depths of my seminary,” he told the marquis, “a poor young man who, unless I am mistaken, is going to be harshly persecuted there. If he were merely a simple religious, he would already be in pace.

“So far, this young man knows only Latin and Holy Scripture; but it is not impossible that one day he may display great talents either for preaching or for the direction of souls. I do not know what he will do, but he has the sacred fire; he may go far. I had intended to give him to our bishop, if ever we had been sent one who shared something of your way of judging men and affairs.”

“Where does your young man come from?” said the marquis.

“He is said to be the son of a carpenter from our mountains, but I would sooner believe him the natural son of some rich man. I saw him receive an anonymous or pseudonymous letter with a bill of exchange for five hundred francs.”

“Ah! That is Julien Sorel,” said the marquis.

“How do you know his name?” said the astonished abbé; and when he blushed at his own question:

“That is something I shall not tell you,” replied the marquis.

“Well then,” the abbé resumed, “you might try making him your secretary; he has energy and judgment; in short, it is an experiment worth trying.”

“Why not?” said the marquis. “But would he be the sort of man to let the prefect of police or anyone else grease his palm to act as a spy in my house? That is my only objection.”

After Abbé Pirard’s favorable assurances, the marquis took out a thousand-franc note:

“Send this traveling money to Julien Sorel; have him come to me.”

“The habit of living in Paris must indeed, Monsieur le Marquis, produce this illusion in your mind; because you occupy a high social position, you do not know the tyranny that weighs upon us poor provincials, and particularly upon priests who are not friends of the Jesuits. They will not be willing to let Julien Sorel leave; they will know how to cloak themselves in the cleverest pretexts. I shall be told that he is ill, the post will have lost the letters, and so on and so forth.”

“One of these days I shall obtain a letter from the minister to the bishop,” said the marquis.

“I was forgetting a precaution,” said the abbé. “Although this young man was born very low, he has a proud spirit; he will be of no use whatsoever in your affairs if his pride is alarmed; you would make him stupid.”

“I like that,” said the marquis. “I shall make him my son’s companion; will that suffice?”

Some time later, Julien received a letter in an unfamiliar hand and bearing the Châlon postmark. In it he found a payment order upon a merchant in Besançon and instructions to go to Paris without delay. The letter was signed with an assumed name, but upon opening it Julien had started: a large blot of ink had fallen in the middle of the thirteenth word. It was the signal he had agreed upon with Abbé Pirard.

--Que m'importe? il m'a regardé.

peut-être même il va venir vous parler. Je lui ai dit que vous êtes un
parent de ma mère, et que vous arrivez de Genlis. Lui est Franc-comtois
et n'a jamais dépassé Dole, sur la route de la Bourgogne; ainsi dites ce
que vous voudrez, ne craignez rien.

Julien hésitait encore, elle ajouta bien vite, son imagination de dame
de comptoir lui fournissant des mensonges en abondance:

--Sans doute il vous a regardé, mais c'est au moment où il me demandait
qui vous êtes; c'est un homme qui est manant avec tout le monde, il n'a
pas voulu vous insulter.

L'oeil de Julien suivait le prétendu beau-frère; il le vit acheter un
numéro à la poule que l'on jouait au plus éloigné des deux billards.
Julien entendit sa grosse voix qui criait, d'un ton menaçant: Je prends
à faire. Il passa vivement derrière Mlle Amanda, et fit un pas vers le
billard. Amanda le saisit par le bras:

--Venez me payer d'abord, lui dit-elle.

C'est juste, pensa Julien; elle a peur que je ne sorte sans payer.
Amanda était aussi agitée que lui et fort rouge; elle lui rendit de la
monnaie le plus lentement qu'elle put, tout en lui répétant à voix
basse:

--Sortez à l'instant du café, ou je ne vous aime plus; et cependant, je
vous aime bien.

Julien sortit en effet, mais lentement. N'est-il pas de mon devoir, se
répétait-il, d'aller regarder à mon tour en soufflant ce grossier
personnage? Cette incertitude le retint une heure sur le boulevard
devant le café; il regardait si son homme sortait. Il ne parut pas, et
Julien s'éloigna.

Il n'était à Besançon que depuis quelques heures, et déjà il avait
conquis un remords. Le vieux chirurgien-major lui avait donné autrefois,
malgré sa goutte, quelques leçons d'escrime, telle était toute la
science que Julien trouvait au service de sa colère. Mais cet embarras
n'eût rien été s'il eût su comment se fâcher autrement qu'en donnant un
soufflet, et si l'on en venait aux coups de poing, son rival, homme
énorme, l'eût battu et puis planté là.

Pour un pauvre diable comme moi, se dit Julien, sans protecteurs et sans
argent, il n'y aura pas grande différence entre un séminaire et une
prison; il faut que je dépose mes habits bourgeois dans quelque auberge,
où je reprendrai mon habit noir. Si jamais je parviens à sortir du
séminaire pour quelques heures, je pourrai fort bien avec mes habits
bourgeois revoir Mlle Amanda. Ce raisonnement était beau; mais Julien,
passant devant toutes les auberges, n'osait entrer dans aucune.

Enfin, comme il repassait devant l'hôtel des Ambassadeurs, ses yeux
inquiets rencontrèrent ceux d'une grosse femme, encore assez jeune,
haute en couleur, à l'air heureux et gai. Il s'approcha d'elle et lui
raconta son histoire.

--Certainement, mon joli petit abbé, lui dit l'hôtesse des Ambassadeurs,
je vous garderai vos habits bourgeois et même les ferai épousseter
souvent. De ce temps-ci, il ne fait pas bon laisser un habit de drap
sans le toucher. Elle prit une clef et le conduisit elle-même dans une
chambre, en lui recommandant d'écrire la note de ce qu'il laissait.

--Bon Dieu! que vous avez bonne mine comme ça, monsieur l'abbé Sorel,
lui dit la grosse femme, quand il descendit à la cuisine, je m'en vais
vous faire servir un bon dîner, et, ajouta-t-elle à voix basse, il ne
vous coûtera que vingt sols au lieu de cinquante que tout le monde paye;
car il faut bien ménager votre petit _boursicot_.

--J'ai dix louis, répliqua Julien, avec une certaine fierté.

--Ah! bon Dieu! répondit la bonne hôtesse alarmée, ne parlez pas si
haut; il y a bien des mauvais sujets dans Besançon. On vous volera cela
en moins de rien. Surtout n'entrez jamais dans les cafés, ils sont
remplis de mauvais sujets.

--Vraiment! dit Julien, à qui ce mot donnait à penser.

--Ne venez jamais que chez moi, je vous ferai faire du café.
Rappelez-vous que vous trouverez toujours ici une amie et un bon dîner à
vingt sols, c'est parler ça, j'espère. Allez vous mettre à table, je
vais vous servir moi-même.

--Je ne saurais manger, lui dit Julien, je suis trop ému, je vais entrer
au séminaire, en sortant de chez vous.

La bonne femme ne le laissa partir qu'après avoir empli ses poches de
provisions. Enfin Julien s'achemina vers le lieu terrible; l'hôtesse, de
dessus sa porte, lui en indiquait la route.

translation.text:
“Do speak more quietly,” she said to him with a frightened look. Julien was trying to recall the phrases from an odd volume of the _New Heloise_ that he had found at Vergy. His memory served him well; for ten minutes he had been reciting the _New Heloise_ to a delighted Mademoiselle Amanda, and he was happy in his boldness, when suddenly the beautiful woman from Franche-Comté assumed an icy air. One of her lovers had appeared at the door of the café.

He approached the counter, whistling and swaggering his shoulders; he looked at Julien. At once, Julien’s imagination, always running to extremes, was filled with nothing but thoughts of a duel. He turned very pale, pushed his cup away, put on a confident expression, and looked at his rival very attentively. As this rival lowered his head while familiarly pouring himself a glass of brandy at the counter, Amanda ordered Julien with a glance to lower his eyes. He obeyed and, for two minutes, remained motionless in his place, pale, resolute, and thinking only of what was about to happen; he was truly admirable at that moment. The rival had been surprised by Julien’s eyes; having swallowed his glass of brandy in one gulp, he said a word to Amanda, put both hands into the side pockets of his heavy overcoat, and approached a billiard table, puffing and looking at Julien. Julien rose, carried away by anger; but he did not know how to go about being insolent. He put down his little bundle and, with the most swaggering air he could manage, walked toward the billiard table.

In vain prudence told him: But with a duel as soon as you arrive in Besançon, your ecclesiastical career is ruined.

What does it matter? It shall not be said that I let an insolent fellow escape me.

Amanda saw his courage; it formed a pretty contrast with the ingenuousness of his manners; in an instant, she preferred him to the tall young man in the overcoat. She rose and, while pretending to be following someone passing in the street with her eyes, quickly came and placed herself between him and the billiard table:

“Take care not to look askance at that gentleman; he is my brother-in-law.”

“What do I care? He looked at me.”

“Do you want to make me unhappy? Of course he looked at you; perhaps he is even going to come and speak to you. I told him that you are a relative of my mother’s and that you have just arrived from Genlis. He is from Franche-Comté and has never gone beyond Dole on the road to Burgundy; so say whatever you like, and do not be afraid.”

Julien was still hesitating; she added very quickly, her imagination as a woman behind a counter supplying her with lies in abundance:

“Of course he looked at you, but that was when he was asking me who you were; he is a man who is boorish with everyone; he did not mean to insult you.”

Julien’s eye followed the supposed brother-in-law; he saw him buy a number in the pool being played at the farther of the two billiard tables. Julien heard his loud voice cry in a threatening tone, “I’ll take the play.” He passed quickly behind Mademoiselle Amanda and took a step toward the billiard table. Amanda seized him by the arm:

“Come and pay me first,” she said to him.

That is fair, thought Julien; she is afraid I shall leave without paying.

Amanda was as agitated as he was and very red; she gave him his change as slowly as she could, all the while repeating to him in a low voice:

“Leave the café this instant, or I shall no longer love you; and yet I love you dearly.”

Julien did leave, but slowly. Is it not my duty, he kept asking himself, to go and stare at that coarse fellow in my turn, puffing as I do so? This uncertainty kept him for an hour on the boulevard in front of the café; he watched to see whether his man would come out. He did not appear, and Julien went away.

He had been in Besançon for only a few hours, and already he had acquired a remorse. The old surgeon-major had once given him, despite his gout, a few fencing lessons; that was all the skill Julien could find to put at the service of his anger. But this difficulty would have been nothing if he had known how to become angry otherwise than by administering a slap in the face; and if it came to fisticuffs, his rival, an enormous man, would have beaten him and then left him there.

For a poor devil like me, Julien said to himself, without protectors and without money, there will not be much difference between a seminary and a prison; I must leave my civilian clothes at some inn, where I shall put my black coat back on. If I ever manage to get out of the seminary for a few hours, I can quite easily put on my civilian clothes and see Mademoiselle Amanda again. This reasoning was excellent; but as Julien passed all the inns, he did not dare enter any of them.

At last, as he passed the Hôtel des Ambassadeurs again, his anxious eyes met those of a stout woman, still fairly young, ruddy, with a happy and cheerful air. He approached her and told her his story.

“Certainly, my pretty little abbé,” the landlady of the Ambassadeurs said to him, “I shall keep your civilian clothes for you and even have them dusted often. At this time of year, it is not wise to leave a woolen coat untouched.” She took a key and herself led him to a room, recommending that he write down a list of what he was leaving.

“Good Lord! How handsome you look like that, Monsieur l’Abbé Sorel,” the stout woman said to him when he came down to the kitchen. “I am going to have a good dinner served to you, and,” she added in a low voice, “it will cost you only twenty sous instead of the fifty everyone else pays; for you must take care of your little nest egg.”

“I have ten louis,” Julien replied with a certain pride.

“Oh, good Lord!” the kind landlady answered in alarm. “Do not speak so loudly; there are many bad characters in Besançon. They will steal that from you in no time. Above all, never go into the cafés; they are full of bad characters.”

“Really!” said Julien, to whom this remark gave food for thought.

“Never go anywhere but here; I shall have coffee made for you. Remember that you will always find a friend here and a good dinner for twenty sous; that is plain speaking, I hope. Go and sit down at the table; I shall serve you myself.”

“I could not eat,” Julien told her. “I am too agitated; I am going to enter the seminary when I leave here.”

The good woman did not let him leave until she had filled his pockets with provisions. At last Julien set out for the terrible place; from her doorway, the landlady pointed out the way to him.

Och då spricker trollet!

tvekande.

Tillräckligt att börja med! Följ mig, för jag kan inte resa ensam

translation.text:
She goes to the washbasin and washes her face and hands.

There! Give me a towel!—oh—the sun is rising!

JEAN

And then the troll bursts!

MISS

Yes, it is the trolls who have been abroad tonight!—But Jean, listen! Come with me, for now I have the means!

JEAN

hesitating.

Enough?

MISS

Enough to begin with! Come with me, for I cannot travel alone today. Just think, Midsummer Day, on a stifling train, packed in among crowds of people who will gape at one; standing still at the stations when one wanted to fly—no, I cannot, I cannot! And then the memories come; childhood memories of Midsummer Days, with the church decked in greenery—the birch leaves and lilacs; dinner with the table laid, the relatives, the friends; the afternoon in the park, dancing, music, flowers, and games! Oh, one flees, flees, but the memories follow in the baggage van, and remorse and pangs of conscience!

JEAN

I shall go with you! But now, at once, before it is too late! This very moment!

MISS

There! Get dressed, then!

Takes the birdcage.

JEAN

But no luggage! Then we shall be discovered!

MISS

No, nothing! Only what one can take in the compartment!

JEAN

has taken his hat.

What sort of thing have you there? What is it?

MISS

It is only my greenfinch! I do not want to leave it!

JEAN

Well, there we are! Are we to bring a birdcage now too! You are out of your mind! Put down the cage!

MISS

The only thing I am taking with me from home; the only living creature that is fond of me, since Diana was unfaithful to me! Do not be cruel! Let me take it with me!

JEAN

Put down the cage, I say—and do not speak so loudly—Kristin will hear us!

MISS

No, I will not leave it in strangers’ hands! Kill it instead, then!

JEAN

Bring the wretched creature here, then, and I shall wring its neck!

MISS

Yes, but do not hurt it! Do not—no, I cannot!

JEAN

Bring it here; I can!

MISS

takes the bird out of the cage and kisses it.

Oh, my little Serine, are you to die and leave your mistress now?

JEAN

Please do not make a scene; it is your life, your welfare, that is at stake! Come, quickly!

Snatches the bird from her; carries it to the chopping block and takes the kitchen axe.

Miss turns away.

JEAN

You should have learned to slaughter chickens instead of shooting a revolver—

strikes

Then you would not have fainted at a drop of blood!

MISS

screams.

Kill me too! Kill me! You who can slaughter an innocent animal without your hand trembling. Oh, I hate and loathe you; there is blood between us! I curse the hour when I saw you, I curse the hour when I was born in my mother’s womb!

JEAN

Yes, what good does it do for you to curse! Go!

MISS

approaches the chopping block as though drawn there against her will.

No, I do not want to go yet; I cannot—I must see—quiet! There is a carriage driving outside—

Listens toward the outside, all the while keeping her eyes fixed on the block and the axe.

Do you think I cannot look at blood! Do you think I am so weak—oh—I should like to see your blood, your brain on a wooden block—I should like to see your whole sex swimming in a lake like that—I think I could drink from your skull, I should like to bathe my feet in your chest and I could eat your heart roasted whole!—You think I am weak; you think I love you because the fruit of my womb desired your seed; you think I want to carry your offspring beneath my heart and nourish it with my blood—bear your child and take your name—do you hear, what is your name?—I have never heard your surname—you probably have none, I suppose. I should become Mrs. “Gatehouse”—or Madam Dunghill—you dog who wears my collar, you farmhand who wears my owner’s mark on your buttons—I, share with my cook, rival my maid—oh! oh! oh!—You think I am cowardly and want to flee! No, now I shall stay—and let the thunder roll! My father comes home—finds his escritoire broken open—his money gone—then he rings—that bell—twice for the valet—and then he sends for the sheriff—and then I tell everything! Everything! Oh, it will be good to have an end—if only it would end—and then he has a stroke and dies!—then we shall all be finished—and then there will be calm—peace—eternal rest—and then the coat of arms is shattered against the coffin—the count’s line is extinguished and the valet’s line continues in a foundling home—wins its laurels in a gutter and ends in a prison!

JEAN

Now it is the royal blood speaking! Good, Miss Julie! Just put the miller in the sack too!

Kristin enters, dressed for church, with a hymnbook in her hand.

MISS

Hurries toward her and falls into her arms as though seeking protection.

Help me, Kristin! Help me against this man!

KRISTIN

motionless and cold.

What sort of spectacle is this on a holy-day morning!

Looks at the chopping block.

And how you have fouled things up here!—What is the meaning of this? And all this screaming and noise!

MISS

Kristin! You are a woman and you are my friend! Beware of this scoundrel!

JEAN

abashed.

While the ladies discuss matters, I shall go in and shave!

Slips out to the right.

MISS

You must understand me; and you must listen to me!

KRISTIN

No, I really do not understand this sort of sluttishness! Where is Miss going, dressed for travel like this—and he is standing there with his hat on—eh?—eh?—

MISS

Hear me, Kristin; listen to me, and I shall tell you everything—

KRISTIN

I do not want to know anything—

MISS

You must hear me—

KRISTIN

What is it about? Is it about the foolishness with Jean! Well, you see, I do not care about that at all! For I do not meddle in it. But if Miss means to trick him into running away, we shall put a stop to that!

MISS

extremely nervous.

Try now to remain calm, Kristin, and listen to me! I cannot stay here and Jean cannot stay here—we must therefore leave...

KRISTIN

Hm, hm!

MISS

brightening.

But you see, I have just had an idea—what if all three of us were to go—abroad—to Switzerland and set up a hotel together—I have money, you see—and Jean and I would run the whole thing—and you, I had thought, would take care of the kitchen—would that not be good!—Say yes now! And come with us, and then everything is arranged!—Say yes! Do!

Embraces Kristin and pats her.

KRISTIN

cold and thoughtful.

Hm, hm!

MISS

presto tempo.

BALETT

Bondfolket in högtidsklädda, med blommor i hattarna; en
fiolspelare i spetsen; en ankare svagdricka och en kutting brännvin
sirade med grönt läggs opp på bordet; glas tagas fram. Därpå
drickes. Sedan tar man i ring och sjunger och dansar dansleken: "Det
kommo två fruar från skogen."

När detta är gjort gå de igen sjungande.

Fröken in ensam; ser förödelsen i köket; slår ihop händerna;
därpå tar hon upp en pudervippa och pudrar sitt ansikte.

JEAN

in; exalterad.

Där ser ni! Och ni har hört! Anser ni det möjligt att stanna här?

FRöKEN

Nej! Det anser jag inte! Men vad skola vi så göra!

JEAN

Fly, resa, långt härifrån!

FRöKEN

Resa? Ja, men vart?

JEAN

Till Schweiz, till Italienska sjöarna; - där har ni aldrig varit?

FRöKEN

Nej! är det vackert där?

JEAN

åh, en evig sommar, oranger, lagrar, åh!

FRöKEN

Men vad ska vi sedan göra där?

JEAN

Där sätter jag opp ett hotell med första klassens varor och första
klassens kunder.

FRöKEN

Hotell?

JEAN

Det är ett liv skall ni tro; oupphörligt nya ansikten, nya språk;
inte en minuts ledighet till grubbel eller nerver; intet letande efter
sysselsättning, då arbetet ger sig själv; natt och dag klockan som
ringer, tåget som blåser, omnibussen som kommer och går; under det
guldstyckena rulla på byrån. Det är ett liv!

FRöKEN

Ja, det är att leva! Och jag?

JEAN

Husets härskarinna; firmans prydnad. Med ert utseende, och ert
sätt - åh - det är en given succés! Kolossal! Ni sitter som en
drottning på kontoret och sätter slavarne i rörelse med att trycka på
en elektrisk knapp; gästerna defilera inför er tron och lägga blyga
sin skatt på ert bord - ni kan aldrig tro vad mänskorna darrar när de
få en räkning i sin hand - jag skall salta notorna och ni skall sockra
på dem med ert vackraste leende - ack! låt oss resa härifrån -

tar upp en kommunikationstabell ur fickan

genast, med nästa tåg! - vi äro i Malmö klockan sex och trettio;

i Como genom Gotthardbanan om, låt mig se, tre dar! Tre dar!

tvekande.

blygt, sant kvinnligt.

Det är visserligen sant; men det är därför jag söker en

Det kan jag inte, och jag äger intet själv.

Då förfaller hela saken ---

Och ---

Det blir som det är!

BALLET

The country folk enter in festive dress, with flowers in their hats; a
fiddler at their head; a keg of small beer and a small cask of brandy,
decorated with greenery, are set on the table; glasses are brought out.
Then they drink. Afterward they form a ring and sing and dance the singing
game: “There Came Two Ladies from the Woods.”

When this is over, they leave, still singing.

Miss Julie enters alone; sees the devastation in the kitchen; clasps her
hands; then picks up a powder puff and powders her face.

JEAN

enters; exalted.

There, you see! And you have heard! Do you consider it possible to remain
here?

MISS JULIE

No! I do not! But what, then, are we to do?

JEAN

Flee, travel, far away from here!

MISS JULIE

Travel? Yes, but where?

JEAN

To Switzerland, to the Italian lakes;—you have never been there?

MISS JULIE

No! Is it beautiful there?

JEAN

Oh, an eternal summer, orange trees, laurels, oh!

MISS JULIE

But what shall we do there afterward?

JEAN

There I shall establish a hotel with first-class goods and first-class
customers.

MISS JULIE

A hotel?

JEAN

That is a life, believe me; constantly new faces, new languages; not a
minute’s leisure for brooding or nerves; no searching for something to do,
for the work presents itself; night and day, the bell ringing, the train
whistling, the omnibus coming and going; while the gold pieces roll onto
the bureau. That is a life!

MISS JULIE

Yes, that is living! And I?

JEAN

Mistress of the house; the ornament of the firm. With your looks and your
manner—oh—it is a certain success! Colossal! You sit like a queen in the
office and set the slaves in motion by pressing an electric button; the
guests file past your throne and timidly lay their tribute on your table—you
would never believe how people tremble when they are handed a bill—I shall
salt the accounts, and you shall sugar them with your loveliest smile—ah!
let us travel away from here—

Takes a timetable from his pocket.

at once, on the next train!—we shall be in Malmö at six thirty; Hamburg at
eight forty early tomorrow morning; Frankfurt—Basel in one day, and in Como
by the Gotthard Railway in, let me see, three days! Three days!

MISS JULIE

All that is well and good! But Jean—you must give me courage—say that you
love me! Come and embrace me!

JEAN

hesitating.

I want to—but I dare not! Not here in this house anymore! I love you—without
a doubt—can you doubt it?

MISS JULIE

shyly, truly womanly.

Not “you”!—Say “thou”! There are no barriers between us anymore!—Say “thou”!

JEAN

in anguish.

I cannot!—There are still barriers between us, as long as we remain in this
house—there is the past, there is the Count—and I have never met anyone for
whom I have such respect—I need only see his gloves lying on a chair, and I
feel small—I need only hear the bell upstairs, and I start like a skittish
horse—and when I now see his boots standing there so straight and
self-assured, I feel my back bending!

Kicks the boots.

Superstition, prejudices that we have been taught since childhood—but that
one can forget just as easily. Just come to another country where there is
a republic, and people fall flat on their faces before my doorman’s livery—on
their faces they shall fall, you see; but I shall not! I was not born to
fall on my face, for there is substance in me, there is character, and once
I get hold of the first branch, you shall see me climb!

I am a servant today, but next year I shall be a proprietor, in ten years I
shall be a man of independent means, and then I shall travel to Romania,
have myself decorated, and may—mark well, I say may—end as a count!

MISS JULIE

Beautiful, beautiful!

JEAN

Ah, in Romania one buys oneself the title of count, and then you will be a
countess after all! My countess!

MISS JULIE

What do I care about all that, which I am now casting behind me!—Say that
you love me, otherwise—yes, what am I otherwise?

JEAN

I shall say it a thousand times—afterward—only not here! And above all, no
feelings, unless everything is to be lost! We must approach the matter
coldly! Like sensible people!

Takes out a cigar, clips and lights it.

Now sit down there! Then I shall sit here, and we shall talk as though
nothing had happened!

MISS JULIE

despairingly.

Oh my God! Have you no feelings, then?

JEAN

I! There is no one as full of feeling as I am; but I can restrain myself.

MISS JULIE

Just now you could kiss my shoe—and now!

JEAN

harshly.

Yes, that was then! Now we have other things to think about!

MISS JULIE

Do not speak harshly to me!

JEAN

No, but sensibly! One folly has been committed; do not commit more! The
Count may be here at any moment, and before then our fates must be decided.
What do you think of my plans for the future? Do you approve of them?

MISS JULIE

They seem quite acceptable to me, but just one question: so large an
enterprise requires considerable capital; do you have it?

JEAN

chews the cigar.

I! Certainly! I have my professional knowledge, my vast experience, my
knowledge of languages! That is capital of real worth, I should think!

MISS JULIE

But with that you cannot even buy a railway ticket.

JEAN

That is certainly true; but that is why I am looking for a backer who can
advance the funds!

MISS JULIE

Where will you find one in such haste?

JEAN

You shall find one, if you are willing to become my partner!

MISS JULIE

I cannot, and I own nothing myself.

Pause.

JEAN

Then the whole matter falls through—

MISS JULIE

And—

JEAN

Things will remain as they are!

MISS JULIE

Do you think I shall remain under this roof as your mistress? Do you think
I am willing to let the people point their fingers at me; do you imagine I
can look my father in the face after this? No! Take me away from here: from
the humiliation and the disgrace!—Oh, what have I done, my God, my God!

Konen gløttet paa døren, møtte fra sengen Simons

Han skulde unde dem godt forsprang. Ellers saa

— Straks han kom ind i stuen og la av sig ytter

Og istedet kom mindet om den anden sønnen hans

Erling — han vilde ha været fjorten vintrer nu.
Naar Andres engang drog saa nær mandsalderen, var

Aaja, Halfrid — du hadde det ikke for godt med

Erlend Nikulaussøn hadde sagtens maattet bøte med
livet for sin letsindighet da. Og Kristin sittet enke paa
Jørundgaard nu —.
Og han seiv hadde kanske gaat og treget paa det
at han var gift mand. Der var ingenting saa ufor
standig at han ikke trodde sig seiv til det nu —.
Blaasten hadde stilnet, men store vaate filler av vaar
sne faldt endda, da Simon red fra tavernsgaarden. Og
nu mot kveld tok fuglen til at fløite og trille i skog
snarene, trass i snefaldet.
Som en flænge i holdet sprækker op igjen ved en
braa rørsel, gjorde et litet minde vondt — forleden, i
paaskegildet hans, hadde de staat ute og latt sig bake
av middagssolen, en flok. Høit i bjerken over dem sat
en rødstrupe og fløitet mot den lune blaa luft. Geir-
mund kom haltende omkring hushjørnet, slæpte sig
frem ved staven sin, med en haand paa sin ældste
søns skulder. Han saa op, stanset og hermet efter
fuglen. Gutten ogsaa spidset mund og fløitet. De
kunde gjøre efter næsten alle fuglestemmer. Kristin
stod litt ifrå, inde mellem nogen andre koner .Hun
smilte saa vakkert mens hun lydde paa.
Frem imot soleglad letnet skyerne i vest — valt
gyldne indover de hvite fjeldsider, fyldte skar og smaa
daler som graa skodde. Elven glittret mat lik messing
— den bruste aapen og mørk omkring stenene i strøm
men, og paa hver sten laa en liten hvit pute av nysne.
Det gik ikke fort med de trætte hester paa det
tunge føre. Det var melkehvit nat med fuldmaane som
gløttet ut mellem drivende dis og skyer, da Simon red
nedover brækkerne ved Ula-aaen. Da han var kommet
over broen og ut paa de flate furumoer, hvor vinter
veien gik, strakte hestene bedre ut — de visste det bar
mot stalden. Simon klappet Digerbeins dampende vaate
hals. Han var glad likevel, denne færden snart var til
ende. Ramborg sov vel forlængst.
Hvor veien brat dreier ut av skogen laa der en liten
stue. Han var like indpaa den, da han blev vår at
nogen mænd tilhest holdt foran døren. Han hørte Er
lends stemme rope:
«Det er visst da, du kommer første dag over hel
gen — jeg kan si det til konen min —?»
Simon ropte en hilsen. Det vilde se altfor rart ut
ikke at stanse og ride videre i følge med dem, men
han bad Sigurd fare i forveien. Saa red han op til de
andre: det var Naakkve og Gaute. Erlend kom frem
fra husdøren i det samme.
De hilstes igjen — de tre andre noget tvungent. Han
kunde se deres ansigter, men ikke ganske tydelig i
det dæmrende lys — det tyktes Simon at deres miner
var usikre, spændte og uvillige paa en gang. Saa sa
han det straks:
«Jeg kommer fra Dyfrin, maag.»
«Ja jeg hadde spurt, du skulde ha reist sydover.» Er
lend stod med haanden paa sadelbuen og saa ned.
«Du har faret fort da,» la han til, som fordi tausheten
blev pinlig.
«Nei vent litt,» sa Simon til de unge drengene, de
vilde tit at ride. «Dere ogsaa bør høre paa dette. Det
var min brors segl, du saa paa brevet, Gaute. Og jeg
skjønner at det maa tykkes dig, de holdt daarlig sin tro
med far din, han og de andre herrerne som hadde be
seglet dette brevet til junker Haakon, som din far
skulde føre til Danmark —»
Gutten saa ned og taug. Erlend mælte:
«Ett tænkte du vel ikke paa, Simon, da du f6r til funds

ordholden og trofast mand. Nu mener vel Gyrd
Darre, at end ikke det navnet har jeg berget -—»
Skamfuld bøiet Simon hodet. Dette hadde han ikke
tænkt paa.
«Det kunde du sagt til mig, Erlend, da jeg lot om
at jeg vilde fare til Dyfrin —»
«Du maatte vel seiv kunne se det, jeg var saa vild
og rasende, jeg duget ikke til at tænke eller raade, da
jeg red ut av gaarden din —»
«Jeg var ikke aldeles besindig jeg heller, Erlend —»
«Nei, men jeg synes du kunde hat tid til at sanse
dig paa den lange veien. Ikke heller kunde jeg godt
bedt dig la det fare at spørre din bror uten at røbe
ting som jeg hadde svoret dyrt paa at tie om —»
Simon taug litt — første stund syntes han den
anden hadde ret. Men saa slog det ham — nei nu
var Erlend rent urimelig. Skulde han gaat her og latt

«Jeg har aldrig ymtet ett ord om det, maag, hverken
til mor eller til brødrene mine,» sa Gaute og vendte
sit vakre, lyse aasyn mot mostermanden.
«Ja sidst fik de da vite om det likevel,» svarte Simon
stædig. «Jeg mener, efter alt det som hændte den
dagen hos mig, maatte vi klare op saken. Og jeg skjøn
ner ikke, det kunde komme din far saa uventet — stort
mere end barnet er du ikke, Gaute min, og rent ung
var du, da du blev blandet ind i disse — lønraad.»
«Min egen søn maatte jeg vel tro jeg kunde lite
paa,» mælte Erlend heftig. «Og jeg hadde ikke to
kaar at vælge mellem, da jeg skulde berge brevet. Det
var at gi det til Gaute eller la sysselmanden finde
det —»
Det syntes Simon nytteløst at snakke mere om saken.
Men han kunde ikke holde sig fra at si:
«Litet likte jeg det da jeg skjønte, hvad gutten har
gaat her og trodd om mig i fire aar. Jeg har altid tykt
godt om dig, Gaute.»
Gutten drev sin hest nogen skridt frem, rakte ut
haanden, og Simon saa at hans aasyn mørknet, som
om han rødmet:
«I faar tilgi mig, Simon!»
Simon klemte barnets haand. Stundimellem kunde
Gaute være saa lik sin morfar i ansigtet, saa Simon
blev rent underlig tilmote. Han var noget hjulbent og
liten av vekst, naar han gik, men han var en ypper
lig rytter, og tilhest saa han ut som det fagreste mands
emne nogen far kunde glæde sig over.

«Ja — med tid og stunder skal jeg da faa hende til

hadde sovnet, det var mørkt i loftet, men du kom bort

og saa kveiket du lyset og skar er, sphnt og ståk om

Simon la sin haand paa hendes node, presset det

for tandverk —. .

Simon løftet hende lempe.ig ned av fanget sit, re>ste

«Tal ikke mere om søster din nu, Ramborg -paa

du sier. Tænker du ikke jeg frygter Gud - kan du
tro om mig a. jeg skulde være saa uræd for skam og
den værste synd, eller at jeg ikke skulde komme . hug

er da bonden din, Ramborg - glem .kke det, og tal
